I built this utility because there have been a ton of times I started a claude session and then wanted to go for a walk, or a coffee break, while thinking about whatever I was working on, and keep prompting the agent.

I used a hacky VPS + Termius setup while I was backpacking / nomading across Europe and Asia, which allowed me to be modestly productive, but connections kept dropping, and the transfer of files, context, etc from my laptop to VPS was annoying.

tui2web basically mirrors any terminal UI application (claude, opencode, omp, even bash or vim) to the web. I know claude and codex (?) has remote sessions, but I never managed to get it working and none of the other open source harnesses do, and they all require way too much setup on my phone when I already have a mobile browser I quite like.

All traffic runs through a relay I'm hosting and providing for free. I was using this for a few days myself before it became too sketchy to run this through public internet, so I added first class Tailscale support.

I think the security is definitely top of mind. Anything on public internet feels prey at this point, curious to hear if anyone has any feedback to make this more locked down.

Hey HN, I'm Shreyash from Feyn. We help companies build custom models from their data. Today we're releasing Critic, a change review platform that lets you engage directly with the AI that wrote the code.

Agents write most of our code. While that has made us more productive, understanding a change and its consequences has become incredibly difficult. As our company adopted more agentic tools, we found it harder to loop people in on the impact of a PR and the state of a project. We built Critic to fix this.

Critic lets AI agents present their code, annotate key blocks, and include relevant evidence (like screenshots and instructions to run locally). Anyone viewing that change can talk directly to the agent that wrote it. See a demo here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U2--lytmOtQ.

Critic works through a plugin for Codex or Claude Code. When your agent writes code, the plugin asks it to also write a narrative describing the story behind the change, and highlight any assumptions, decisions, or complex code. You can then view the change at critic.run or have your agent pull it via the bundled MCP. Every feature in Critic is available over MCP, so your agent gets all the same context without leaving its harness.

From the dashboard or MCP, you can chat with the authoring agent directly. When Critic receives a question, it forks the authoring session and forwards your question there. That way your main thread stays clean and keeps working.

Local changes are visible only to the owner. Anything pushed to GitHub is mirrored and visible to anyone with permission to view that change on GitHub.

When building Critic, security was a big priority for us. AI agents often run in auto mode and can take many actions on your computer. We wanted to ensure that giving people access to your agent doesn't mean giving them access to your computer. All Critic forked sessions are stripped of their write tools. They can only answer questions about the change and in-progress work in that workspace.

Critic has helped us catch several incidents before they hit production. The most common is a model not reusing artifacts, like existing styles, components, or functions. Because it's so easy to dig into an agent's work and question it, we've also caught more cases of models misdiagnosing issues or writing unhelpful code. Since Critic's UI is faster and friendlier to agents than GitHub, our team is returning feedback quicker as well.

Critic is free to use. Sign up at https://critic.run. Let me know if you have feedback or questions.

I built ETF Copilot (https://etf-copilot.com/go/show-hn) as analytical support for my own investing. It answers what financial screeners and platforms do not: which valuation, growth, quality and risk metrics matter for each ETF, and how do they compare to own history and peers. It covers 1,000+ US-listed equity ETFs and updates every night with fresh data.

Free version without signup offers 5 fund views. Overlap, concentration, and theme pages are unlimited. Pro $20/month tier adds unlimited views, full rankings, watchlists, alerts, and twice a week ETF market newsletter. For Show HN I opened a broader access showing most functionality for free.

> > > Background: About a year ago I became much more interested in investing in ETFs. I have been in Finance for many years and saw many systems and tools from Yahoo Finance to expensive enterprise solutions. They all gave plenty of data, but getting to ETF-level conclusion still took hours.

> > > How it grew into a system: I started building a small tool for myself. Rolling up stock level analysis to an ETF level was a key requirement, which enabled answering questions like “Is this ETF expensive” or “How profitable are companies in this ETF”. I automated it to run daily for US-listed equity ETF universe, which enabled ETF rankings based on valuation, growth, quality, and risk. I added features people were asking about on forums and social media: multi-fund comparison, overlap and concentration. Over time it evolved into an app.

> > > Technical problems solved: 1) Mapping ETFs to stocks. ETFs hold many companies listed on international exchanges, reporting in different currencies, having different classes of securities. Tickers, ISIN, FIGI and company names can vary or be missing. I ended up building a fairly long set of rules to resolve the inconsistencies and map the data, as mapping quality directly influenced metrics downstream.

2) Metrics aggregation and rankings. Negative P/E, missing data, abrupt changes in some metrics caused wild swings in early versions, and a straightforward weighted average approach worked in some cases but broke in others. Developing a system of calculation and coverage rules was an integral part to raise quality of outputs. For rankings, “Gate first, weight second” filtering to remove poor performers proved to be a much more effective and stable approach than a seemingly logical weighted average across all.

3) LLM explanations grounded in facts and without hallucinations. I wanted to provide short daily explanations on each ETF and the market, instead of pushing the user to analyze dozens of metrics. I ran data analysis deterministically and built compact “factpacks” on each ETF and sector, as the only data LLM sees. Then fed those to LLM to write explanations and put a deterministic validator checking numerical claims against the source data, as well as a separate semantic LLM validator checking unclear or misleading wording.

> > > Questions: 1. Can you quickly get the needed data in app to tell “what sets ETF X apart from similar funds”? 2. What would you improve to make it more actionable and useful for individual ETF investors? 3. Which steps and data points do you use, when you consider investing in ETFs?

Hello everyone, I wanted to share with you one of my crazy ideas that I have been working on for the last couple of months.

The platform is a collectible card platform, like Pokemon TCG, where you use your cards to build a website. Each day you get a new pack, with HTML tags, attributes, CSS elements, etc. and you have to make the most of those to compete against other devs. The idea is to figure out how to do more with less and to learn from others.

As for some background on this... I have many crazy ideas, my brain can't stop sometimes. Using AI to write code for me has scratched some of the itches that my brain has farted through the years and have been living rent free in there for way too many years. Now they can land into the world (and maybe they shouldn't?) and I can free some mental space for new crazy ideas.

I have develop my career in security (cybersecurity, couldn't hurt a fly even if I tried) and one common thing I saw when dealing with a free text field is that users could insert some HTML tags, but only from a shortlist. Things like <b> or <i> but never <script> or <video>. Well, my brain thought: "what if they add 1000000000e56 <b>s? Don't we want to limit that too?" and that thought has been in my head for too long.

That is why, to test some of the AI coding capabilities, I created the html-allowlist npm package[0] early this year. Once I had that done my brain was happy and I was happy. A library that does what I always thought it was the best way of filtering content: you can add some flourish to your comment/textfield but not _too much_. Not sure if anyone will ever use it, but now they can.

Then another thought came in: what is that make us scratch that pleasure of achieving more with less? With AI you have all that stream of code pouring without any effort but there was some pleasure on the struggles to get things to work when resources where limited or finding creative ways to do things on our own.

As a bit of a gamer myself, quickly thought on the Pokemon TCG mobile app, where you get daily packs, build your deck and you battle. And because I have now the library that prevents more than N tags/elements to be present in an HTML page, I could apply that here and build something similar.

So I did, I have been trying to apply all my learning from years of working as a security engineer in different companies to try and build a website that allows people to have a simple personal website but also showcase their web kung-fu skills. I was very happy when I saw a few days ago here about CSS Zen Garden[1] because this website was an early career inspiration for me, as well as being a type of scenario where I could see this platform going: small web mastercrafted by hand.

I know people will come and say "if you didn't code it yourself why should we bother with it?" and you are more than welcome to do so. But for me this is about finally getting that idea out into the world, which maybe doesn't need a website like this, but maybe there's some joy on opening a random pack, slowly improving ones webpage, learning about an obscure CSS trick and appreciating others' skills.

Anyway, I hope you give this a go, it is my first attempt to release something that feels, hopefully, like a final product, so happy to hear what you all have to say and see what you get to build.

I’ve been building Ox, a local, open-source agent that uses the internet for you.

Ox acts as an intelligent proxy between you and the internet. It uses websites and apps on your behalf, freeing you from attention-hungry interfaces and slow legacy services. As it works, it can turn what it learns into reusable actions (basically function calls), making future interactions deterministic and way faster.

Most service integrations today are still built ahead of time: someone writes an API integration, connector, MCP server, or browser automation and then maintains it as the service changes.

But the internet is becoming more dynamic so have our agents.

With Ox, instead of waiting for a connector, you can say something like:

“Connect to <service>.”

Ox can study a website or workflow through capabilities it already has, turn what it learns into typed actions and reusable skills, validate them, and make them available immediately.

That pushed me toward local agents.

A local agent operates from your own device, network, and existing authenticated browser sessions instead of relying on shared datacenter infrastructure. This also makes it less likely to hit blocks aimed at datacenter IPs or centralized browser automation.

The model doesn’t need your passwords, cookies, or session tokens. Authentication and browser state are owned by the Host, while the agent interacts through explicit actions that could be gated.

Ox is completely free and open source. You can use any model provider, including local or self-hosted models, while keeping your agent’s data on device. As local models improve, I think this architecture becomes increasingly useful because the agent can become more capable without requiring more of your data to leave your device.

The security model is also a big part of the design. Ox asks before taking sensitive actions, keeps credentials isolated from the model, limits what agent code can access, and lets you stop execution at any time.

Underneath the app is OpenOx, an open protocol for self-evolving agents. It separates the interface, agent, model provider, persistent state, execution environment, and external capabilities.

The agent can run JavaScript inside a capability-limited VM. The VM has no direct network access, Host filesystem access, shell, Node.js, or DOM. Anything outside the VM has to go through an explicit ox.* capability exposed by the Host. Services provide typed actions for websites, device capabilities, or MCP servers. Skills provide reusable instructions for combining those actions. New services and skills can be attached at runtime without waiting for a new version of the app.

They can remain local or be recorded in Git and shared through repositories, so each Ox can evolve independently while benefiting from capabilities learned by others.

The agent’s persistent state lives in a portable Ox Profile containing its identity, memory, skills, artifacts, and conversations. The goal is for that state to stay independent of any particular interface, including Ox itself, or model provider. File over app.

The first implementation is an iOS app. It’s available on the App Store, and the whole thing is open source:

https://openox.ai/

https://github.com/ziyzhu/openox

If you’re interested in the broader motivation behind the project, I wrote about it here:

https://ziyzhu.com/a-technology-for-free-will

This is still early. I’m especially interested in feedback on the security model and self-evolution.

Hi HN!

I'm Michael and I built HookDeploy. HookDeploy is a webhook infrastructure tool that captures webhooks at the edge, allows for inspection, transformation and fanout to multiple destinations including to your own private infrastructure with our first-party (source-available) mTLS agent. Runs as a service on Linux, lives in the tray on Windows and in the menu bar on Mac.

As I'm sure most of you you have felt webhooks kind of suck if things don't go exactly as planned. Dropped webhooks or failures are likely silent. What actually drove me to build this was cleaning up after major cloud outages more than once. Cross referencing what System A knew against what System B actually had and reentering data by hand or trying to simulate events firing again. I have spent weeks of my life cleaning up webhook failures. HookDeploy solves that problem with a button and intelligent grouping of failed requests into incidents. If you've ever seen or had to clean up after a ransomware attack - you understand why I'd prefer to keep my firewall as tight as possible too.

Our agent enables developers and teams to keep ports closed - if there is nothing to scan, there is nothing to attack. Getting to our own mTLS agent was a journey of trying to integrate existing solutions: first WireGuard (too much operational overhead), then Tailscale which was excellent, but it had real drawbacks on the required memory per joined tailnet and the additional cost to a user's Tailscale bill. It took several months to get it right, but it was worth every week of it.

A few things to note at launch: we are launching with security measures in place: data is encrypted at rest with org-scoped keys rotated weekly (BYOK is on the roadmap), segregated databases for US, EU, APAC and AU so customer data stays where customers are not traversing underwater fiber to come to the US. We have 7 private delivery exit regions: San Francisco (us-west), New York (us-east), London (uk-london), Amsterdam (eu-west), Frankfurt (eu-central), Singapore (ap-southeast) and Sydney (au-southeast).

Our platform is built primarily on Cloudflare for speed and security utilizing workers, KV, R2, Queues, Tunnels/VPC, and of course DNS and security.

This has been some time in the making and I am excited to answer your questions and get feedback! Thank you in advance!

as I kept getting confused by having multiple Claude sessions open, last weekend I decided to combine two of my favorite emerging technologies and give it a try: Software Factory and JEV.

The idea is simple, inspired by GitHub Actions, I wanted a way to "queue" agent work on my local laptop, with the ability to define different pipelines via YAML.

Each pipeline runs in its own Git worktree, so it's isolated from the others.

I'm using some pipelines:

  dev: code → test → commit
  plan: plan → human review → code → test → commit
  security: code → human review → test → security review → commit
  frontend: code → React test → build → commit
A request can move up and down the pipeline and be reworked if an agent or JEV flags it!

I'm also using JEV to check if a potential secret is leaked, if the coding agent output asks for human review, etc.

The real magic happens when you take a single Agent session as the main driver. You can then plan and queue multiple features at once.

I think it worked out pretty well, so I open sourced it:

https://github.com/stratonext/software-factory

You can try it yourself with:

     uv tool install software-factory
Note: You need a JEV key if you want to use the judging steps.

# Audit des prérequis Phase 6

## 1. Les sources historiques nécessaires existent

Phase 1 fournit les observations marché persistées et reconstructibles.

Phase 2 fournit l’historique de marché dérivé depuis les observations, avec :
- temporalité explicite ;
- fingerprint d’état ;
- répétition vs changement d’état ;
- évolution observationnelle des ordres ;
- conservation de la fraîcheur et de la provenance.

Phase 3 fournit les données Player character-scoped :
- identité ;
- wallet ;
- journal ;
- transactions ;
- assets ;
- active orders ;
- provenance ;
- timestamps ;
- disponibilité / couverture / santé.

Phase 4 fournit une analyse économique déterministe et explicitement simulée.

Phase 5 fournit :
- identité stable d’opportunité ;
- observations temporelles ;
- provenance et scope ;
- liens vers les snapshots/orders utilisés par l’analyse ;
- outcomes séparés de la simulation ;
- statuts d’observation et de réalisation ;
- persistance PostgreSQL idempotente.

Aucun nouveau endpoint ESI n’est requis pour commencer la Phase 6.

# 2. Point critique découvert : la persistence Phase 5 n’est pas encore un dataset d’entraînement

Phase 5 a livré le **contrat de persistence**, mais pas un pipeline complet de production qui alimente automatiquement et continûment cette persistence depuis le worker d’analyse.

Le dépôt contient actuellement :
- les contrats Opportunity ;
- le domaine de reconstruction ;
- le repository PostgreSQL ;
- la migration `004_opportunity_tracking.sql`.

En revanche, le worker actuel orchestre toujours principalement :
- ingestion marché ;
- synchronisation Player.

Il n’existe pas encore de chaîne complète démontrée :

```
observations marché/player
        ↓
Trade Analysis
        ↓
Opportunity Observation
        ↓
Outcome evidence
        ↓
Prediction Dataset
```

**Conséquence :**

Phase 6 ne doit jamais fabriquer des prédictions de production à partir de données absentes.

Le modèle doit pouvoir retourner explicitement un état tel que :

```
INSUFFICIENT_DATA
```

plutôt qu’une probabilité, une moyenne ou une prédiction synthétique.

Les fixtures/tests peuvent permettre de certifier l’algorithme, mais ne constituent pas un dataset de production.

La première responsabilité de Phase 6 est donc de définir une **matérialisation déterministe du dataset de prédiction à partir des observations réellement persistées** et de son seuil minimal d’éligibilité.

Two of the five items below are confirmed, deterministic, and trivially triggerable by any local unprivileged user against a root daemon; a third crashes the daemon outright. The other two are real but lower-urgency. Recommend fixing all five in one pass since they're the same bug shape, but treat the first three as the ones that actually need to ship soon.

## Background

These five findings came out of triage of an external code-scan report (Claude Code + Mythos, against `wazuh` `tag-v4.14.5`). Each one is the same underlying pattern: a length calculation that fills a fixed-size buffer to capacity without leaving room for its own terminator, so the terminating write lands one byte past the allocation. All five were independently re-verified against the current `5.0.0`/`main` source (all present, none of these have prior fixes).

## 1. Whodata `readlink()` off-by-one heap write — **confirmed exploitable, live-reproduced**

`get_parent_process_info()` (`src/syscheckd/src/whodata/audit_parse.c:409`) allocates `parent_name`/`parent_cwd` with `os_malloc(OS_FLSIZE, ...)` (256 bytes) and calls `readlink(path, *parent_name, OS_FLSIZE)`. `readlink()` does not NUL-terminate and returns up to `bufsiz` on success; when the target path is ≥256 bytes, `tam_ppname == 256`, and `parent_name[0][tam_ppname] = '\0'` writes at index 256 of a 256-byte allocation — one byte out of bounds. Same bug for `parent_cwd`.

**Reproduced against the real, unmodified `wazuh-syscheckd` binary** (5.0.0 branch, built clean, run under Valgrind with real kernel `auditd` and a real whodata-monitored directory): placing a binary at a path ≥256 bytes and having it (as parent) touch a file in the monitored directory reliably produces:
```
Invalid write of size 1
   at get_parent_process_info (audit_parse.c:413)
Address is 0 bytes after a block of size 256 alloc'd
```
This requires no special privilege — any local user can create a deeply nested directory and run a binary from it. `wazuh-syscheckd` never drops root on Linux (`Privsep_SetGroup` only, no `Privsep_SetUser`), so this is a heap-corruption primitive in a root process, reachable by any local account.

**Fix**: pass `OS_FLSIZE - 1` to `readlink()`.

## 2. Whodata audit-cache off-by-one heap write — **confirmed exploitable (verbatim-source harness)**

`src/syscheckd/src/whodata/syscheck_audit.c:759` (`cache` buffer, `os_malloc(BUF_SIZE)`, `BUF_SIZE = OS_MAXSTR = 65536`): the guard `cache_i + len + 1 <= BUF_SIZE` allows a line whose length leaves exactly zero slack. **Fix**: change the guard to `cache_i + len + 1 < BUF_SIZE` (or explicitly reserve 2 bytes: newline + terminator).

EXTERNAL-1's blind packet numbers its items in arm order: the item id carries the arm

`external1_packet.py` numbers its items in arm order and shuffles the list afterwards, so the item id carries the arm it was drawn from.

The builder appends 100 sampled accusations, then 15 gate-VERIFIED decoys, then 15 synthetic contradictions, assigning `E1-{len(items):03d}` as each is added, and calls `rng.shuffle(items)` only after all 130 exist. Shuffling the order does not renumber anything: ids 000-099 are the accusation arm, 100-114 the verified decoys, 115-129 the synthetic ones.

It is demonstrable from the committed `papers/closed-model-frontier/external1_packet.json` alone, with no sealed key: the fifteen items whose claim text or detail carries the builder's `zz_` path perturbation — the synthetic arm, identifiable because the perturbation is visible in the item — are exactly `E1-115` through `E1-129`. The other two arms follow the same ordering by construction.

Why it matters: `PROTOCOL_oath_external_corpus_2026_08_27.md` states that blinding is structural rather than promised, and that decoys exist precisely so membership carries no status ("an adjudicator cannot infer status from inclusion because inclusion no longer carries it"). For the id, that is not true, and the decoy arm is what measures the miss rate.

What it does not mean: the adjudicator was not handed the builder source, and EXTERNAL-1's published headline is a precision of 0.23 against a 0.95 floor — the direction that counts against the instrument — so the leak is not a plausible explanation for that figure. Whether any seat exploited it cannot be established after the fact. The honest statement is that the blinding was weaker than the protocol asserted, and that is disclosed rather than quietly fixed.

Repair, for whoever takes it: assign ids after the shuffle, from the shuffled position, and assert at build time that the arms do not cluster in id order. `compat2_packet.py` (COMPAT-2) does this and carries the assertion; `external1_packet.py` is unchanged here because rebuilding a packet that has already been adjudicated would destroy the record. A re-run under the repaired builder is a new cycle with its own preregistration.

Found by re-implementing the packet for COMPAT-2, not by reading the original.

[Feature]: Honor exec approvals autoAllowSkills for gateway-host exec

### Summary

Honor exec approvals `autoAllowSkills` for gateway-host exec, not only on node hosts. Skills already declare the binaries they need (`metadata.openclaw.requires.bins`), but an agent whose commands run on the Gateway host still gets `exec denied: allowlist miss` for those binaries.

### Problem to solve

With `security: "allowlist"`, a Gateway-hosted agent (for example a single container running the Gateway, with workspace skills) needs every skill binary listed twice: once in the skill's `requires.bins`, and again by hand in the exec approvals allowlist. `autoAllowSkills: true` looks like the fix, but it only applies on nodes (per the docs: "executables referenced by known skills are treated as allowlisted on nodes"). On the Gateway host it has no effect.

Source (main at 168d454d32):
- `src/node-host/invoke-system-run.ts:563-581` reads `approvals.agent.autoAllowSkills`, fetches `skillBins`, and passes both to the allowlist evaluation.
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.ts:425` calls `evaluateShellAllowlistWithAuthorization` with `safeBins` and `trustedSafeBinDirs` but **no `skillBins` / `autoAllowSkills`**, so `allowSkills` in `src/infra/exec-approvals-allowlist.ts:714` is always false for gateway-host exec.
- The Gateway already computes the bin list for nodes (`skills.bins`, `src/gateway/server-methods/skills.ts:275`).

### Proposed solution

In the gateway exec host, when the effective agent approvals have `autoAllowSkills: true`, resolve the skill bins for that agent (the same source `skills.bins` uses, scoped to the agent's eligible skills) and pass `skillBins` + `autoAllowSkills` into `evaluateShellAllowlistWithAuthorization`, exactly as the node host does. The existing trust index (resolved-path matching in `buildSkillBinTrustIndex`) and the `security audit` warning for `autoAllowSkills` apply unchanged. Default stays `false`.

### Alternatives considered

- Hand-maintained allowlist entries per skill binary (today's only option): duplicates skill metadata and drifts when skills change.
- `security: "full"`: works, but then nothing stops `apt-get`/`pip install` from an agent turn.

### Impact

Anyone running the Gateway as the exec host (containers, servers, most self-hosted setups) who wants `allowlist` mode with workspace skills. It makes the documented setting work where these users expect it and removes a source of drift.

### Evidence/examples

2026.9.5, Gateway in a Kubernetes pod (gateway-host exec), workspace skill `dinero` with `"requires": {"bins": ["dinero"]}`:

```
openclaw exec-policy set --security allowlist --ask off --ask-fallback deny
# approvals: agents.main = { autoAllowSkills: true, allowlist: [] }
openclaw agent --agent main -m "Use the exec tool to run exactly: dinero /accounts"
→ exec denied: allowlist miss
```

With a manual allowlist entry for `/usr/local/bin/dinero`, the same turn runs, so the skill binary resolves and is otherwise allowed.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself

### Additional information

Execution-permission change, so I expect the security-sensitive review path; the PR will keep the change to the gateway exec host and reuse the node-host code path and tests as the reference.

build: a release build without the signing variables is debug-signed, not unsigned

## What

`app/app/build.gradle.kts:43-47` says:

> Without these variables a release build comes out unsigned (not installable) rather than silently signed with the debug key.

That is not true. Without `KEYSTORE_PATH`/`KEYSTORE_PASSWORD`/`SIGNING_KEY_ALIAS`, `./gradlew :app:app:assembleDefaultRelease` produces `app-default-release.apk` **signed with the debug key**:

```
V2 Signer: certificate DN: C=US, O=Android, CN=Android Debug
```

Measured locally on 2026-09-25 (commit 52421daa7). It also showed up in CI: the first manual `release.yml` run of #134 (36126367572) checked for an unsigned APK and failed on this.

## Why

`buildTypes.release` sets `signingConfig = if (releaseSigningAvailable) … else null`. A null signing config on a build type is not "unsigned": AGP merges it with `defaultConfig`, and `defaultConfig` sets `signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("debug")` (line 40). The debug build type needs no explicit config, since it signs with the debug key anyway.

## Safety boundary: releases are not affected

- **The tag path always has the key.** `release.yml` decodes the keystore on every tag push.
- **The debug key cannot pass anyway.** Its verify step fails the build if the signer is the debug key (`! grep -qi "androiddebugkey\|CN=Android Debug"`).
- **Nothing debug-signed is uploaded.** With #134, manual runs no longer upload an APK, and they assert that no key other than the debug key reached them.

No released APK was ever debug-signed. This is a local and developer-machine problem, not a shipped vulnerability.

## Why fix it rather than correct the comment

A keyless "release" build carries the real application id `org.andashi.home` (no `.debug` suffix) and the debug key. It is the input to the failure mode documented in `AGENTS.md` § Emulator (#135):
1. Replace a release-signed install with it. The signature mismatch forces an uninstall first.
2. The per-user external directory survives the uninstall, still owned by the previous install.
3. Config ingest then fails permanently in every secondary zone (`IOException: Permission denied` in `ConfigIngestProvider.newTempFile`) until that user is cleared.

The comment tells you that you built something that *cannot* be installed, so you would never expect to be in that state.

A genuinely unsigned APK is refused by `adb install`, which is the behavior the comment promises.

## Proposed fix

- Move `signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("debug")` from `defaultConfig` to `buildTypes.debug`, so a keyless release build is actually unsigned.
- Check `nightly` (`initWith(release)`, `signingConfigs.findByName("gh-actions")`) for the same fallback.

Test by breaking what it guards:
- A keyless `assembleDefaultRelease` must produce an APK that `apksigner verify` rejects. Red today.
- With the variables set, the APK must be signed by the release key.
- The debug build must stay debug-signed (control).

Then relax #134's manual-run check back to "unsigned" only.

This umbrella issue iterates lenses the other way round: each lens is written from ONE concrete miss shape that has a dev-corpus twin (design source, in-distribution) and a held-out twin (the test), and is measured only on the held-out twin. Scan the independently published apigen module with govulncheck

## Impact
CI scans the root and client Go modules for known reachable vulnerabilities, but never runs `govulncheck` from the separately published `apigen` module. A vulnerability reachable only through an apigen API outside root/client usage can be missed before that module is released.

## Evidence
[`apigen/go.mod`](https://github.com/calypr/syfon/blob/4612d42fc8353b9ea8be19253f0d1cd9b6736e83/apigen/go.mod#L1) declares its own module. The [CI static-check job](https://github.com/calypr/syfon/blob/4612d42fc8353b9ea8be19253f0d1cd9b6736e83/.github/workflows/ci.yaml#L302-L318) scans only root and client with `govulncheck`. This is a coverage gap at development commit `4612d42fc8353b9ea8be19253f0d1cd9b6736e83`, not a claim that a current dependency is vulnerable. The local vulnerability database was unreachable during this audit.

## Acceptance criteria
Run `govulncheck ./...` from `apigen` in CI and make a reported reachable vulnerability fail the static-check job.

### Problem

Host service self-inspection must distinguish a matching service, a provider-unknown observation, and a mismatched/foreign process. A live PID alone is insufficient. The inspection must bind SCM state, exact service configuration, PID, process creation identity, and approved image path, while keeping DACL/owner/group verification separate from installer-only SACL work. A `Partial` observation from the generic P-01 status path must not be silently treated as an accepted Host match or lose the reason for uncertainty.

### Current source assessment

The issue remains structurally current in one path, but its original runtime diagnosis is incomplete on current `main` `12eae28aa4154fd4f8deed21cde8b3c9c0e5094a`. The typed two-sample runtime path exists in `crates/kernel/eliot-platform-windows/src/lib.rs:5133-5182` and `:5200-5377`: `classify_service_runtime_observation` checks state/PID shape, process identity and exact image path, while `inspect_service_registration_runtime` re-reads SCM after opening the process, rejects unstable samples, rechecks configuration, and compares the second process identity. The installation consumer exposes this runtime API through the platform adapter.

Therefore the current runtime API does not prove that the legacy registration inspection used by installation is repaired. The implementation proposal is to route Host self-inspection through the typed capsule or an exact adapter that preserves the same semantics; it must never accept the legacy partial sample by fiat.

[Engineering] api_middleware.py cites a 60 req/s figure measured on the terminated CPX31, and it is the only such number in shipping code

Round 20's `>= 60 req/s` citation sweep ([core#778], founder decision 2026-09-25: publish the measured ~50 and stop citing 60) enumerated 107 citations across the fleet. **106 were Infra's to change. This is the one that is not**, so it is routed rather than edited — Infra does not edit application code.

## The line

`datanika/services/api_middleware.py:10-11`, identical on `origin/master` and `origin/dev`:

```python
# a Granian async worker. k6 Run 4 (2026-04-18) measured 60 req/s at 100
# VUs with 4 workers — theoretical max was 97.
```

## Why it is being raised rather than left alone

It is a **dated measurement**, not a floor claim, so it may legitimately survive the sweep. ⚠️ **But it should survive by decision, not by having been missed** — that is the whole reason this issue exists. Three things make it worth a deliberate look:

1. **The machine it describes no longer exists.** Run 4 ran on the Hetzner **CPX31**, which was terminated **2026-07-14**; production moved to pointer.gr on 2026-07-17 — a different host, a different network path, and **Apache instead of nginx**. `docs/slo_targets.md` carries a callout saying exactly this about every figure that traces to that machine. This comment carries no such marker.
2. **It is the only `60 req/s` figure in shipping application code.** Every other live citation was in `scripts/loadtest/`, `docs/` or tests. A reader in the middleware has no reason to suspect the number is about hardware we sold.
3. **It rides on five refs.** `master`, `dev`, and it was on the stale branches `1076-eol-guard-discrimination`, `486-inode-stale-config`, `835-image-cve-signal` and `923-ci-mergegroup-cloud-ref` at sweep time.

## What the sweep established, so this is not re-derived

- **`~50 req/s under neighbour load`, measured 2026-09-24 on the current host**, is the published figure now: 5,991 requests in 120 s at a mean **49.92/s**, `http_req_failed` **0.00%**, zero 429s, p95 **26.57 ms**.
- **60 is not wrong — it is unmeasured**, because the ladder that produced it never held a rate ([core#1560]). No knee was observed below 60.
- **A third number is also in circulation**: `~48 req/s` (Run 5/6, 2026-04-18) is `slo_targets.md`'s *"newest conclusive datum"* — also the terminated CPX31. `~48`, `~50` and `60` are not interchangeable.

## Suggested resolutions — Engineering's call, all three are defensible

1. **Keep it and date its hardware.** Add *"on the terminated Hetzner CPX31"* so the number cannot be read as current capacity. Cheapest, and it preserves the reasoning the comment exists to give.
2. **Repoint it at the current figure** if the surrounding argument only needs *an* order of magnitude — but then it is a new claim and needs the neighbour-load label, which is a lot of prose for a comment.
3. **Drop the number and keep the mechanism.** If the point is *"a sync handler blocks a Granian async worker"*, the argument stands without any req/s figure, and no figure means nothing to rot.

⚠️ **Whichever is chosen, do not delete the reasoning** to satisfy the sweep. A comment that explains *why* the middleware is shaped as it is earns its place; the defect is an undated capacity number, not the explanation around it.

```

1. **CI cannot see it.** Runners resolve `graph.facebook.com`, so `test` is green on every PR — I

bug: get-analytics-overview is missing from the api:read automation catalogue

## Description

`GET /api/v1/analytics` already exists as the `get-analytics-overview` operation, but the operation is not included in the automation catalogue used to authorize workspace-scoped `api:read` tokens.

As a result, a correctly scoped read-only API token can access other allowed workspace resources but receives `403` when requesting the stored analytics endpoint.

The endpoint itself appears to be a read operation over analytics already stored by OpenPost, so this looks like an authorization-catalogue omission rather than a request for new analytics functionality.

I have also confirmed that the catalogue entry remains absent in OpenPost v6.1.3 and current `main`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create or use an API token scoped to a workspace with `api:read`.
2. Confirm that the token can access an allowed workspace read endpoint, for example:

   `GET /api/v1/workspaces`

3. Request:

   `GET /api/v1/analytics`

4. Observe that the request is rejected with `403`.

5. Inspect:

   `apps/server/internal/automationcatalog/catalog.go`

   The catalogue includes workspace-scoped read operations such as `list-accounts`, but does not include `get-analytics-overview`.

A minimal catalogue entry that resolves the authorization gap is:

```go
withSelectors(read("get-analytics-overview", ExposureAlpha), workspaceSelector()),
```

I have tested this change in a downstream compatibility build. With no other authorization change, the same workspace-scoped `api:read` token changes from `403` to a successful analytics response, while write operations remain unavailable.

## Expected Behavior

A workspace-scoped `api:read` token should be able to call the existing stored-data analytics endpoint for its permitted workspace.

The authorization should remain workspace-scoped and read-only.

## Actual Behavior

`GET /api/v1/analytics` returns `403` to a valid workspace-scoped `api:read` token because `get-analytics-overview` is absent from the read automation catalogue.

## Screenshots

N/A — this is an API authorization issue.

## Environment

- OpenPost version: reproduced on v5.1.2; catalogue omission also confirmed in v6.1.3 and current `main`
- Deployment method: Docker
- Operating system: Linux
- Go version (if building from source): N/A
- Browser (if web UI issue): N/A

## Logs

```text
GET /api/v1/workspaces -> 200
GET /api/v1/analytics  -> 403
```

Sensitive token and workspace details omitted.

## Additional Context

The analytics route already exists and is registered as operation `get-analytics-overview`.

The proposed change is therefore limited to admitting that existing GET operation to the read automation catalogue with the existing workspace selector:

```go
withSelectors(read("get-analytics-overview", ExposureAlpha), workspaceSelector()),
```

This preserves the intended boundary:

- read-only access;
- workspace-scoped access;
- no publishing permission;
- no provider credential access;
- no additional provider mutation capability.

I would be happy to submit the corresponding small PR with a regression test if that would be useful.

perf(core): optimise DiracOperator omega table initialisation and memory footprint

### Problem Statement
In `DiracOperator::DiracOperator(int p, int q, int dim)`, `initOmegaTable4()` is called unconditionally during object construction. 

For $(p,q) = (3,3)$, $N = m\_num\_matrices = 32$, resulting in:
- A 4-level nested loop iterating $32^4 = 1,048,576$ times.
- Evaluating `trace((*m_omegas)[i] * (*m_omegas)[j] * (*m_omegas)[k] * (*m_omegas)[l])` per iteration, which performs **3,145,728 complex matrix multiplications** for $8 \times 8$ matrices.
- The sub-product `(*m_omegas)[i] * (*m_omegas)[j]` is recomputed over 1 million times instead of $32^2 = 1,024$ times.
- `m_omega_table_4` allocates $32^4 \times 16 \text{ bytes} \approx 16.8 \text{ MB}$ of heap storage, growing as $O(N^4)$.
- **Testing Bottleneck:** `m_omega_table_4` is only ever read by `derDirac4()` during action derivative calculations. Basic unit tests asserting dimensions, matrix counts, or eigenvalues do not access this table, yet bear the multi-second instantiation cost repeatedly.

### Proposed Solution
1. **Lazy Initialisation:**
   - Defer computing `m_omega_table_4` until the first invocation of `getOmegaTable4()` or `derDirac4()`.
   - Unit tests that do not evaluate action derivatives will instantiate `DiracOperator` in sub-milliseconds.
2. **Loop Hoisting:**
   - Hoist invariant intermediate products out of the inner loops:
     - `ij = omega[i] * omega[j]` (computed $N^2$ times)
     - `ijk = ij * omega[k]` (computed $N^3$ times)
     - `trace(ijk * omega[l])` (computed $N^4$ times)
   - Micro-benchmarks demonstrate a **10x speedup** (860 ms down to 83 ms for $(3,3)$).
3. **Trace Cyclicity & Sparsity:**
   - Exploit cyclic trace invariance ($\text{Tr}(ABCD) = \text{Tr}(DABC)$) to eliminate redundant matrix products.
   - Investigate flat sparse storage for non-zero trace products to reduce the 16.8 MB memory footprint.

Engine retries LiteLLM budget refusals as rate limits on LiteLLM 1.84+ (429)

## What changes
From LiteLLM 1.84, the proxy refuses an exhausted key, customer or team budget with **HTTP 429**. 1.83.14 answered **400** for the same error, with the same `ExceededBudget` / `Budget has been exceeded` wording. Both proxies move to `v1.102.1` for CVE-2026-49468 / CVE-2026-59822 (research-os #1930, prbe-backend #387).

## What breaks
The engine classifies any 429 as a transient rate limit:
- `engine/shared/embeddings.py:473-481`: a 429 becomes `EmbeddingRateLimited`, which the batch loop (~`:356`, `:442`) retries about 5 times, around 30 s of sleep per batch.
- `engine/ingest/inferred_edges/extractor.py`: backs off 5-60 s per attempt on 429.
- 429 handling also exists in `engine/shared/llm.py`, `engine/shared/llm_tools.py` and `engine/retrieval/agent/jev.py` (not traced).

So when a budget is exhausted, ingestion stalls and requeues instead of failing fast. The research-os side of the same change was fixed in research-os #1929.

## When it can trigger
Only when a LiteLLM budget refuses the engine's calls. On the managed gateway, `managed-shared-data-plane` has `max_budget` 1000 per 30 days, with $878.82 spent as of 2026-09-25 (resets 2026-10-01). On the research gateway, the engine uses the master key, which has no budget.

## Fix
Check the refusal wording before the status code: a 400 or 429 whose message contains `ExceededBudget` or `Budget has been exceeded` is terminal (or a postpone-until-reset). A 429 without that wording stays a rate limit. See research-os `app/generation/llm.py` `budget_exhausted` for the matcher and its tests.

Research report: Product Composition (SBOM / HBOM)

**Proposed owner:** Tyler Van Heerden (needs GitHub handle)  ·  **Wave:** 1 — research  ·  **Depends on:** #P1  ·  **Feeds:** #D1, #D4 (radar vs model), #D3 schema

> Deep external search producing the research report **"Product Composition."** Covers SBOMs, HBOMs, and the technical references, tools, and open-source projects around them. Same multi-agent, self-improving shape. Nothing accepts a `DEC-*`.

## Goal
A survey of **software/hardware composition**: SBOM and HBOM formats, the standards and tooling, and how composition data becomes threat-model input (components → weaknesses/vulnerabilities).

## Deliverable
`research/0004-product-composition/report.md` (versioned): **comparison table first**, then sections per format/tool. Sources → library records; a mapping of **composition → model input** feeds #D1/#D3.

## Scope & questions
- **SBOM**: CycloneDX, SPDX, SWID; Syft, Grype, Trivy, Dependency-Track; how `tradar` already uses these.
- **HBOM**: CycloneDX HBOM, hardware/firmware bills; buses, compute cores, firmware components.
- Technical references, open-source tools, and commercial products with real usage.
- How composition yields **Components** and links to **Weaknesses/Vulnerabilities** (CWE/CVE/NVD) — the bridge into the model.
- Identity of a "build": commit/hash/SBOM — how composition pins a specific product version.

## Multi-agent plan
1. **Scope** — formats + tools + dimensions (coverage, ecosystem, identity model, license).
2. **Fan-out search** (parallel per format/tool) → sources; log queries.
3. **Ingest** → library records (#P1); pin OSS repos + licenses.
4. **Distill** → per-format field notes + the composition→model-input mapping.
5. **Snowball** references.
6. **Adversarial review** — coverage + accuracy + citations.
7. **Synthesize** → report: table + sections + the bridge to the object model.

## Self-improving loop
- Start with CycloneDX + SPDX to tune template/rubric; then scale to HBOM + tools.
- Re-queue gaps; log rejects.

## Human review gate
- Format/clarity + correctness of the composition→model mapping.

## Definition of done
- [ ] Sources as complete library records
- [ ] Report: table + per-format/tool sections
- [ ] Composition→model-input mapping drafted for #D1/#D3
- [ ] Adversarial + human review signed off

The code of conduct says exactly how to report, and where a report goes

**What should be true when this is done**
The Enforcement section of CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md tells someone how to report privately and what happens next:
- To report, use “Report content” in the … menu of an issue, pull request or comment, or “Report abuse” on a person's profile.
- Those reports go to GitHub's staff, not to the maintainer, because this repository belongs to a personal account.
- The maintainer acts on conduct they see here by hiding or deleting it, locking a conversation, blocking someone or limiting interactions.
- There is no private channel for behaviour away from GitHub.
- Security problems go through SECURITY.md.
The page publishes no email address.

**Why it matters**
Decided in #294. Today the page promises privacy and a route “through GitHub” without naming one, and anything written in an issue is public. Someone reporting harassment should know where their report goes.

**Watch out**
- Do not promise that the maintainer reads reports. GitHub's setting that sends reports to maintainers (Settings → Moderation options → Reported content) exists only for public repositories owned by an organisation.
- Use GitHub's own names for the buttons, and keep the Contributor Covenant 2.1 attribution and link.
- Do not send conduct reports to private vulnerability reporting; that route is for security (SECURITY.md).

**How to check it**
Read the rendered page on GitHub, and find each named button on a real issue and a real profile. Run `pnpm test` in `companion/web`, because `docs.test.ts` checks the paths that root-level Markdown files name.

#294.

Bootstrap airgapped mirror registry as podman pod via MachineConfig

## Problem

In airgapped OpenShift environments, there is a chicken-and-egg problem: the cluster needs a container registry to pull images, but deploying a registry (e.g., Quay) as a workload on the cluster requires pulling its images from a registry that doesn't yet exist on the network.

Currently, the airgapped workflow assumes a registry is already available, but on a freshly provisioned "cluster 0" (the first cluster in a disconnected environment), there is no registry to pull from.

## Design Principle

The podman-hosted mirror registry on cluster nodes is the **permanent** registry solution — not a temporary bootstrap step. It must never be removed because the cluster depends on it to pull images at the node level, before Kubernetes workloads (including any in-cluster registry) can start. Removing it would recreate the original chicken-and-egg problem.

By default, the operator does **not** deploy a full Quay instance on the airgapped side. The podman-hosted registries on the nodes are sufficient for serving mirrored content. A full Quay deployment (with its UI, vulnerability scanning, etc.) is an optional add-on that can be enabled if needed, but it is never a replacement for the node-level registries — those remain the primary image source regardless.
## End-to-End Workflow

```
1. Physical media (USB/disk) transferred into airgapped network
        ↓
2. Bastion host: run import bash script to create a temporary
   mirror registry and import the tar bundle into it
        ↓
3. Bastion mirror registry used to install cluster 0
   (install-config points to bastion registry)
        ↓
4. Cluster 0 operational, pointing to bastion temp registry
        ↓
5. Mirror operator installed, configured as airgapped
   DisconnectedPlatform
        ↓
6. Operator generates MachineConfigs to deploy podman-hosted
   mirror registry on at least 2 nodes
        ↓
7. Initial tar mirror content imported into both node-hosted
   registry instances
        ↓
8. IDMS/ICSP rewritten to mirror to BOTH node registries
   (failover: if one node is down, cluster uses the other)
        ↓
9. Bastion temp registry can be decommissioned
        ↓
10. Ongoing imports go directly to the node-hosted registries
    (this is the permanent steady-state architecture)
```

## Phase 1: Bastion Bootstrap (Pre-Operator)

Before the operator exists on the cluster, a bastion host handles initial bootstrapping:

- Import bash script creates a temporary mirror registry on the bastion
- Tar bundle from physical media is imported into this bastion registry
- Cluster 0 is installed using the bastion registry as its image source
- This is a manual/scripted process, not operator-managed

## Phase 2: Operator Takes Over (Post-Install)

Once the mirror operator is installed on cluster 0 and configured as an airgapped `DisconnectedPlatform`:

GA gate, unfiled: the KVM battery must be green on the SHIPPING cut's tip, and its static half carries a check that cannot fail (#1414)

## Why this is an issue

#394's release checklist carries three unticked gates that are **runs, not code** — the KVM battery
green per cut, the 7-day soak, and the release lane exercised end to end. None of them was an issue,
so none had a milestone or an owner, and a milestone-keyed queue could not see them. Filed so the
release cannot read as ready while they are outstanding. This is the battery half.

## The gate

`tests/os/run.sh` is the release gate and `tests/os/verify-image.sh` its static half. Per #394 the
battery must be green **on the current tip, per cut** — not on the tip it was last run against.

Phases per #394: boot · update (A/B + rollback + commit gate) · install (one-page installer, reinstall
tiers) · provision (headless from pre-seed; wizard with one-time token) · fault injection (power cuts
mid-write and mid-commit, corrupt bundle). It now also carries identity-survival, hugepage, and honest
fault-C asserts.

## Two things to settle before the run, not during it

**1. The static half has a known blind spot on the very artifact it gates — #1414.**
`verify-image.sh:189` asserts the baked RigForge ref was *recorded*, never that it matches the pin, so
it passes for any ref including a stale one. Measured on the appliance bench today: the running image
reports `version=1.14.0`, and the check is green on it. **A battery run that includes a check which
cannot fail on the thing it guards reports a stronger result than it earned.** #1414 is in this
milestone; land it before the gating run, or record in the run's result that this assertion was known
vacuous at the time.

**2. Which tip.** "Per cut" means the battery is re-run for the cut being shipped. #1649 is a CVE fix
that changes the compiled binaries in the image, so the gating run is on the post-#1649 tip. A green
battery from before it does not carry.

## Relationship to the other two gates

Run the battery **first**. It is hours, the soak is seven days, and starting a seven-day soak on an
image the battery has not passed risks spending the week to learn something the battery would have
said the same morning.

## What was NOT checked

I have not run the battery and I am not reporting a result. This issue records the gate, its two
preconditions, and its ordering against the other two. Bench dedication is with the operator.

[POSTMORTEM] Échec migration slides pptx→slidev (CoursIA) — exploiter les squelettes partagés pour postmortems cross-machine (affûte #807)

## Contexte

Pendant plus d'un mois, les **agents CoursIA** (Claude Code + Roo dans le workspace CoursIA) sur **po-2025** et **ai-01** ont travaillé à migrer les slides du cours Epita de **pptx vers slidev** (avec passage intermédiaire par Marp), pour les **3 premiers decks** du premier cours.

**Résultat :** Échec cuisant. Le 8 avril 2026, l'utilisateur a dû donner son cours avec les slides pptx d'origine. Aucune des versions slidev livrées n'était utilisable.

Ce n'est pas un incident isolé — l'utilisateur signale « bien d'autres catastrophes » du même type.

**Cette issue est dans roo-extensions** car l'objectif est de permettre à notre harnais de **faire les postmortems de telles catastrophes** (y compris sur d'autres workspaces comme CoursIA) afin d'**affermir** les règles, protocoles et outils multi-agents.

## Faits observés (reality/reports mismatch)

Le dashboard `workspace-CoursIA` (consulté depuis roo-extensions le 2026-04-08) rapporte, dans les heures précédant le cours :

- **ai-01 (agent CoursIA) @ 2026-04-08T00:58:15Z** : commit `a1cd841a` « Corrections visuelles des 3 decks EPITA » avec travail détaillé Deck 01/02/03
- **po-2025 (agent CoursIA) @ 2026-04-08T00:28:23Z** : « Review visuelle slides EPITA 01-02-03 TERMINEE » (via GLM-5, note « Playwright non disponible »)
- **ai-01 (agent CoursIA) @ 2026-04-08T05:23:06Z** : « Slidev servers online localhost:3030/3031/3032, User en revue finale »
- **Status dashboard CoursIA** : « 183 slides EPITA revues : 3/3 decks PROPREs »

**Réalité :** l'utilisateur n'a pas pu utiliser ces slides et est revenu au pptx.

Ce décalage entre rapports d'agents (tout vert) et expérience utilisateur (inutilisable) est **le cœur du problème harnais** à investiguer. Il signale une rupture de l'auto-évaluation des agents sur des livrables visuels/complexes — un défaut transversal qui concerne tous les workspaces, pas seulement CoursIA.

## Architecture disponible — les squelettes sont déjà partagés

**Rappel architectural :** les **squelettes de tâches** (`ConversationSkeleton`) sont stockés sur le **répertoire partagé** (GDrive `.shared-state/`). Cela signifie que, **architecturalement, toutes les conversations de toutes les machines sont accessibles depuis n'importe quelle machine d'investigation** — il « suffit » que les outils exploitent cette réalité.

**Le problème n'est donc pas architectural, il est outillage :**
- `conversation_browser` ne lit actuellement que le filesystem local et ignore les squelettes partagés des autres machines.
- `roosync_search(action: "semantic")` devrait pouvoir exploiter ces squelettes via Qdrant mais est actuellement dégradé (API embeddings vLLM qwen3-4b en 503 au 2026-04-08, lié à #1171).

C'est exactement le type de capacité que #807 cherche à renforcer pour les méta-analystes.

## Chemins possibles

### Chemin A (principal) — Mettre les outils à niveau

**A.1 — Accès direct aux squelettes partagés (browsing/view)**

Permettre à `conversation_browser` (ou un équivalent) d'exploiter les squelettes sur le répertoire partagé pour offrir, depuis une machine d'investigation unique, les actions habituelles (`list`, `view`, `tree`, `summarize`) sur **toutes les conversations de toutes les machines et de tous les workspaces**.

Travail attendu :
1. Cartographier la structure actuelle des squelettes sur le partagé (format, index, métadonnées par machine/workspace)
2. Étendre `conversation_browser` avec une option `source: "shared"` ou équivalent
3. Gérer les cas de squelettes manquants (task récente non encore synchronisée sur le partagé) avec un fallback explicite
4. Documenter le protocole dans `.claude/rules/conversation-browser-guide.md`

**A.2 — Recherche sémantique cross-machine correcte (outil alternatif)**

En parallèle ou en fallback : rendre `roosync_search(semantic)` véritablement utilisable pour les postmorte

# Compiler: make mixed-SSA KIR the single optimized and verified production middle end

## Summary

Make one canonical, target-neutral, mixed-SSA Kernel IR graph the program that
fe2o3 both optimizes and verifies before lowering. Extend the current bounded
optimizer into a modular scalar, control-flow, loop, memory, interprocedural,
and target-specific pipeline; validate every mutation; and require every
runnable/compiler-produced kernel published by `fe2o3-kernels` to compile
through this sole production route.

This is the successor roadmap for the mixed-SSA and optimizer work under #175
and #178. It must preserve the owner/session safety boundary in #140, the
semantic-refinement work in #106, and the honest community-launch policy in
#267.

## Why this issue exists

The production pipeline has made substantial progress:

- rustc owns parsing, typing, borrow checking, const evaluation, layout, and
  monomorphization;
- the backend collects fully monomorphized device MIR into canonical semantic
  MIR;
- `ProductionSemanticSsaOwnerV1` runs the shared bounded SSA planner for every
  semantic function;
- ranked Pliron runs the immutable nine-stage verification sequence;
- semantic MIR is lowered to versioned target-neutral KIR;
- target binding selects an exact AMDGPU profile; and
- the production V2 optimizer executes SCCP, CFG simplification,
  `select(c, x, x)` canonicalization, DCE, same-block pure CSE, DCE, and CFG
  simplification before LLVM lowering.

The remaining architectural gaps are important:

1. The semantic SSA owner retains unchanged semantic MIR plus a construction
   plan. It is not a reusable, materialized optimization IR.
2. Ranked verification and executable KIR are separately constructed
   representations. Exact correspondence checks reduce risk but do not make
   duplicated program graphs desirable permanent architecture.
3. Production target-KIR optimization currently happens after earlier ranked
   and formal-memory evidence was established. Structural replay and output IR
   verification do not by themselves prove semantic preservation or carry all
   earlier safety conclusions across mutation.
4. The symbolic index, Presburger, ownership, uniformity, and memory analyses
   are primarily verification services. Their facts do not yet enable general
   bounds-check removal, global value numbering, loop optimization, or
   alias-driven memory optimization.
5. The current five distinct optimizer pass implementations are not yet a general
   optimizing middle end. SROA, fixpoint canonicalization, global CSE/GVN,
   inlining, loop transformations, interprocedural cleanup, and memory
   optimization remain absent or deliberately restricted.
6. The tutorial website has an evolving mixture of compiler-produced kernels,
   CPU/simulator examples, design snippets, and external comparison baselines.
   The compiler lacks one machine-readable gate that prevents a runnable lesson
   from bypassing the production optimizer or silently falling out of coverage.

## Architectural decision

Mixed SSA is an invariant of the canonical middle-end IR, not a one-time
terminal conversion. SSA values remain single-definition throughout the
pipeline; address-observable storage remains explicit memory. Passes such as
inlining and SROA may expose new promotable storage, so bounded promotion and
cleanup may run again.

The target architecture is:

```text
authenticated Rust source
  -> rustc fully monomorphized device MIR
  -> canonical semantic MIR ownership
  -> bounded SSA construction plan
  -> one canonical target-neutral mixed-SSA KIR/Pliron graph
  -> target-neutral optimization + checked transformation records
  -> complete ranked/safety/semantic verification of that exact graph
  -> exact AMDGPU target binding
  -> target-specific GPU optimization + affected-analysis replay
  -> final verified canonical target-KIR snapshot
  -> AMDGPU LL

组织数字化的下一跃：从 AI 对话到企业轻应用落地 ## 引言：当"写一个应用"突然变得很便宜 Vibe Coding 大幅降低了应用开发成本，过去因"不值得投入专业研发"而长期积压的部门台账、活动报名、检查工具等长尾需求，第一次具备经济可行性。但人人都能生成应用之后，瓶颈从"谁来开发"转向"如何治理"。 ## 第一章 应用生产权正在下沉 ### 1.1 从"提需求"到"自己解决" 过去一个内部应用的诞生路径是固定的：业务提需求 → IT 评估 → 排期 → 产品设计 → 开发 → 测试 → 上线。这条链路的每一环都有存在的理由，但它有一个无法回避的属性——**它有固定的最低成本**。 即使是一张最简单的表单加一个审批，走完这条链路也意味着若干人天的投入和一个排期窗口。这个最低成本，构成了企业内部应用的**供给门槛**。 AI Coding 改变的第一件事，是让这条链路第一次**可以被绕过**。业务人员用自然语言描述意图，工具直接产出可运行的前端代码。他不需要理解组件、状态管理或构建流程，他需要理解的只是自己的业务。 这不是"IT 决定放权"，而是成本结构变化的自然结果。 ### 1.2 真正改变的不是开发效率，而是应用供给曲线 ![应用供给曲线](https://regulusun.github.io/images/app-supply-curve.png) 外界谈 AI 编程，习惯用"提效"来衡量——把 10 天缩短到 2 天。这个视角本身没错，公开数据也支持效率提升：GitHub 与微软研究院的随机对照实验显示，使用 Copilot 的开发者完成同一个编程任务比对照组快约 55%；GitHub 官方也披露过 Copilot 用户约 30% 的代码由 AI 建议生成。 但对企业数字化而言，提效只是次要效应。**主要效应是供给曲线的位移。** 把企业内部所有数字化需求按"业务价值"从高到低排开，会得到一条长尾分布：左端是少量高价值的核心系统需求，右端是大量低价值但数量庞大的长尾需求。IT 的开发成本在这条曲线上画出一条水平线——线以上的需求值得做，线以下的需求永远不值得做。 线以下堆积的是什么？ - 部门临时台账 - 一次性活动报名与统计 - 门店检查与巡检记录表 - 项目 checklist - 内部信息收集与投票 - 小型计算与换算工具 它们不是没有价值。它们的困境只有一句话：**开发成本 > 需求价值**。 所以它们的真实归宿不是"被拒绝"，而是被 Excel、微信群接龙、纸质表格和人工汇总替代——也就是说，这部分需求从来没有消失，它只是**以非数字化的方式被消耗掉了**，消耗的是业务人员的时间。 AI Coding 做的事情，是把那条水平线往下压。线一下移，原本躺在线下的大片需求，第一次进入了"值得做"的区间。 > **这不是效率问题，是经济可行性问题。** > 过去我们没有解决这些需求，不是因为不会做，而是因为不划算。现在它划算了。 这也解释了一个即将出现的现象：**企业内部应用的数量，会在未来两到三年出现数量级的增长**，而这个增长与 IT 人力规模无关。 ### 1.3 于是，生产权天然下沉 过去 IT 同时握着四种权力：需求解释权、开发权、部署权、数据访问权。这四者被同一条研发流程捆在一起，所以从来不需要被分开讨论。 AI Coding 松动的是其中一项——**开发权**。它是四者中唯一可以被通用工具替代的，因为写代码是一项有明确输入输出、可以被模型泛化的技能，而部署、数据与身份天然依附于企业自有的基础设施。 所以这里要说清楚一个容易被误读的点： > **下沉的是生产权，不是全部。** 一个业务人员今天可以生成一个能跑的前端，但他仍然没有能力、也不应该被要求去决定：这个应用用谁的身份登录、数据存在哪个库、谁可以读、域名怎么分配、上线前该检查什么、三年后谁来下线它。 这就构成了一个结构性的错位——**生产能力已经扩散到组织边缘，而治理能力仍然集中在中心**。旧的治理模型之所以有效，是因为它默认"只有专业开发者才能生产软件"，治理是研发流程的副产品；当这个前提不再成立，副产品也就随之消失。 这个错位，就是第二章要处理的问题。

第二章 真正的问题不是 AI，而是责任边界

2.1 应用数量上来之后，会暴露什么

第一章的结论是：生产权在下沉，内部应用的数量会出现数量级增长。

接下来要问的是：这些应用带来的问题，究竟是什么性质的问题。

一个用 AI 生成的轻应用，从上线那一刻起就需要回答七个问题：

  • 用户用什么身份登录？
  • 数据存在哪里、归谁所有？
  • 谁能读、谁能写？
  • 访问凭证放在什么位置？
  • 它能访问到哪些系统？
  • 谁是这个应用的负责人？
  • 三年后它还在不在跑，由谁关掉？

这七个问题，没有一个是关于业务逻辑的，全部是工程与治理问题。而提出需求、也最清楚业务逻辑的那个人，恰恰是最没有能力回答这七个问题的人。

这就是问题的全部来源。它与 AI 生成的代码质量高低无关——即使 AI 写出完美的业务代码，这七个问题依然悬空。

2.2 一个公开案例：当"默认安全"这个假设不成立

海外的 AI 应用生成平台 Lovable 提供了一个值得引用的教训。

它的架构与本文讨论的场景高度相似：AI 生成纯前端代码，前端用一个公开的客户端密钥直接访问后端数据库，数据访问权限由数据库的行级安全策略（RLS）控制。这是一套标准且合理的 BaaS 架构。

问题出在责任归属上。写对行级策略这件事，被留给了使用者。

结果是 CVE-2025-48757：生成的应用用公开密钥从浏览器直连数据库，却没有对应的行级策略约束，攻击者不需要任何凭证就能读写数据表。安全研究者扫描了 1645 个用该平台生成的应用，发现其中 170 个存在同样问题，泄露了姓名、邮箱、财务信息和 API 密钥。

更值得注意的是修复方式：平台随后上线了一个安全扫描器，但它检测的是"行级策略是否存在"，而不是"策略是否正确"。

这个案例有三层含义，逐层递进：

第一层，基础设施的安全不等于应用的安全。 PostgreSQL 的行级安全机制本身是可靠的、经过长期验证的。出事的不是机制，是机制没有被正确配置。凡是"默认安全"的说法，都要追问一句：默认安全的是基础设施，还是策略本身？

第二层，把安全配置交给不具备判断力的人，等于没有配置。 使用者无法验证一条策略写得对不对，因为验证需要的知识恰恰是他所缺少的。他只能看到"应用能用"，而"应用能用"和"应用安全"是两个独立的状态。

第三层，检测存在性不等于检测正确性。 这一点对你我尤其重要——它意味着在设计平台的检查环节时，"每张表都开启了 RLS"只是一个及格线，真正的安全来自策略本身不由使用者编写。

2.3 这不是 AI 的问题，是治理模型的前提失效了

有一种常见的解读是：AI 生成的代码不够安全，所以要谨慎使用 AI。

这个解读是错的，而且会导向错误的对策。

过去二十年企业软件治理之所以有效，依赖一个隐性前提：只有专业开发者才能生产软件。

在这个前提下，治理不需要被单独设计，它是研发流程的副产品——代码评审、安全扫描、权限设计、上线审批、资产登记，全都挂在研发流程这根主干上。一个应用要上线，必然经过这根主干，也必然被治理顺带覆盖。

AI Coding 拆掉的不是安全机制，而是这个前提。生产能力扩散到了组织边缘，主干却还在中心。于是应用可以在不经过主干的情况下诞生并上线——治理没有被突破，它是被绕过了。

所以对策也不该是"限制业务使用 AI"。限制只会把这件事逼到台面之下：业务同学依然会用公网工具做出应用，只是 IT 不再知道它们的存在。影子 IT 从来不是被创造出来的，它是被管出来的。

正确的对策是：把治理从研发流程里剥离出来，做成一条独立的、所有应用都必须经过的通道。

2.4 新的责任边界

结论可以收敛成一句话：业务负责业务意图，平台负责工程正确性。

具体的划分是：

  | 业务侧 | 平台侧 -- | -- | -- 负责 | 需求判断、业务逻辑、界面与流程、应用的持续有用性 | 身份、数据、权限、域名、发布、网络边界、生命周期 需要理解 | 自己的业务 | JWT、RLS、CSP、OAuth、凭证管理 决策方式 | 在平台提供的选项中选择 | 设计选项本身

这里有一个关键的设计原则，后文的所有护栏都由它推导而来：

凡是业务人员无法验证对错的事情，都不应该交给业务人员决

The wave audit (#662) has not produced an `APPROVED` since **2026-07-28**. Every wave since has exited 4, failed open, and chained its un-audited range into the next one — which makes the next range larger and more certain to fail the same way. The watermark cannot advance on its own, so the mechanism that is supposed to review propagated canonical content is structurally a no-op.

```

```

## The adapter's own words

```
[phase-4b] ERROR: diff (2242097 bytes) exceeds the 800000-byte review budget and
cannot be reduced by omitting policy-allowlisted bulk sections
(phase_4b_automation.diff_omit_globs) — refusing to omit unreviewed code (#636);
omission is also refused outright when the diff touches .github/review-policy.yml,
because the PR may have rewritten the very allowlist this run would trust (#668);
pass a curated --diff-file or extend the allowlist; falling back to the manual handoff
```

Both refusals are correct in isolation. #636 will not silently drop unreviewed code, and #668 will not trust an allowlist the PR under review may have edited. Neither is the bug.

## Why exit 4 is the wrong classification, and why that matters

`wave-audit.sh` maps orchestrator exit 4 to *"reviewer unavailable — quota, timeout, automation off"* and applies the documented fail-open: proceed on CI + lane, do not advance the watermark, chain the range forward.

That disposition is right for a **transient** cause. A quota lapse or a timeout clears; retrying later works; chaining costs one extra cycle.

This cause is **deterministic**. The reviewer was never asked — the run refused before dispatch because the payload exceeds a fixed byte budget. Retrying changes nothing, and the fail-open's remedy (chain into the next audit) actively makes it worse, because the next range is a superset of this one. Five weeks of that produced the 2.8x overage above.

So the audit reports the same outcome for "ask again in an hour" and for "this will never succeed again", and only the first is survivable.

## Consequences worth stating plainly

- **Nothing has audited the propagated canonical range since 2026-07-28.** Every wave in that window fanned out on CI + lane alone. CI and the lane verify that the mirror is byte-identical to the hub; neither reads the code.
- **The gap is self-reinforcing** in exactly the way mergepath#1086 was (weekly drift audit failing *because* there was too much drift to report). Same shape, different surface.
- It is also why invoking Codex on the canary keeps surfacing real findings against canonical content — see #1185 and #1166. With the audit inert, the mirror trigger is the only thing reading that range at all, which is an argument that the findings are signal rather than churn.

🟡 Auto-update workflow adopts latest dependencies with no quarantine window (.github/workflows/quality.yml)

<!-- finding-id: SEC-a3f19c02d8e1 -->
<!-- cwe: CWE-829 -->

`.github/workflows/quality.yml:24-25` runs `deno outdated --update --latest` unconditionally, then (lines 51-63) auto-commits and pushes whatever changed — including any resulting `deno.json` import-map bump — with no minimum-age / quarantine gate on the newly-adopted dependency versions.

## Why this matters

The repo has no Renovate config, no Dependabot config, and no `bump-deps.sh` (confirmed by search — none exist in this repository). `deno.json` also carries no native `minimumDependencyAge` field. `quality.yml` is therefore the repo's only auto-update path, and it adopts whatever version the registry reports as "latest" at the moment the workflow runs, with zero delay between a package being published and this repo trusting and shipping it. This is exactly the "supply-chain:quarantine-missing" gap the 2025–2026 npm/JSR supply-chain wave (Shai-Hulud, node-ipc dormant republish, TanStack CI hijack) makes concrete: a malicious or hijacked release published moments before this workflow runs is adopted immediately, with no human review before it can be executed (see the related exploit-chain finding for how it gets executed and what it can then reach).

## Attacker model

A supply-chain attacker able to publish a malicious release of any package this repo imports (directly via `@std/assert`, `@std/cli`, `@std/yaml`, or any of their transitive dependencies), timed to be "latest" when a collaborator with push access next triggers this workflow.

## Trigger

Any `push` to any branch other than `Develop` (`on.push.branches-ignore: [Develop]`, line 4-6) runs this job, which unconditionally executes `deno outdated --update --latest`.

## Exploit sketch

1. Attacker publishes a compromised version of a dependency (or a new transitive dependency).
2. A collaborator pushes a branch (routine activity — no special trigger needed).
3. `quality.yml` runs `deno outdated --update --latest`, adopting the compromised version into `deno.json` / the resolved import graph with no age check.
4. The subsequent `deno test --allow-all test/*.ts` step (line 39) executes code that transitively resolves through the newly-adopted dependency tree.
5. If the diff is non-empty, the workflow auto-commits and pushes the change (lines 51-63), so the compromised pin can even land in the branch history without human review.

## Suggested fix

Add a quarantine gate before `deno outdated --update --latest` runs unattended — e.g. adopt Deno's native `minimumDependencyAge` in `deno.json` (with `stSoftwareAU/*`-scoped deps excluded from the wait), or replace the unconditional `deno outdated --update --latest` step with a scheduled, human-reviewed PR (Renovate/Dependabot-style) rather than an unattended auto-commit-and-push on every push.

**Scope.** #29 tracks **Terabithia patches**; #106 tracks **`devel` commits**. **One line = one artifact, always** — one patch, or one commit. **A bundle is a group, not a line**: give it a heading, put each member on its own line beneath it, and let the heading carry what is true of all of them (see *Grouping* and *Group headings*). Analysis true of only some members is written once, on one of them, and **referenced** from the others (`see <id>`) — never restated, per *No repetition*. Dependencies are expressed the same way — see *Sequencing*. The same underlying change may appear on both — as a patch on #29, as a commit on #106 — linked by cross-reference, never by ownership.

*Sub-items:* a bullet that only elaborates its parent (a step, a caveat, a sub-task) is **not** a separate artifact and needs no verdict, checkbox or cross-reference of its own.

## L1 — Leer Archivos

Un detector de malware que no sabe leer archivos es un decorado. Vamos a arrancar por lo aburrido pero necesario: cargar una transmisión como **una sola cadena limpia**.

Los archivos vienen con saltos de línea (`\n`, y en Windows también `\r`). Esos saltos **no son parte de la transmisión**, así que hay que quitarlos antes de buscar nada, o las posiciones saldrán chuecas.

**Concepto nuevo:** `open()` con `with` cierra el archivo solo. `str.replace(a, "")` borra caracteres. (Aquí sí se vale usar `replace` porque no resuelve el problema del algoritmo, solo limpia.)

## L2 — El Método Lento

Antes de KMP hay que entender por qué existe. Imagina buscar `AAAAB` en `AAAAAAAAAAAB`: el método ingenuo compara 4 A's, falla en la B, **retrocede** y vuelve a empezar una posición más adelante. Repite eso n veces → **O(n·m)**.

## L3 — La Tabla de Prefijos

Este es el cerebro de KMP. Necesitas entender un concepto: **borde**.

**Concepto nuevo:** un *borde* de una cadena es un trozo que es a la vez prefijo y sufijo (sin ser toda la cadena). En `ABCAB`, `AB` es borde. La tabla `pi[i]` guarda el largo del borde más largo de `s[0..i]`.

Ejemplo para `s = "ABABC"`:

| i | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| s[i] | A | B | A | B | C |
| pi[i] | 0 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 0 |

### Tarea (función paso a paso) — en `src/kmp.py`
1. Firma y tabla inicial:
```python
def prefix_function(s: str) -> list[int]:
    pi = [0] * len(s)
    k = 0  # largo del borde actual
```
2. Recorre `i` de `1` a `len(s)-1`.
3. Mientras `k > 0` y `s[i] != s[k]`, retrocede: `k = pi[k-1]`. *(Por qué: si el borde actual no se puede extender, probamos con el borde del borde; nunca retrocedemos en `s`, solo en `k`.)*
4. Si `s[i] == s[k]`, incrementa `k`.
5. Guarda `pi[i] = k`.
6. Devuelve `pi`.

> Esta función también la usará Fabian (Parte 3). **No cambies la firma.**

### Pruébalo tú mismo
```python
assert prefix_function("ABABC") == [0, 0, 1, 2, 0]
assert prefix_function("AAAA") == [0, 1, 2, 3]
assert prefix_function("ABCD") == [0, 0, 0, 0]
```

### Criterios de aceptación
- [ ] Los 3 asserts pasan.
- [ ] `prefix_function("")` devuelve `[]` sin error.
- [ ] Sin usar `find`, `in`, `re`.

ops: persist attachment blobs on a durable volume with a content-root-relative path

### Context

Attachment binaries (certificates, photos, control-chart exports linked to production records) back the shopfloor evidence behind Genealogy and the audit trail. Today they are not durable: LocalFileStorage resolves the default relative RootPath (App_Data/attachments) with Path.GetFullPath against the process working directory, and docker-compose.yml mounts no volume for the storage root (only postgres_data, pg_backups, seq_data exist). Every api/api-prod container recreate therefore wipes uploaded blobs while the Attachment metadata rows (with StorageKey) survive in Postgres, leaving orphaned keys and broken downloads. A manufacturing customer loses proof-of-quality files on each redeploy.

### Glossary terms

- Tenant (Attachment metadata is tenant-scoped; on-disk blobs are GUID-sharded keys and tenant isolation stays enforced by metadata plus handler authorization from issue #315)
- Genealogy (attachments may evidence traceability records that must survive redeploys)

### Scope

- **In scope:**
  - Resolve a relative Attachments:LocalStorage:RootPath against the content root (IHostEnvironment.ContentRootPath) instead of the process CWD; absolute paths keep working unchanged.
  - Add an attachments_data named volume in docker-compose.yml mounted at the storage root on api and api-prod, with an env-overridable path variable.
  - Document the volume and the override in .env.example and docs/deployment.md.
  - Log the resolved absolute blob root at startup so operators can verify the mount.
- **Out of scope:**
  - Migrating to S3/object storage or changing the StorageKey format.
  - Per-tenant quota, malware-scan hook (issue #348), object-level authorization (issue #315), upload attribution (issue #354) - all done; must not regress.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With default config the resolved blob root is <content-root>/App_Data/attachments regardless of the process working directory.
- [ ] An absolute Attachments:LocalStorage:RootPath keeps working unchanged.
- [ ] docker compose config shows the attachments_data volume mounted into api and api-prod at the configured root.
- [ ] Durability proof: upload a file, docker compose down (volume kept) and up again, download returns byte-identical content.
- [ ] Crafted storage keys containing .. are still rejected (traversal guard, no regression).
- [ ] .env.example and docs/deployment.md document the volume and the override variable.
- [ ] No EF Core migration.

### Multi-tenancy impact

- No new tenant-scoped entities; Attachment already implements ISaasy.
- No new MediatR requests, so no ITenantRequest / IAllowAnonymousRequest change; on-disk layout is unchanged (GUID-sharded keys) and tenant isolation stays in metadata plus handler authorization.

### Test plan

- **Unit tests** (tests/AsistOff.MES.Shared.Tests/Attachments/): root-resolution cases - relative path resolves under the content root independent of CWD, absolute path passes through, traversal keys still rejected.
- **Endpoint integration tests** (tests/AsistOff.MES.Integration.Tests/, Testcontainers PostgreSQL, extend IntegrationTestBase): upload then download round-trip happy path plus 404 for an unknown key.
- **Manual compose proof** recorded in the PR body (upload, down/up, byte-compare download) since Testcontainers cannot prove compose mounts. Follow .github/instructions/testing.instructions.md.

### Affected areas

- Backend: AsistOff.MES.Attachments.Infrastructure/Storage/LocalFileStorage.cs, LocalFileStorageOptions.cs, DependencyInjection.cs (content-root resolution).
- Ops: docker-compose.yml (attachments_data volume plus mounts), docker-compose.override.yml (dev convenience), .env.example, docs/deployment.md.
- EF Core migration: no.

Unprotected initialize() — front-runnable admin takeover on any future deployment

**Suggested complexity: High (200) points** — flagged with the extreme-difficulty label too since a correct fix touches the deploy/init contract lifecycle itself, not just application logic.

## Problem

`initialize()` (`lib.rs:109`) is callable by anyone — it only requires `admin.require_auth()`, proving the caller controls whatever address they pass in as `admin`, never that the caller is the intended deployer. Soroban deployment and `initialize()` are separate transactions in this repo's actual workflow (manual `stellar contract deploy`, then a separate `initialize()` invoke — confirmed no script bundles them atomically).

## Exploit scenario

An attacker watches the ledger for a freshly-deployed `OracleEscrow` WASM instance (matching the known contract hash), before the operator's own `initialize()` call lands. The attacker submits `initialize(attacker_addr, real_usdc_token, attacker_addr, 1)` first, self-signing as admin — using the *real* token address so it looks legitimate. The operator's subsequent `initialize()` then fails with `AlreadyInitialized`. Any user who trusts the published contract ID and calls `submit()`/`deposit()` has their funds resolvable to the attacker via `resolve()`.

## Important context

The currently-live contract is almost certainly safe — it's been settling real transactions all session using the real platform key, which wouldn't work if it had been front-run. This is a risk for any *future* redeploy, not an active compromise right now.

## Suggested fix

Use soroban-sdk's constructor pattern (`__constructor`, invoked atomically by `CreateContractV2` in the same operation as deployment) instead of a free-standing `initialize()` callable in a later, separate transaction — this closes the race structurally. If staying on the current pattern for now, at minimum document/enforce that deploy and initialize must be the same submitted (multi-op) transaction operationally.

## Out of scope

Does not require touching the currently-deployed instance — this is about how any *future* deployment happens.
