🟡 Privileged push PAT persisted to disk before an --allow-all test run (.github/workflows/quality.yml)

<!-- finding-id: SEC-7b4d0e9f2a63 -->
<!-- cwe: CWE-522 -->

`.github/workflows/quality.yml:16-18` checks out the repo with a privileged, non-default PAT (the `ACTIONS_PUSH` secret) via the `token:` input, and does not disable credential persistence. `actions/checkout`'s default behaviour is to persist credentials, so this PAT is written to the runner's on-disk git credential store (`.git/config`) and stays there, readable, for the rest of the job.

## Why this matters

The sibling workflow `.github/workflows/update-package-version.yml:25-37` does the opposite deliberately, with an explicit comment explaining that the default credential-persistence behaviour would write the `ACTIONS_PUSH` secret (a privileged PAT) into `.git/config` for every subsequent step, and that any future step invoking a PR-controlled script would silently open a PAT-exfiltration vector. `quality.yml` shows the exact pattern that comment warns about: the PAT is persisted, and a later step (`deno test --allow-all test/*.ts`, line 39) runs with unrestricted filesystem, network and env permissions — any code executing there (including via a compromised dependency, see the related quarantine-missing finding) can read the persisted credential from disk and use it to push, or exfiltrate it over the network.

## Attacker model

Any code that executes later in the same job with filesystem/network access — most concretely, a compromised dependency pulled in by the `deno outdated --update --latest` step at line 25 and then executed during `deno test --allow-all` at line 39.

## Trigger

Any `push` to a non-`Develop` branch runs the job; the credential is persisted at the checkout step (lines 16-18) and remains valid for every subsequent step.

## Exploit sketch

1. Checkout (lines 16-18) persists the `ACTIONS_PUSH` PAT to `.git/config` on the runner (credential persistence is left at its default, on).
2. `deno test --allow-all test/*.ts` (line 39) runs with `--allow-all`, i.e. full read/write/net/env/run access.
3. Any code executing during that test step — attacker-controlled via a compromised dependency, or simply a bug in test code — can read `.git/config`, obtain the PAT, and either `git push` directly (credentials are already configured) or exfiltrate the token over the network.

## Suggested fix

Explicitly turn credential persistence off on this checkout step, matching the pattern already used in `update-package-version.yml`, and re-introduce the PAT only at the specific push step via a per-command auth header (as `update-package-version.yml:143-151` already demonstrates).

Design a safe multi-asset settlement mechanism without a token-substitution trust hole

## Problem
The contract is hardcoded to one settlement token (set once at `initialize()`). There's no way to support multiple assets without deploying an entirely separate contract instance per asset, and no analysis of what a pluggable-asset design would need to stay safe.

## Why this is hard
A naive "let the caller pass any token address" design is a real vulnerability — it would let a malicious caller substitute a fake/malicious SAC that lies about balances or blocks transfers, effectively rugging the escrow. A safe design needs an explicit, admin-gated asset allowlist (or equivalent trust boundary), careful handling of differing token decimals, and proof that per-question accounting can't be confused across assets.

## Acceptance criteria
- A designed and implemented multi-asset mechanism with an explicit trust boundary (e.g. admin-curated allowlist) preventing arbitrary token substitution
- Tests proving cross-asset accounting can't be confused (e.g. a question escrowed in asset A can never be resolved/refunded against asset B's balance)
- Decimal-handling correctness tests for at least one non-7-decimal SEP-41 token

This issue is the live coordination surface for autonomous completion workers launched repeatedly (approximately every few minutes).

Minimize `DISTANCE_TO_FINISHED_SCRIPTURE_ARCHIVE`.

Workers have no permanent role. Each run must reconstruct live state and choose the highest-value unowned release-critical role: BUILD, REPAIR, CONTENT, SOURCE_QA, CONVERGE, TEST, SECURITY, ACCESSIBILITY, WINDOWS, CONSTRUCTOR, INTEGRATION_READINESS, INTEGRATE, RELEASE, RECOVERY, CLOSE.

The product is not finished until a real packaged Windows 11 x64 user journey works with canonical content: launch packaged app → keyboard/NVDA navigation → Bible reader/search/research workspace → campaign/mission/tasks → evidence/witness/timeline mechanics → deterministic grading/hints/branching → mastery/review → persistence/restart → usable constructor create/validate/preview/publish/version/export/import → content packs/search/export → recovery/update/rollback → final package fidelity → physical NVDA acceptance.

One canonical implementation per capability. Reuse → repair → converge → compose → extend. Do not mutate main casually. A run does not earn delivery credit for status-only reporting, repeated unchanged-head review, duplicate CI/evidence, broad audit without repair when repair is possible, cosmetic cleanup while a release blocker exists, or a duplicate implementation.

Post only material transitions when useful: CLAIM, REAL_DEFECT_PROVEN, BLOCKER_REMOVED, HEAD_CHANGED, CI_TERMINAL, REVIEW_VERDICT, READY_FOR_INTEGRATION, INTEGRATED, HANDOFF, RUN_END. Avoid comment spam.

[Security] Hard-Coded Django Secret Enables JWT Forgery # Hard-Coded Django Secret Enables JWT Forgery Hello AI Story maintainers, AI Story's production Compose configuration omits `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY`, so Django falls back to the public value `django-insecure-dev-key-change-in-production`. The same value is configured as Simple JWT's HS256 signing key. An attacker who can reach an instance using the shipped deployment configuration can forge access tokens for existing active users and call authenticated APIs as those users. This affects deployments using the shipped Compose configuration without an external `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY` override. ## Evidence - [`base.py:14`](https://github.com/xhongc/ai_story/blob/6072cc8b6035bc42c2fb543527af33eb35a40e63/backend/config/settings/base.py#L14) defines the public fallback secret. - [`production.py:5-8`](https://github.com/xhongc/ai_story/blob/6072cc8b6035bc42c2fb543527af33eb35a40e63/backend/config/settings/production.py#L5-L8) imports the base settings. [`docker-compose-deploy.yml:25-32`](https://github.com/xhongc/ai_story/blob/6072cc8b6035bc42c2fb543527af33eb35a40e63/docker-compose-deploy.yml#L25-L32) selects production settings but does not set `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY`. - [`base.py:199-220`](https://github.com/xhongc/ai_story/blob/6072cc8b6035bc42c2fb543527af33eb35a40e63/backend/config/settings/base.py#L199-L220) sets `ALGORITHM` to `HS256`, uses `SECRET_KEY` as `SIGNING_KEY`, and maps the token's `user_id` claim to the Django user `id`. - [`RegisterView`](https://github.com/xhongc/ai_story/blob/6072cc8b6035bc42c2fb543527af33eb35a40e63/backend/apps/users/views.py#L46-L72) allows unauthenticated registration and returns the user's ID ([`UserSerializer`](https://github.com/xhongc/ai_story/blob/6072cc8b6035bc42c2fb543527af33eb35a40e63/backend/apps/users/serializers.py#L8-L14)). The shipped Compose configuration also omits the registration-code override, leaving its public default `charles` ([`base.py:188`](https://github.com/xhongc/ai_story/blob/6072cc8b6035bc42c2fb543527af33eb35a40e63/backend/config/settings/base.py#L188)). Authenticated API views use JWT authentication by default ([`base.py:142-149`](https://github.com/xhongc/ai_story/blob/6072cc8b6035bc42c2fb543527af33eb35a40e63/backend/config/settings/base.py#L142-L149)). ## Proof of concept Run in the backend's Django environment. Use the ID of an existing active account: ```python import os import django os.environ.setdefault("DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE", "config.settings.production") django.setup() from rest_framework_simplejwt.tokens import AccessToken token = AccessToken() token["user_id"] = 1 # Replace with an existing active user's ID. print(str(token)) ``` Send the printed token as `Authorization: Bearer ` to an authenticated API endpoint. The server verifies its signature with the same public fallback key and resolves the selected user ID. ## Remediation Require a unique, high-entropy `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY` in production and fail startup if it is absent. Rotate the key to invalidate tokens signed with the exposed value. ## Related works - [Arcade MCP — CVE-2025-66454](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g2jx-37x6-6438) - [Bambuddy — CVE-2026-25505](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gc24-px2r-5qmf) - [AstrBot — CVE-2025-55449](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4m32-cjv7-f425) - [Apache Superset — CVE-2023-27524](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5cx2-vq3h-x52c) - [Label Studio — CVE-2023-43791](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f475-x83m-rx5m) - [Redash — CVE-2021-41192](https://github.com/getredash/redash/security/advisories/GHSA-g8xr-f424-h2rv) - [PPress — CVE-2025-54761](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-54761) - [WeRSS — CVE-2026-2215](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4rf7-rfqf-gw8j) This report is part of my ongoing security research. # Mail-man retirement architecture v5 — CANDIDATE

## Decision status
`CANDIDATE — NOT YET FROZEN`

This ADR supersedes Issue #26 **as the current planning baseline only**. Issue #26 and all prior receipts remain historical authority for work already executed under them.

The purpose of v5 is to simplify the system around what is now empirically proven:

- GitHub durable receipts work as shared authority.
- `CODEX_DESKTOP_AGENT` can execute the Desktop↔Web long-loop experiment (#42), currently at Round 2.
- `INDEPENDENT_CONNECTOR_REVIEWER / CONNECTOR` has a PASS capability receipt (#40 `5230481784`).
- `CROSS_FAMILY_CLI_REVIEWER / CODEX_OPENAI / CLI` has a PASS capability receipt (#41 `5230507790`).
- GitHub maintains the official `github-mcp-server` with installation guides for OpenCode and OpenAI Codex, including read-only mode.

This ADR does **not** declare either Desktop or CLI/MCP the final winner. It defines a small common architecture and two evidence tracks.

---

# 1. Core principle

`GitHub = durable authority`

AI chat, Desktop UI, CLI stdout, browser messages, and doorbells are transport only.

Every agent must re-read GitHub before acting on a task/review transition when a durable receipt exists.

No persistent autonomous AI Control Tower is required.

---

# 2. Architecture layers

## 2.1 Authority plane — GitHub

Canonical state:
- Issues/cards
- exact comment/receipt IDs
- exact commits/heads
- PR/run/job/artifact identities when applicable
- machine-readable PASS | FIX_REQUIRED | BLOCKED and routing receipts

Mutable chat history, browser prose, labels, and local summaries do not override durable exact receipts.

## 2.2 GitHub access substrate

Use existing maintained transports instead of inventing another generic CLI↔GitHub bridge.

Preferred order:

1. **ChatGPT Web / Control / formal Reviewer**
   - use the connected GitHub app/connector directly.

2. **CLI AI agents (OpenCode, Codex, later Gemini if needed)**
   - prefer GitHub's official `github-mcp-server`.
   - use least-privilege toolsets.
   - Worker/read-only lanes MUST expose only read operations (`read-only` mode or equivalent server-side restriction).
   - secrets/tokens must never appear in prompts, receipts, or repo files.

3. **Deterministic publication / watcher glue**
   - GitHub REST / `gh api` / Actions may remain for bounded deterministic publication, read-back, scheduling, or fallback when MCP does not cover the required operation.

MCP is an **access substrate**, not a Reviewer identity and not a new review-policy transport enum. Issue #38's `CONNECTOR | CLI | WEB` review-route taxonomy remains conceptually valid.

## 2.3 Executor planes

### A. Proven Desktop baseline lane
`CODEX_DESKTOP_AGENT`

Used where the card explicitly selects the Desktop long-loop path.

Current proof card: Issue #42.

Desktop/Web messages are not authority. Desktop must re-read GitHub result receipts before repair/next-task action.

Direct code publication rights demonstrated by #42 are synthetic-canary-specific and MUST NOT be generalized to the production Worker plane without a later explicit decision.

### B. Primary CLI Worker lane
`OpenCode CLI + approved DeepSeek family`

Production-oriented Worker principle remains:
- bounded card
- exact base/scope
- no Reviewer self-approval
- no ORCA
- no broad GitHub write authority inside the model process
- GitHub MCP read-only is the preferred future GitHub intake mechanism after admission PASS
- artifacts/results cross a deterministic publication boundary when write authority is needed

## 2.4 Reviewer plane

Formal authority remains:
`fresh-context ChatGPT 網頁版（GPT-5.6 Sol）Reviewer`

Requirements:
- independent fresh context for each formal round
- direct GitHub evidence read
- exact head/generation binding
- durable result written to GitHub first

Additional lanes already capability-proven:
- primary/independent connector lane: #4

> "we do not have a place to store projects. If i want to start a new project in a new repo, and make some specs, we have no good place to store my projects. I think we need to make this an app that installs and is hosted with a db. we should have users and projects and can expand the feature set."

I think someone started with idea and stopped after a few days. lets use that name as the core opensource repo. we have two layers of opensource openDox and openXdox. The openXdox is openDox tuned for use with openXfactory. we will make openDox work to just manage documents and ideas. it will keep the integration with git and notebook lm etc and have all tools that help for document management and ideation. then openXdox will integrate with openXfactory."
>
> Earlier in the same sitting: "We then further pin that down to medxDox and CodeXdox for use in those domain factories. If I install MedxFacotry, then I get a medXdox install running in the installed tenand with its own db."

## What the ruling settles

1. **Two open-source layers, two repositories.** `opensoft/openDox` — the neutral core: a hosted, installable app with its own database; users and projects; document and idea management; git and NotebookLM integration and the document-management/ideation tooling. `opensoft/openXdox` — openDox tuned for openxFactory: the corpus reader, doc-health and lifecycle integration, gates, the apply lane. Domain descendants (`MedxDox`, `codexDox`, …) pin openXdox in the `<Domainx><Product>` form; a domain-factory install brings its own descendant instance with its own database in the tenant.
2. **The name `openDox` is taken deliberately.** `docs/openxdox-naming.md` (ratified 2026-08-13) rejected `openDox` as "taken"; Brett has ruled the existing use dead (a near-empty repo abandoned after days) and accepted the name for the core. The record owes an **Amendment 3** carried by the change that creates the repository: it must state the collision facts as measured today — a GitHub organization `opendox` exists, and small repos named `opendox` exist including one active 2026 project in the adjacent agent-written-docs space — and Brett's acceptance of them.
3. **A departure from the wallet precedent, ruled.** `split-openxwallet-repo` kept the integration seam inside openxFactory; here the integration layer is its own open-source repository (`openXdox`). The seam openxFactory keeps is the corpus itself and its governance; what moves to openXdox is the code that reads it.

## Why this is filed as an issue

It is the governing object for the lane's claims (Rule 1) and the place the ruling lives outside a chat transcript. The engineering record it supersedes in part: `openxdox-install-app-provisioning` (staged 2026-08-14, gate met, exit unraised) and codexFactory #89 (standalone migration, open since 2026-08-25) — both fold into the topic this issue commissions.

CI: scope the changelog app key to main

### Problem

`.github/workflows/changelog.yml` mints a token from `CHANGELOG_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` for a GitHub App that the `main` ruleset names as a bypass actor. Because it is a repository secret rather than an environment secret, it is available to `workflow_dispatch` runs from any ref (which run the workflow file from that ref) and to any `push`-triggered workflow on any branch. `create-github-app-token` is also called without `permission-*` inputs, so the minted token carries every permission the installation has.

Net effect: anyone with push access to any branch (including a leaked fine-grained PAT with `contents` + `workflows` write) can push to `main` without a PR. While the owner is the only writer this is hardening, not an exploit.

### Fix (needs repo-admin settings, so not done in #101)

1. Create a GitHub Environment (e.g. `changelog`) whose deployment branches are restricted to `main`, and move `CHANGELOG_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` (and the app ID if it's a secret) into it.
2. Add `environment: changelog` to the job.
3. Pass `permission-contents: write` to `actions/create-github-app-token` so the token is scoped.

[Bug]: iOS Native App: mTLS Client Certificate Support for WebSocket / URLSession connections

### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

### Is there an existing issue for this?
- [x] I have searched the existing issues.

### Summary
When exposing an OpenClaw instance behind a Reverse Proxy (such as SWAG/Nginx) with **mTLS (Mutual TLS)** enabled (`ssl_verify_client optional` or `on`), the native OpenClaw iOS app fails to connect over cellular/5G and is dropped with an HTTP 444 / 400 error. 

While iOS Safari correctly prompts the user for the installed client certificate (`.p12` profile from Keychain) and establishes a successful connection, the native OpenClaw iOS app's underlying network stack (`URLSessionWebSocketTask`) does not supply the client certificate during the TLS handshake.

### Environment
- **OpenClaw Version:** 2026.9.4
- **Client OS:** iOS 19.x (iPhone / iPad)
- **Deployment:** Reverse Proxy (SWAG / Nginx) with mTLS CA validation.

### Expected Behavior
The native OpenClaw iOS app should either:
1. Allow importing/selecting a client certificate (`.p12` / `.pfx` or via system Keychain) in the app's connection settings, OR
2. Properly implement a `URLSessionDelegate` (`didReceive challenge` with client certificate authentication challenge handling) so iOS can securely pull the client certificate from the device's system keychain during the WebSocket handshake.

### Additional Context
Without native mTLS support in the iOS app, users who want zero-trust perimeter security via mutual TLS are forced to bypass mTLS for mobile app traffic (e.g. relying solely on GeoIP/LAN restrictions), leaving native app users unable to leverage client certificates.

At 15:09:06Z alignment was signed onto this identity-less state. The separate completion ledger still named the run, but it is a different, lower-authority carrier.

The cause is now reproduced at the function boundary: `commands/implement-fix.md` F1 initializes `state` without `session_id`, while full mode includes one. After SubagentStop, `hooks/unified_session_tracker.py` calls `ensure_sentinel_heartbeat(session_id)`. For parseable state without an owner, `lib/pipeline_completion_state.py` treats the owner mismatch as recoverable and atomically replaces the *entire* run-bearing state with `{session_id,recovered,recovered_at}`. A local replay using the shipped `atomic_write_json` and `ensure_sentinel_heartbeat` reproduced the same key loss and `[SENTINEL-HEARTBEAT-MISSING]` result. The exact native filesystem write from the original run was not independently captured, but this is a sufficient deterministic reproducer for the failure class.

An independent bootstrap negative control exposed a second identity gap before specialist work: `verify_state_hmac(state, wrong_session_id)` returned `True`; changing or removing `state['session_id']` also returned `True`. Source inspection confirms `_compute_state_hmac` signs start time, mode, run ID, explicit-invocation flag, alignment fields and nonce, **not session ID**; `verify_state_hmac` uses the per-run secret and treats its `session_id` argument as a legacy fallback. Thus the current HMAC authenticates some run fields but not the owner. Do not describe the whole run identity as signed until owner binding is proven. The full-mode STEP-0 command also attempts an inline `PIPELINE_STATE_FILE=` assignment and the live PreToolUse hook refused it under #557. Later the coordinator hand-wrote the missing identity fields using `atomic_write_json` and re-ran alignment. Supervisor rejected that reconstructed authority and marked the run **INVALID FOR CONTINUATION**. A valid HMAC after a coordinator rewrite proves the write used a signing-capable API, not that the missing identity is authentic. No implementation from that resumed state may be accepted.

Thanks for gocryptfs, it has been solid and I appreciate the care that has clearly gone into it. I package it downstream, via Alpine's `community/gocryptfs`, in a Docker-based encrypted backup tool.

**This is not a CVE report.** Your answer on #973 is correct and I checked it before filing: `govulncheck ./...` at v2.6.1 reports 0 vulnerabilities called, with 22 in required-but-uncalled modules, and `go list -deps ./...` shows no `x/crypto/ssh` anywhere in the build graph. The `x/crypto v0.33.0` scanner noise downstream is a module-granularity artifact, and #1018 already resolves it on `master`.

**What I want to raise is provenance.** Every release asset is built on your machine and signed there by hand, with `package-release-tarballs.bash` stopping at a printed `gpg --detach-sig` hint. Nothing connects a published artifact to a commit except the signature, which attests who uploaded it and not what went into it.

I verified v2.6.1's `src-deps` tarball against the git tag by hand:

- all 206 `.go` files byte-identical
- `go.mod` and `go.sum` identical
- `go mod verify`: all modules verified
- shipped `vendor/` reproduces exactly from a fresh `go mod vendor`

That is a clean result, and better than many projects would give. But it only holds because I did it manually, for one release. Nothing in the process establishes it, a future tarball could diverge from its tag with nothing noticing, and the static binaries cannot be checked this way at all: there is no way for anyone to confirm how they were built.

This matters more than it would for most projects, because Alpine pins and builds the tarball you produce locally rather than the git tag, so your machine is in the supply chain for every distribution that follows Alpine. I have raised that side separately: https://gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/aports/-/issues/18435

**The request:** please consider producing release artifacts in CI, with GitHub build attestations, so what you ship is verifiable against a commit. `ci.yml` already cross-builds static binaries, so the artifacts largely exist; the gap is that releases do not come from them. Signing can stay exactly as it is, done by you, after the fact, on CI-produced tarballs.

If you would ever want CI to sign as well, a dedicated signing subkey of 23A02740 keeps you in control: the primary key stays offline, only the subkey sits in Actions secrets, and it is revocable on its own without touching your identity or asking users to re-trust anything.

If you want a hand with the workflow, I am happy to write it and send a draft PR.

Workboard: expired claims still block all non-owner mutations (verified on main); expired-claim sweep in dispatch not in stable release; token-less owner release undocumented

### Environment
- OpenClaw **2026.8.2 stable (0965053)**, bundled workboard extension (`dist/extensions/workboard/`)
- Cross-checked against `main` on 2026-09-03 (`extensions/workboard/src/store.ts`, `src/store-card-helpers.ts`) — per-gap status marked below
- Single gateway, multi-agent board (multiple agent sessions sharing one board), SQLite store

### Summary
A card that was finished, reviewer-approved and ready to close got deadlocked for ~4 hours by its own **expired** claim. Three related gaps in the claim lifecycle turned a routine reviewer handoff into a board-level blocker. All observations come from a live incident on 2026.8.2; the code paths below were additionally verified against `main`.

### Gap 1 — Expired claims still block every non-owner mutation — **still present on `main`**
The mutation guard (`assertCanMutateClaimedCard` on `main` / `canMutateCard` in the 2026.8.2 dist) never considers `claim.expiresAt`:

```ts
if (claim.ownerId !== ownerId && !safeEqualSecret(token, claim.token)) {
  throw new Error(`card is claimed by ${claim.ownerId}.`);
}
```

After the claim's TTL had passed (2026.8.2), we tested the mutation paths as a non-owner (the reviewer): `workboard_proof`, `workboard_comment`, `workboard_reassign`, `workboard_block`, `workboard_complete` — all rejected with `card is claimed by <owner>` (6/6). Only the owner can act (and see gap 3 for how even that can fail on 2026.8.2).

**Proposed fix:** treat claims with `expiresAt < now` as absent for non-owner mutations — or at minimum include the claim's remaining/expired state in the error so agents know the claim is dead, not active.

### Gap 2 — `workboard_dispatch` sweep of expired claims on non-running cards — **fixed on `main`, missing from 2026.8.2**
On `main`, `dispatch()` (src/store.ts) has a non-status-gated `else if (claimExpired)` branch (`isWorkboardClaimReclaimable`) that clears expired claims on any card, including `review`. On 2026.8.2 stable we observed two dispatch runs with `reclaimed=[]` while an expired claim sat on a `review` card; the sweep only covered `running`. **Ask: ship this in the next stable release** (it resolves the owner-absent deadlock path for review cards).

### Gap 3 — Token-less owner release exists but is undocumented
Claim validation is dual: a passed token must match (`claim token does not match`), and omitting the token while matching `ownerId` is a valid owner release/reclaim/heartbeat — this is what eventually freed our stuck claim (validated live). Two sharp edges on 2026.8.2:

- Passing a transformed/invalid token **fails even for the owner**. We hit this because our secret-redaction middleware rewrote the `token` argument to `***` in tool params — 7 consecutive release attempts failed until we understood omission was the intended path. (The tool-payload redaction itself was since fixed on `main` per #130355's closure; the documentation gap remains.)
- Nothing in the docs states that the token is **optional for owners**, or that a wrong token hard-fails owner operations.

**Proposed fix:** document token-less owner validation (`ownerId` match) for `release`/`reclaim`/`heartbeat`/mutations, and the wrong-token hard-failure.

### Gap 4 — (minor, governance) move/complete events carry no actor attribution — **still present on `main`**
`updateEvent` emits `{ kind: "moved", fromStatus, toStatus }` with no actor field. A board-level "who moved this?" question is unanswerable from the event log. **Proposed fix:** include the acting agent/session id in moved/completed events.

### Proposed fixes (any/all)
1. `assertCanMutateClaimedCard`: expired claims → treated as absent for non-owner mutations (or expiry-aware error message).
2. Ship the `main` dispatch sweep (expired claims on non-running cards) in the next stable release.
3. Docs: token-le

[Program] Independent module delivery: selective publishing through the 4.0 stable release

## Purpose

Ship each Elsa module on its own: a module gets a new version only when it changed, only changed packages publish, dependency floors are honest, and consumers follow one release number. End with a stable 4.0 release from which real upgrades begin.

This is a planning program. It adds no new design: every decision below is already recorded, and the implementation issues already exist. Its job is to hold the order and the gates.

## Decisions of record

- [ADR 0067](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/blob/main/docs/adr/0067-package-versioning-uses-two-lines-with-computed-patch.md) (as amended in #1977): two version lines, a computed patch, selective publishing, and last-published state kept on a `publish-state` branch.
- Spec 149 (the canonical dependency map) and spec 150 (version computation).
- #1976: migrations are regenerated until 4.0 ships stable, then frozen as baselines.

## Workstreams

### A1 — Version numbers and selective publishing ([#1144](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/1144))
- **Phase 1 (done 2026-09-26):**
  - #2076: no hand-written project versions.
  - #2077: the one reviewed Line A list and its closure guard.
  - #2075: the canonical dependency map.
  - #2078: public-API tracking on Line A.
- **Phase 2 (dry run; publishes nothing):**
  - #2079: the version calculator.
  - #2080: pack-time changes, meaning ranges with an upper bound, fingerprints and labels.
- **Phase 3 (touches public feeds):**
  - #2081: bootstrap the publish-state record.
  - #2082: selective `packages.yml`.
  - #2083: the repair workflow.
  - #2084: Workbench's Elsa shares in CI-built images.

### A2 — Clean host ([#1145](https://github.com/elsa-workflows/elsa-foundation/issues/1145))
Foundation.Host shares the ten Line A contracts with its features, as Workbench already does. This depends on A1, because a source-built host can't declare Elsa package versions until per-package versioning exists.

### A3 — The 4.0 stable release
- #1976: freeze each module's `Initial` migration as its baseline, with a guard that stops a shipped migration being edited.
- #2085: the release cut: the full surface gate, release promotion and the release manifest.

## Sequence and gates

1. **M1: versions computed.** Deliver #2079 and #2080. Output is inspectable, and nothing is pushed.
2. **Gate: the owner creates the `publish-state` ruleset.** Settings: restrict deletions, block force pushes, no bypass, targeting branch `publish-state`. Nothing in Phase 3 starts before it exists, and each Phase 3 step is confirmed with the owner before it runs.
3. **M2: selective publishing live on the preview feed.** Delivers #2081–#2084.
4. **M3: Foundation.Host shares Line A.** Delivers #1145.
5. **M4: 4.0 stable.** Delivers #1976 and #2085.

## Relationship to the cluster rollout program (#2093)

4.0 does **not** wait for the cluster schema-rollout program, #2093. Until 4.0, migrations are regenerated, so there are no real between-version schema upgrades to coordinate. That program must land before the first schema-changing release *after* 4.0. Until then, 4.0.x release notes state that schema-changing updates are single-host or coordinated by hand.

## Acceptance

- A module whose files did not change keeps its version and is not republished.
- A changed module publishes with a computed version and honest, upper-bounded dependency ranges.
- Consumers can pin one release number, and the release manifest maps it to package versions.
- Every host shares Line A.
- 4.0 ships with frozen migration baselines, guarded against edits.

### Description

### Summary

The Laya Engine FastAPI server binds to `127.0.0.1:8420` by default and protects itself mainly through TrustedHostMiddleware plus a restricted CORS allowlist. Most REST endpoints (events, cards, settings, actions, egress, workspace, audit, and others) do not require any authentication token or shared secret. As a result, any process running on the same machine can call these endpoints very freely!!

### Why this is a problem

Because the API is unauthenticated, a malicious or compromised local process does not need to break out of the browser sandbox or forge Host headers to interact with the engine. It can:

- Ingest arbitrary events via `POST /events`
- Read, modify, archive, or delete cards and related data
- Change settings, spaces, rules, and budget configuration
- Trigger egress actions (send email, post to Slack, comment on PRs, etc.) once staged
- Call sensitive MCP management routes such as token reveal and config updates

TrustedHostMiddleware and the CORS list reduce the chance of a pure DNS rebinding attack from a remote page. They do not stop other local processes, browser extensions with local network access, or any future change that widens the bind address.

### Impact

An attacker who can run code on the user’s machine (malware, a compromised dependency, a malicious IDE extension, etc.) gains full control over the engine’s data and outbound actions without needing the OS keychain or the Tauri UI. Because Laya holds OAuth tokens, API keys (via keychain), and notification content from Gmail, Slack, Jira, GitHub and similar services, this expands the blast radius of any local compromise.

## Summary
Add `EpssKevClient`, a network adapter implementing `ExploitabilityRepository` via batched EPSS lookups against FIRST.org and a single CISA KEV catalog fetch, soft-failing on any error so a failed exploitability lookup never aborts SBOM generation.

Part of #812

## Why
- Distinct architectural layer (`src/adapters/outbound/network/`) from the port it implements (#876) — the only subtask that touches actual HTTP calls, so network-specific concerns (batching, rate limiting, timeouts) stay isolated from the trait definition and its consumers.

## Scope
**In**
- `EpssKevClient` implementing `ExploitabilityRepository`.
- EPSS: batched `GET https://api.first.org/data/v1/epss?cve=CVE-A,CVE-B,...`, capped at `OsvClient::MAX_BATCH_SIZE` (100) to bound URL length.
- KEV: single `GET` of the CISA KEV JSON feed, parsed once into a `HashSet<String>` of CVE IDs for membership checks.
- Only IDs matching `^CVE-\d{4}-\d+ are looked up; non-matching IDs (e.g. GHSA-only findings) are skipped.
- Soft-fail per `CheckAbandonedPackagesUseCase`'s per-package soft-fail convention: a failed fetch never aborts the run.
- Reuse `OsvClient`'s existing rate-limit/timeout constants (30s timeout, 100ms/10 req/sec).

**Out**
- GHSA→CVE alias resolution — explicit v1 limitation per parent Issue #812, not in scope here or anywhere in this split.
- Wiring into `GenerateSbomUseCase`/CLI (next subtask)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `EpssKevClient` batch-fetches EPSS scores for CVE-pattern IDs only, respecting the 100-item batch cap
- [ ] `EpssKevClient` fetches the CISA KEV catalog once and checks membership via a `HashSet`
- [ ] A failed EPSS or KEV fetch soft-fails: `exploitability: None` for affected vulnerabilities, run continues
- [ ] Rate limiting and timeout match `OsvClient`'s existing constants exactly (no new tunables introduced)

node: build listen and RPC addresses with net.JoinHostPort so IPv6 literals work

## Summary

The listen addresses are built by string formatting rather than `net.JoinHostPort`, so an IPv6 literal cannot be used as a listen host: `"::1"` becomes `::1:35995`, which `net.Listen` rejects with `too many colons in address`. `net.JoinHostPort("::1", "35995")` gives `[::1]:35995`, which listens. Writing the bracketed form `[::1]` into `ListenHost` happens to work today because the formatting passes the brackets through; a `JoinHostPort` change must strip an existing bracket pair first so that workaround keeps working. The same pattern is used for the RPC endpoints. Pre-existing; raised by edgepillar on #94, which makes `--host` reach the P2P listen host and so makes the form of that value matter on the command line as well as in the file.

## Where

- `node/node.go`, the switcher's `ListenAddr`: `fmt.Sprintf("%v:%v", netConfig.ListenAddr, netConfig.ListenPort)`.
- `node/config.go`, `HTTPEndpoint` and `WSEndpoint`: `fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d", host, port)`.
- The legacy backend passes the joined string to `net.Listen` and to discovery's UDP listener; the libp2p backend splits it again with `net.SplitHostPort` in `parseListenAddr`, which handles the bracketed form and already accepts an IPv6 address.

## Backend difference

`parseListenAddr` in `p2p/libp2p/server.go` accepts only an empty host, `0.0.0.0` or an IP literal and rejects hostnames, while the legacy backend resolves `localhost`. A hostname in `ListenHost` therefore works before the transport spork and fails after it. Worth a line in the flag usage or the config documentation; #94 states the accepted forms in the `--host` usage text.

## Proposed change

Use `net.JoinHostPort(strings.Trim(host, "[]"), strconv.Itoa(port))` in the three places above. It is a no-op for IPv4 and hostnames, brackets a raw IPv6 literal, and keeps the already-bracketed form working. A table test over `"0.0.0.0"`, `"127.0.0.1"`, `"localhost"`, `"::"` and `"::1"` that checks `net.Listen` (or `net.ResolveTCPAddr`) accepts each built address would pin it; the libp2p side can be covered by `parseListenAddr` on the same inputs.

# Hardening: cap the reports API pagination, and add HTTP timeouts / narrow defaults

A couple of defense-in-depth gaps I noticed while reading the code. None are
exploitable by themselves, but they're cheap to close — especially while #153 is
adding OAuth to the dashboard.

## 1. `/api/reports?limit=` has no upper bound (MCP tool caps the same query)

`internal/api/server.go` parses `limit` with `strconv.Atoi` and passes it
straight to the storage query:

```go
limit, err := strconv.Atoi(r.URL.Query().Get("limit"))
```

There is no clamp. The sibling MCP tool `getReports` already caps the same
query at 100 rows (`internal/mcp/tools.go:107-109`) — the HTTP API should do the
same. With no cap, one unauthenticated request against a large database buffers
the entire result set into memory before responding (a 5000-row table is ~1 MiB
per request). Rate-limiting or auth (once #153 lands) doesn't fully cover it,
since a single response is already the whole table.

**Suggested fix:** clamp to the same ceiling the MCP tool uses.

```go
const maxAPILimit = 100
limit, err := strconv.Atoi(r.URL.Query().Get("limit"))
if err != nil || limit <= 0 || limit > maxAPILimit {
    limit = maxAPILimit
}
```

## 2. Dashboard `http.Server` has no timeouts (the MCP server already does)

`internal/mcp/server.go:182-185` sets `ReadTimeout: 15s`, `WriteTimeout: 15s`,
`IdleTimeout: 60s`. The dashboard server in `internal/api/server.go` sets none of
them. Every TCP connection can therefore be held open indefinitely, which is a
slow-loris-shaped risk on the operator-facing surface and a trivial resource
exhaustion vector if the port is ever exposed. Copying the same values would
make the two servers consistent.

## 3. Default bind + CORS should be tightened once #153 ships auth

- `SERVER_HOST` defaults to `""` (all interfaces). The README already warns to
  keep the port behind a reverse proxy or VPN, but binding loopback by default
  (`127.0.0.1`) would make that the safe path instead of the required one.
- `Allow-Origin` is `*`. Fine for a read-only API with no auth, but once #153
  adds OAuth sessions a wildcard origin is a credential-inclusion risk, so it
  should be narrowed as part of that work.

Happy to split these into separate issues if that's easier to triage — I kept
them together because they're the same "harden the operator-facing surface while
auth is being added" theme.

Frontend security review dated 27 September 2026, against commit `6eaa8a7ce9a42565f58a0e77df71c67b6b2c5d6e`.

**Priority:** P2 / medium availability risk; production impact and edge mitigation remain unverified.

## Finding and remediation

**Primary locations:** `hacksnap/web/lib/data.ts:175–184`, `hacksnap/web/app/api/stories/[id]/route.ts:4–8`, and `hacksnap/web/lib/stories-api.ts:4–18,36–43`.

Every successful detail request calls `getStory()`, including `hacksnap_ranked_stories`, recent rank history, and the all-retained-history metrics query. `publicStory()` omits all these ranking fields. The route is explicitly dynamic, and its local 200 response supplies no explicit cache lifetime. React's `cache()` here does not provide a persistent cross-request API cache.

The ranking view computes `row_number()` over all eligible stories before filtering the requested story. A local `EXPLAIN` showed `Subquery Scan on r → Filter (r.hn_id = …) → WindowAgg → Sort → scans/joins across candidate stories`. The history metrics CTE also reads all retained observations for that story; its 168-point chart limit only bounds the returned chart. Three valid calls to the detail handler invoked three data reads.

**Impact:** Repeated anonymous requests for an existing ID can repeatedly trigger work proportional to retained data, consume the one-connection pool in each instance, and increase database load and hosting costs. Statement and connection timeouts limit individual waits but do not limit request rate or aggregate work. This is an availability risk established by data flow and query planning, not a measured production denial of service. Deployment-level rate limits were not inspected.

**Fix:** Give the public API a minimal parameterized query that selects only its response fields. Add an explicit bounded cache for public responses and safe negative results, and verify rate limits at the deployed edge, including origin access. Bound expensive rendering paths separately where freshness requires uncached responses.

**Related exposure to address in the same work:** `/markdown` and `/feed.xml` explicitly disable response caching; archive/category pagination permits up to page 9,999,999, translating to a very deep SQL `OFFSET`. A local `/archive?page=9999999` returned 404 only after entering the database path. Prefer cursor pagination or a verified maximum page before querying. The repository's Cloudflare scanner Worker filters selected probe paths; it does not throttle these legitimate routes. External WAF rules could reduce this risk and must be verified before assigning deployment-specific severity.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The detail API selects only fields in its response and does not compute unused ranking/history aggregates.
- [ ] Public detail responses and safe negative responses have a documented, bounded caching policy; failures remain uncacheable.
- [ ] Invalid IDs are rejected before database access, and current public response fields remain compatible.
- [ ] Archive/category pagination cannot trigger arbitrary deep offsets without a justified bound or cursor design.
- [ ] Review freshness and abuse controls for Markdown and RSS, preserving content negotiation.
- [ ] Verify deployed rate limits and direct-origin restrictions; document any remaining exposure.
- [ ] Compare query plans and repeated-request database work with representative synthetic data. Do not load-test production as part of the regression suite.

Escrow `deposit` accepts zero/negative/uncapped amounts and post-deadline deposits

## Context
Soroban escrow contract, `contracts/soroban/contracts/escrow/src/lib.rs:37-55`.

## Problem
`deposit` has no `amount > 0` check, no per-deposit cap, accepts deposits after `target` has been reached, and the deadline boundary uses `>=` (off by one). `platform_fee` is also never validated against the total.

## Impact
Invalid or abusive states: zero deposits, donations after funding ends, overshoot beyond target with no cap.

## Suggested solution
Validate `amount > 0`, enforce a per-deposit cap, reject deposits after the campaign is funded or past deadline (with clear boundary semantics), and validate fee amounts.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Reject zero/negative amounts
- [ ] Reject deposits after target reached or deadline passed (exact boundary)
- [ ] Enforce a per-deposit maximum
- [ ] Validate platform fee against deposit amount

Registre des executions automatisees — qui a fait quoi, et quand

Le compte GitHub est **partagé**. Une action ne dit donc pas qui l'a faite, et l'attribution après coup est impossible : le 21/08, trois sessions ont attribué à Bertrand du travail qui n'était pas le sien, et six issues ont été fermées sur une preuve fabriquée sans qu'on puisse dire d'où venait la fermeture.

**Ce fil est le registre.** Chaque exécution planifiée y dépose son compte rendu : quel agent, quelle tâche, quand, et ce qu'elle a touché.

## Les agents planifiés

| tâche launchd | agent | cadence | ce qu'il a le droit de faire |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fr.mozaiklabs.tune-tri` | `tune-tri` | forum modifié, contrôle toutes les 10 min | **créer** des issues, commenter. Jamais fermer, jamais répondre à un testeur, jamais toucher une branche |
| `fr.mozaiklabs.tune-tag` | `tune-retour` puis `tune-parole` | nouveau tag publié | fermer des issues **avec preuve**, écrire aux testeurs |

## La règle qui vaut pour tous

**Ne jamais présenter comme vérification ce qui n'en est pas une.** Une preuve par contenu cite le fichier **du correctif** et un marqueur qui lui est propre — pas un mot du domaine grepé à l'aveugle. `Refs #N` n'est pas `Closes #N`. Et jamais de fermeture en lot : une issue, une lecture.

## Pour ceux qui lisent ce dépôt

Si une action vous surprend, cherchez-la ici d'abord. Si elle n'y figure pas, elle vient d'une session interactive — pas d'un agent planifié.

## Summary

PR #596 adds `every_sent_header_is_one_the_gateway_allow_list_admits`, presented as a guard that
keeps the harness client in step with the gateway's header allow-list. The test is **unsound in two
independent ways**, and between them it gives false assurance about a class of defect it appears to
prevent.

Found by root while reviewing #596. #597 is the companion report; this issue is the part that is
actually fixable without a cross-repo contract change.

## Defect 1: the list contains a name the gateway does not admit

```rust
    const ALLOWED: &[&str] = &[
        "authorization", "connection", "content-length", "content-type", "host",
        "x-mcp-request-id", "x-mcp-session-id", "x-sts2-instance-id", "x-sts2-caller-id",
        "x-sts2-session-id", "x-sts2-lease-id", "x-sts2-lease-epoch",
        "x-sts2-workflow-boot-epoch", "x-sts2-correlation-id",
        "x-sts2-capabilities-version", "x-sts2-episode-profile", "x-sts2-peer-token",
        "x-sts2-recovery-capability",
        // Admitted by the gateway as a non-gateway header.
        "idempotency-key",
    ];
```

The first 18 names are an exact transcription of `header_is_allowed` in
`sts2-gateway`'s `crates/gateway/src/bin/runtime_support/service_authorization.rs`. The 19th is
not in it, and the comment describing it is false — there is no "non-gateway header" category, and
the gateway does not exempt anything from its own check.

A transcription that is 18/18 correct and then adds an invented entry is worse than no
transcription: a future reader diffing the two lists sees a name the gateway lacks and reasonably
concludes the gateway gained it.

## Defect 2: the test never builds the request whose header it is policing

```rust
fn head() -> String {
    request_head("127.0.0.1:1".parse()..., "test-token", "POST", "/v1/workflows", None, 2)
}
```

The fifth argument is the idempotency key, and it is `None`. `request_head` only emits
`Idempotency-Key` in the `Some` branch, so the test asserts over a request that never carries the
header. The fabricated allow-list entry is unreachable from this test: it cannot fail, and it
cannot detect the header it was added to describe.

This matters because the header is genuinely emitted on a real code path —
`request_json_with_idempotency_key` has nine call sites. The test's shape would not notice if a
future change routed that client at the gateway, where the header is refused with
`400 unsupported_header`.

Removing `Idempotency-Key` from `request_head` would be the obvious "fix" and it is **wrong**. It is
required on the hop these callers actually use:

- `http_routes_memory_owner.rs:214` — `idempotency_key(request)` returns

- All nine callers are policy-owner mutations (propose / approve / adopt), which route through it.

  `"in": "header", "required": true` on those operations.

Those callers connect to the harness runtime's own `management_listen` address, not to the gateway,
so they never meet `header_is_allowed` at all. Deleting the header would convert nine passing
mutations into `400`s.

## Problem

The trufflehog step uses the default shallow `checkout`, so it cannot scan history beyond the current commit; a secret committed and later removed would go undetected.

## Recommended change

- Add `fetch-depth: 0` to the checkout used by the trufflehog job.

## Acceptance criteria

- The checkout in that job uses `fetch-depth: 0`.
- The scan runs over full history.

## Guideline

Secret scanning is only as good as the history it can see.

## 🎯 Context & Goal
Running containerized Node.js applications as `root` user inside production Docker containers is a critical security vulnerability: if an attacker achieves remote code execution via an npm vulnerability, they inherit root container privileges and can potentially escape the container or compromise the host filesystem.

Production Docker containers must follow the principle of least privilege, running under an unprivileged user (e.g. `USER node`), utilizing multi-stage builds to exclude build tools and devDependencies, and including health checks.

This issue refactors `backend/Dockerfile` into a multi-stage Docker build. Stage 1 compiles dependencies; Stage 2 copies only production node_modules and source files into a minimal `node:20-alpine` runtime image running under the `node` user with a native Docker `HEALTHCHECK` directive.

## 📂 Target Files
- `backend/Dockerfile → multi-stage production container definition`
- `backend/.dockerignore → exclude tests, logs, and dev files`
- `docker-compose.yml → update container references`

## 📋 Implementation Tasks
- [ ] **Task**: Implement Stage 1 (`builder`): `npm ci` installing all dependencies
- [ ] **Task**: Implement Stage 2 (`runner`): minimal `node:20-alpine`, copy production `node_modules` and source files
- [ ] **Task**: Switch execution user to `USER node` before running `node server.js`
- [ ] **Task**: Add `HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=5s CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1`
- [ ] **Task**: Test build locally and verify container image size is reduced below 150MB

## 🛠️ Technical Guidance
```dockerfile
# Multi-stage production Dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

FROM node:20-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
USER node
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Orphan sweep liveness keys on discovery.lock, which nothing in-tree writes and NEAT-AI spells .discovery.lock (src/discovery_cleanup.rs::is_directory_orphaned)

<!-- finding-id: SEC-bbe3f392d7aa -->
<!-- cwe: CWE-706 -->

The orphan sweep's only liveness signal is a file named `discovery.lock`
(`discovery_cleanup.rs::LOCK_FILE_NAME`), but **no production code in this
crate writes it**, and the one known host — NEAT-AI — writes
**`.discovery.lock`** (leading dot) into each session directory. A host that
calls the FFI `clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs` on NEAT-AI's `.discovery/`
root therefore reads every live session as orphaned and deletes it with its
in-flight data. Severity low (NEAT-AI does not bind the FFI sweep today, so no
live path), confidence high (both names verified, deletion reproduced).

Found by the chunk 11 security sweep, Issue #2234 (tracker #2095).

## Why this matters

- `discovery_cleanup.rs::is_directory_orphaned` treats a directory as
  abandoned exactly when `<dir>/discovery.lock` is absent;
  `clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs_since` then removes every such directory
  older than the scan start.
- `LOCK_FILE_NAME` has no in-tree production writer — only tests create it.
  The contract lives in the caller: `docs/FFI_API.md` § "Orphaned Directory
  Sweep" and the doc comment on `ffi/utilities.rs::clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs`
  say a subdirectory "is considered orphaned when it has no
  `discovery.lock` file".
- NEAT-AI `src/discovery/DiscoveryCleanup.ts` declares
  `const LOCK_FILE_NAME = ".discovery.lock"` and writes it from
  `createDiscoveryLockFile`. The two names never match, so the ownership
  signal the sweep relies on is unenforced: nothing in either repo checks
  that the writer and the reader agree.
- The #1903 age floor only protects directories touched *after* the scan
  starts; a long-running session whose directory was last modified earlier
  gets no protection.

Reproduced against the current tree: a `.discovery/<uuid>/` holding only
`.discovery.lock` is swept with `removed: 1` and the directory is gone.

## Attacker model

No attacker needed — this is an integrity/availability defect triggered by
ordinary host behaviour. The trigger is a host (today's NEAT-AI, or a future
refactor that adopts the Rust sweep in place of its TypeScript one) invoking
the FFI sweep on a root its own sessions populate.

## Trigger

`clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs({"baseDir": ".discovery"})` while NEAT-AI
sessions are running under `.discovery/<creature-uuid>/`.

## Exploit sketch

1. NEAT-AI starts a discovery session: `.discovery/<uuid>/` with
   `.discovery.lock` inside, data being written.
2. Any caller runs the FFI sweep on `.discovery`.
3. `is_directory_orphaned` probes `discovery.lock` → `NotFound` → orphaned;
   the directory predates the scan, so the age floor passes it; the #1903
   re-check probes the same wrong name and passes it too.
4. `fs::remove_dir_all` deletes the live session's recording.

## Suggested fix

Make the sweep fail closed on either spelling: treat a directory as in use
when `discovery.lock` **or** `.discovery.lock` is present (in
`is_directory_orphaned`, and in the `assert_is_discovery_dir` contents
check), document both in `docs/FFI_API.md`, and note the host's spelling
beside `LOCK_FILE_NAME`. The fix ships
`tests/issue_2256_orphan_sweep_host_lock_name.rs`, which **fails before the
fix**: a `.discovery/<uuid>/` holding only `.discovery.lock` must survive
`clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs` (the session directory is the canary) with
`removed == 0`.

Contradiction check: Difficulty rewards versus competency progression

## Goal

Run a bounded contradiction check before importing difficulty-tagged permanent personnel stat rewards, so high-risk assignment incentives remain compatible with Containment Protocol's authoritative competency, specialization, standing, and difficulty models.

## Scope

* evaluate the proposed pattern where harder assignments directly grant flat permanent personnel-stat increases in addition to standing/fame rewards
* compare that pattern against JamesJedi420/containment-protocol#1068 competency/practice progression and current specialization-growth rules
* verify JamesJedi420/containment-protocol#3894 difficulty input ownership and determine which authoritative progression input, if any, may legitimately consume difficulty as a modifier
* preserve completed JamesJedi420/containment-protocol#3282 risk-weighted standing rewards as the existing standing/fame solution rather than recreating it
* test whether risk-adjusted progression can be represented as bounded practice quality, experience weighting, learning opportunity, or another existing progression input without introducing a generic flat-stat ladder
* test exploit pressure from farming nominally high-difficulty work, repeatable trivialized assignments, party-size manipulation, or other ways difficulty labels could become a permanent-stat optimization loop
* determine whether the imported rule should be rejected, translated into existing progression semantics, or requires a genuinely missing implementation boundary

## Constraints

* contradiction-check only until disposition is approved
* no implementation child or new reward umbrella may be created from this candidate before this check closes
* no reopening completed JamesJedi420/containment-protocol#3282 standing rewards
* no parallel level, OVR, generic stat, or difficulty-progression system
* no assumption that a difficulty label itself proves greater learning value
* preserve deterministic progression and existing partial-observability rules

## Required checks

* JamesJedi420/containment-protocol#1068 unified skill, progression, and competency framework
* JamesJedi420/containment-protocol#3894 canonical assignment/operation difficulty inputs
* current specialization/advancement rules, including the no-generic-flat-growth boundary reconciled against JamesJedi420/containment-protocol#1737
* completed JamesJedi420/containment-protocol#3282 risk-weighted agency-standing rewards
* repeatability/farming and difficulty-classification stability
* player-facing explainability if any progression modifier survives

## Acceptance criteria

* the check states whether flat +stat rewards are rejected or translated into an existing progression input
* any surviving translation identifies one authoritative owner and does not duplicate standing/fame rewards
* farming/repeatability risks and difficulty-label stability are explicitly tested
* no hidden generic power score or parallel progression ladder is introduced
* the result identifies whether existing issues fully contain the solution or a genuinely missing bounded child is required
* final disposition is recorded as reject, fold/update existing owner, or reconcile a new bounded implementation issue

## Completion rule

Complete only when the candidate has one explicit CP-native disposition and the authoritative progression/difficulty owner is identified. Until then, downstream implementation remains held.

## Ownership

Design/reconciliation first; Codex implementation only if a bounded CP-compatible mechanic survives the check.

Spécification de #38, écrite à partir du cadrage du 15 septembre 2026 (Q1 à Q38, résumé en commentaire de #38), de l'ADR 0014 et du glossaire (#390), et de quatre choix faits le 26 septembre 2026 : les points de test, l'endroit où le téléphone masque les numéros, l'ordre du consentement et la publication de l'ADR.

## Problem Statement

Quelqu'un qui arrive sur Messagr ne sait pas lesquels de ses proches y sont déjà. Rien ne le lui dit, et rien ne doit le lui dire sans son accord : Messagr promet de ne demander aucun numéro et de n'aspirer aucun carnet d'adresses.

Retrouver un proche passe donc aujourd'hui par une autre messagerie. Il faut lui demander s'il utilise Messagr, lui envoyer un lien d'invitation, puis attendre qu'il l'ouvre dans l'heure. Un proche déjà sur Messagr ne peut pas être invité autrement : l'invitation par lien est la seule porte, et elle suppose un autre canal.

La spécification produit demande une découverte privée des contacts (§4.2, §6.3, écran 29), et la spécification cryptographique n'en admet qu'une qui n'apprenne pas au service qui cherche qui (§8.3). Le porteur veut qu'elle soit la dernière fonctionnalité livrée avant une diffusion large en magasin.

## Solution

Le « + » de la liste ouvre une feuille à deux entrées : « Inviter quelqu'un », le geste d'aujourd'hui, et « Retrouver mes contacts ».

« Retrouver mes contacts » ouvre un écran de consentement qui dit, en cinq points, ce que la découverte fait du carnet et du numéro, avec deux boutons de même poids : « Continuer » et « Pas maintenant ». Renoncer ne fait rien partir du téléphone.

Continuer mène au numéro. L'écran dit si le pays de ce numéro est ouvert et quel fournisseur enverra le SMS, puis un code reçu par SMS prouve que le numéro est à la personne. Le téléphone propose le code de lui-même, et on peut toujours le taper. La personne est alors trouvable : « Numéro prouvé », pour 28 jours.

Vient ensuite la recherche. Un rappel d'une ligne, avec un seul bouton « Continuer », précède la demande d'accès au carnet du système. Le téléphone fait masquer par le service les numéros de ses fiches, sans que le service puisse les lire. Il télécharge la liste des comptes trouvables, masqués de la même façon, et compare lui-même. Il montre d'abord les contacts déjà sur Messagr, sous le nom de leur fiche, puis les autres.

Pour un contact trouvé, « Inviter » envoie une invitation qui arrive dans Messagr, sans lien. Elle vaut sept jours, et le nom de la fiche remplit d'avance le nom donné. Le compte du destinataire reste caché tant qu'il n'a pas accepté.

Pour un contact absent, « Inviter par SMS » ouvre la messagerie du téléphone avec un texte déjà rédigé et un lien valable trois jours, pour cette seule personne. Le service ne voit pas ce numéro. « Autre moyen » ouvre la feuille de partage habituelle.

Chez le destinataire, le téléphone est réveillé sans rien nommer, et l'invitation apparaît en tête de la liste. Un appui ouvre l'écran d'invitation de §13.3, qui affiche :

- « Se présente comme » suivi du nom que l'inviteur se donne ;
- « Paul (dans votre carnet) » quand le numéro prouvé de l'inviteur figure dans ce carnet ;
- deux actions de même rang, « Rejoindre » et « Refuser », plus « Refuser et bloquer ».

L'inviteur n'apprend jamais un refus : pour lui, l'invitation expire au septième jour, comme si personne ne l'avait vue.

Dans les Réglages, « Être trouvable » montre le numéro et l'état de la preuve, et permet de la renouveler ou de retirer le numéro. À partir du 21e jour, Messagr propose le renouvellement à chaque ouverture. Au 28e jour sans renouvellement, la personne cesse d'être trouvable et de pouvoir chercher, et Messagr le lui dit.

Changer la clé de masquage

## Parent

#392

## What to build

Une fois par an, la clé de masquage change sans un SMS de plus. Les deux clés servent ensemble 28 jours, chaque preuve renouvelée passe sur la nouvelle, puis l'ancienne est détruite. Les appareils voient la nouvelle clé publiée et refont une fois leur comparaison. Ce jour-là, le service leur accorde une rallonge de quota.

Après un vol ou une perte, la bascule est immédiate : l'ancienne clé cesse de servir, et les comptes trouvables cessent de l'être jusqu'à leur prochaine preuve. Une phrase le leur dit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Pendant que deux clés sont en service, l'annuaire porte les entrées sous l'une et l'autre. Une preuve renouvelée passe sur la nouvelle clé, avec son compteur de recherche.
- [ ] Au bout de 28 jours, l'ancienne clé est détruite, et ses entrées quittent l'annuaire.
- [ ] Un appareil qui voit un nouveau numéro de clé refait sa comparaison une fois. Le service lui accorde une rallonge ponctuelle le jour du changement.
- [ ] Lors d'une bascule d'urgence, l'ancienne clé cesse aussitôt de servir. Les comptes trouvables cessent de l'être et lisent la phrase qui le dit, dans les sept langues.
- [ ] La documentation d'exploitation décrit les deux gestes, pas à pas.
- [ ] Tests des routes et du module, avec une horloge contrôlée.

[Feature]: Adaptive test-time compute for Swarm populations

## Relationship to #155442 — 2026-09-27

This is now a **separate follow-up policy surface**. #155442 has been narrowed to the generic bounded candidate/verifier launch contract tracked by #156632 and does not contain the energetic/JEV population controller.

This issue should not block review/landing of the generic bounded-launch seam. The archived full composition remains available on `zozo123/openclaw:archive/liquid-adaptive-test-time-compute-full-2026-09-27` for future policy/plugin work.

---

### Summary

Add **adaptive test-time compute for Swarm** so a population of agents can use heterogeneous reasoning/search budgets and converge toward exact verifier-ready candidates, instead of treating every child as an equally expensive static worker.

This is the population-control half of #155442. The bounded verifier/admission contract is tracked separately in #156632.

### Problem to solve

OpenClaw already supports per-child `model`, `thinking`, and `fastMode`, but those choices are static inputs. A multi-agent run has no search-only control layer that can react to the state of the population.

That creates several concrete problems at scale:

- raw agent count is confused with independent search capacity even when trajectories are highly correlated;
- a stuck population can keep spending expensive reasoning on the same basin instead of increasing diversity;
- high disagreement/uncertainty cannot selectively receive deeper compute;
- resource pressure cannot suppress low-value launches before dispatch;
- promising search trajectories have no explicit transition from broad exploration into an exact candidate that can be independently verified.

The missing abstraction is not “more agents.” It is **where the next unit of test-time compute should go**.

### Proposed solution

A search-only population controller over caller-supplied/trusted per-agent observations:

```text
X_t = {energy_i, temperature_i, mobility_i, novelty_i, evidence_i,
       disagreement_i, correlation_i, susceptibility_i, pressure_i}_i

X_t -> assess local regime -> recommend bounded action -> existing launch owner -> X_(t+1)
```

Keep **energy** and **temperature** separate:

- energy = reasoning/tool/compute intensity;
- temperature = exploratory freedom / perturbation / diversity.

Allow local regimes to coexist:

- `gas` — broad decorrelated exploration
- `liquid` — mobile search with partial coordination
- `critical` — disagreement/susceptibility makes more measurement/depth valuable
- `crystal` — stable evidence-rich candidate ready to freeze
- `glass` — expensive but correlated low-mobility search
- `jammed` — resource pressure dominates useful search
- `unknown` — insufficient telemetry

Search-only actions:

- `measure`
- `deepen`
- `reheat`
- `freeze`
- `drain`
- `hold`

The action is applied only to the **next native launch** through existing owners. It can change reasoning budget/search posture or suppress a jammed launch, but it cannot grant tools, credentials, sandbox exemptions, approval, publish, merge, or deploy authority.

Also expose a diagnostic correlation heuristic:

```text
N_effective = N / (1 + (N - 1) * rho)
```

so 100 highly correlated agents are not treated as 100 independent trajectories.

When a candidate reaches a freeze/crystal state, the exact-candidate verifier boundary from #156632 provides the deterministic convergence step.

### Why this is a current OpenClaw product direction

OpenClaw v2026.9.6 introduced per-agent typed Decision Models, including the TypeSafe/Jev path. That establishes decision/model heterogeneity at the individual-agent level. This issue is the next control layer: **allocate test-time compute across a population based on measured/caller-supplied search state**.

This is also consistent with current OpenClaw triage precedent:

- #52803 — multi-agent/subagent orchestration improvement — is **P2** even though its own impact section says it is

bug: MintedKey.GoString prints the credential digest, so %#v writes a verification oracle to any log

## What happens

`application.MintedKey` redacts the one-time token from every formatting verb. `String()` returns `minted key <id> (token redacted)`, and `MarshalJSON` refuses outright. `GoString()` — the `%#v` path — redacts `Token` but prints `Digest` in full:

```go
// apps/console-api/internal/application/identity.go
func (k MintedKey) GoString() string {
	return fmt.Sprintf("application.MintedKey{Key: %s, Token: redacted, Digest: %s}", k.Key.ID, k.Digest.Hex())
}
```

`Digest` is the SHA-256 of the key's secret. The field's own comment says:

```go
// Digest is the recorded form of Token's secret — not secret material
// itself, and therefore the part that may be delivered onward.
```

## What should happen instead

The claim "not secret material itself" is right in the sense that matters for authentication — the digest cannot be used to authenticate, only to *verify a candidate*. That is exactly the property that makes it worth not printing.

`identity.Secret` is treated with care everywhere it appears: `String`, `GoString` and a refusing `MarshalText`, plus a mechanically enforced rule in `internal/arch/secrets_test.go` that it may never be a struct field. `identity.Digest` gets none of that, and the one place its hex is rendered it is rendered deliberately and in a way `%#v` reaches implicitly.

Concretely: with the digest in hand, an attacker holding a candidate `gw_<key-id>_<secret>` string can confirm it with one SHA-256 rather than needing to authenticate. Anything that reaches `%#v` on a `MintedKey` — a debug statement, a structured logger that formats with `%+v`/`%#v`, a test failure message that dumps a struct — puts a verification oracle into whatever sink that is.

This is observed behaviour of the code on `main`, not an observed leak: no caller on `main` currently formats a `MintedKey`, because no HTTP surface mints a key yet. The gap is that the redaction guarantee is uneven across the three verbs, and `MintedKey`'s docblock claims the guarantee is uniform:

```go
// String redacts: a mint result is exactly the value a debug line prints
// wholesale, and its Token field is the one copy of the credential anyone
// will ever hold. Every fmt verb that renders a value (%v, %+v, %s, %q)
// goes through here and shows the key, never the token.
```

`%#v` is the one verb that does not show "the key, never the token and never anything else about the credential".

## Steps to reproduce

1. `cd apps/console-api`
2. `sed -n '/^\/\/ String redacts/,/^}/p' internal/application/identity.go` — read `String` and `GoString`.
3. `grep -n "Digest" internal/domain/identity/keymaterial.go` — note the type and that it is `fmt.Stringer`/`hex`-renderable.
4. Note that `%#v` on a `MintedKey` routes to `GoString`, which emits the digest hex.

## Environment

- Gateway version (or commit): `main` @ `ce0047f`
- Node (`node --version`): v24.16.0
- pnpm (`pnpm --version`): 12.5.0
- Go (`go version`): go1.26.4
- OS: Linux 7.1.8+deb14-amd64

## Anything else

The docblock's own reasoning is the argument for the fix — "a mint result is exactly the value a debug line prints wholesale". A digest is a credential's hash, printed wholesale by the very method written to prevent that.

A test that pins the redaction across all verbs (`%v`, `%+v`, `%#v`, `%s`, `%q`, `json.Marshal`) would make the guarantee mechanical rather than a comment, and would be the same shape as the negative cases in `internal/arch/secrets_test.go`.

I am not claiming this is exploitable today; I am claiming the guarantee is stated as uniform and is not uniform.

security: tenant scope becomes an explicit three-state value that fails closed

## Problem

Tenant authorization in the controller is expressed as a bare string, and an empty
string means "root, allow everything". `isWithinTenantScope` in
`features/controller/api/middleware.go` returns `true` when the caller tenant is `""`.

That intent is correct for a genuine mTLS admin. The defect is that a deliberate root
admin and a plumbing bug are indistinguishable: any path that reads the wrong context
key, forgets to propagate the tenant, or uses `context.Background()` instead of the
request context arrives at the same `""` and is granted unrestricted cross-tenant
access with no error and no log line.

A survey of `features/controller/api` on `origin/develop` found 195 HTTP handlers that
read a caller-supplied identifier, of which 101 never read the caller's tenant at all;
about 77 of those sit behind `requirePermission`, so an authenticated caller reaches
them. The scope helper is correct and is simply not called — 22 of 133 handler files
call it.

Because the default is open, omission is the vulnerability. Adding call sites lowers the
count without removing the class; the next forgotten propagation reopens it.

Caller scope is an explicit value with three distinguishable states — root-scoped,
tenant-scoped, and unset — and unset denies. Only the authentication middleware can
produce the root-scoped state, and only from a verified admin certificate marker. A
handler cannot reach a store call carrying an unset scope. An architecture test fails
the build when a handler reads a caller-supplied identifier without consuming that
value, so the remaining call-site work becomes enumerable and verifiable rather than
hand-audited.

Symlink race in file operations

When lf copies, moves or renames files, it uses the path name and follows symlinks. The path is resolved at every step, which adds the potential of TOCTOU races. This has been attempted to be solved before in #2534

In most cases, this can result in accidentally following symlinks and files ending up where they were not supposed to. The risk depends on how often the user operates on files or in directories with symlinks.

There are two additional more severe cases:
- When a user runs lf as root on files that are writable by a unprivileged user, this issue can lead to privilege escalation and its actually a well documented problem in file operations https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xj38-jxc5-rppx
- when the application runs chmod, this adds another vector to make this problem exploitable, which is why I consider this issue to be a blocker for #2678 which has to use chmod to preserve the permissions during copy 

The "good" news for lf: nearly al file mangers have the same issue (including yazi and ranger)
The only tool that I found to be safe is coreutils `cp` which has taken significant efforts to do this right

There is actually a lot to consider when it comes to file operations and making them reliably and ideally even secure, but I think following the example of coreutils is likely the right call.

[ADR-084] Reviewer personas: a separate reviewer invocation with a declared remit, attached per stage or by an escalation, advisory with ingest-time checks, plus deterministic security checks as concern sources

## Context

ADR-080 #3693 says new crew roles are "reviewer personas", not new stage types (N6). Two alpha epics need one: the **architect** (E78 #3699), a plan-stage reviewer whose remit is the in-repo decision record, and the **security officer** (E80 #3701), a threat-model reviewer on declared sensitive paths. Both epics say "via E55's grammar". ADR-068 #2211 (accepted 2026-07-26) governs that grammar, but it decides something narrower: **workflow-declared conventions injected as supplemental criteria into the existing reviewers' prompt**, with base-ref resolution, subordinate framing, `severity_cap` and attribution. It does not decide a separate reviewer, per-reviewer prompts, attachment by escalation, or choosing records from a directory.

**Verified in code (2026-09-27):**

- **One prompt for every reviewer.** `runPlanReviews` (`server/plan.go` ~1458) builds one `promptText`, and `runPlanReviewLoop` (~2133) sends it to every `reviewerInvocation` (~77), which has no per-reviewer prompt or remit field. The implement side is the same (`runImplementReviewInvocations`, `server/trace.go` ~5111). `spec.AgentReviewer` carries provider, model, effort and version only. Authority is per stage (this repository: two agents plus `human: 1`, so advisory).
- **E55 status.** E55.1 #2242 (the `repodoc` resolver, 32 KiB cap, `FetchFile`-only access with no directory listing) is done. E55.2 grammar #2243, E55.3 rendering #2244, E55.4 hard eval gate #2245 and E55.6 in-process wiring #2797 are open and `milestone:beta`. The in-process review builds never set injected documents, so a declared document reaches no reviewer today. The per-run base ref for code-change runs was unowned until E55.7 #3746.
- **Size.** The ADR corpus is about 606 KB against a 32 KiB injection cap. Whole-record injection is impossible, so selection needs a machine-readable index (E78.1 #3722, amended).
- **Escalations** carry only `approvals` and `max_autonomy` (`escalation_requirements`). They match the approved plan's scope union (`server/escalation_gate.go`), whereas review happens on the diff.
- **Security today.** The implement review prompt has a self-gating security lens (`prompt.go` ~5823); the plan review has none. `securityscan` consumes CodeQL findings (dormant on stock installs; E80.1 #3749). There is no diff secret scanning or permission-drift check. `redaction/`'s pattern set is reusable.
- **E55.4 itself names "a separate reviewer pass"** as the fallback if conventions dilute the standard reviewers' catch rate.

## Options

**Description:**
Add rolling-window outflow caps per token for bond withdrawals, escrow releases, and rescue. When the cap is exceeded, the protocol auto-pauses outflows of that token and emits an alert event, which limits the blast radius of an unknown bug or key compromise.

**Problem Statement & Context:**
`pause()` needs a human to notice. Most DeFi exploits drain funds within minutes, and a rate limiter bounds the loss automatically.

**Scope & Acceptance Criteria:**
- A configurable `(window_secs, max_outflow)` per token, set by the admin behind a timelock, with loosening timelocked and tightening immediate.
- Tracking with a fixed-bucket or leaky-bucket accumulator.
- User-facing fills are *not* rate-limited, because they're solver-to-user. Only contract-held funds are.
- The guardian or admin can lift the breaker.
- Out of scope: cross-token aggregate limits.

3. Edge Cases/Constraints: A legitimate mass deregistration (the cap must be tunable), and window rollover at the boundaries.
4. Testing: Boundary tests, plus a test that every contract-originated transfer goes through the helper (grep-based or type-enforced).
