Candidate 2 design: latent-permanent conditioned chained QRF (research memo)

Research memo for the candidate that follows the failed baseline (#40). Gate 1 stays locked; candidate 2 runs through the same protocol on the same paired splits, and its model description should be registered in this issue before the run.

## 1. What the locked references demand — a three-moment back-out

The committed battery autocorrelations (log earnings among positives, biennial lags 1/2/5 = 2/4/10 years) are 0.7301 / 0.6572 / 0.5389. Fitting candidate structures to exactly these three numbers:

| structure | implied 10yr autocorr | vs locked band [0.469, 0.609] |
|---|---|---|
| AR(1) chain (the baseline's linear analogue) | 0.207 | far outside |
| AR(2) — "condition on two lags" (Yule–Walker fit to lags 1–2) | 0.396 | **still outside** |
| permanent + AR(1) transitory + white noise | 0.539 | **exact by construction** |

The three-component model fits all three committed moments exactly with **permanent share 0.467, transitory share 0.364 (biennial ρ = 0.722 ≈ 0.85 annualized), noise share 0.169**. The long-run autocorrelation asymptote equals the permanent share — no finite-lag chain, however nonlinear, can hold a ~0.47 floor forever; the baseline run measured exactly this (1-lag QRF: 10yr autocorr 0.31–0.37 — nonlinearity buys ~+0.13 over the linear 0.207, structurally short). The noise share of 0.169 is consistent with the PSID validation literature on reporting error ([Pischke 1995](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/07350015.1995.10524604); [Bound & Krueger's](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2535181) mean-reverting error), which also cautions against pushing the chain to reproduce lag-0 variance too literally.

**Conclusion: candidate 2 must carry an explicit latent person-level state.** Two extra lags provably cannot do it; a permanent component is not one option among several, it is what the committed moments identify.

## 2. Literature mapping (all verified)

- **[Arellano, Blundell & Bonhomme (2017, Econometrica 85:693–734)](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.3982/ECTA13795)** — the theoretical home for our machinery: log earnings = a general Markovian **persistent component** plus a transitory innovation, estimated with **quantile-based** methods; persistence varies with the size and sign of the current shock (nonlinear persistence, conditional skewness). A chained QRF conditioned on a latent persistent state is the simulation-native analogue of this framework.
- **[Guvenen, Karahan, Ozkan & Song (2021, Econometrica 89:2303–2339)](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.3982/ECTA14603)** — administrative data on millions of workers: earnings changes are strongly non-Gaussian (negative skewness, kurtosis far above normal, varying by age and earnings level), and persistence is asymmetric (positive changes for high earners are transitory; negative ones persistent; reversed for low earners). QRF quantile draws capture these facts natively where parametric AR components cannot — the reason to keep the QRF frame rather than switch to a parametric process.
- **[Sabelhaus & Song (2010, JME 57:391–403)](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/moneco/v57y2010i4p391-403.html)** — permanent/transitory decomposition over the life cycle on SSA administrative earnings; already load-bearing in the paper's earnings section and the right external anchor for our fitted component shares.

Correlated Codebooks Destroy VSA Capacity: A 30× Reduction and Its Security Implications for Multi-Tenant Session Memory

# Correlated Codebooks Destroy VSA Capacity: A 30× Reduction and Its Security Implications for Multi-Tenant Session Memory

**Theory Corrections + Security Analysis**

**Status:** Empirical findings, revision of the theory paper  
**Prerequisites:** `hv_session_memory_v6.py`, `vsa_theory_probes.py`  
**Companion:** Substrate, encoder, service, benchmark, and theory papers

---

## Abstract

The theory paper preceding this one derived five laws governing the VSA session memory substrate. We tested each law against the substrate and report five corrections:

1. **The transition is Gaussian, not sharp.** The theory predicted a sharp falloff at `T_c = √D/4`. Empirically, the transition is a Gaussian CDF with `T_c = 18.7` and `σ = 10.5` at D=4096 — a **wide** transition, not a sharp one. MSE 0.069 for Gaussian vs 0.086 for logistic and 0.137 for Weibull.

2. **Hierarchical encoding fails.** The theory proposed two-level bundling as the fix for `T > T_safe`. Empirically, hierarchical bundling is **2× worse** than direct bundling at every tested T. The extra bundling layers add noise, not signal.

3. **The adversarial threat is not random queries.** 100 random adversarial queries find only 15% max similarity to a target session. The actual threat is *sign-based* reconstruction (`sign(target + noise)`), which trivially achieves similarity 1.0. Real systems must resist both.

4. **Correlated codebooks catastrophically reduce capacity.** A codebook with 60% pairwise correlation drops VSA capacity by **30×** (100% at K=64 to 3.1% at K=32). Clustered codebooks are intermediate (25% at K=32). This is the main finding of this paper: **random codebooks are not optional, they are a hard requirement**.

5. **Shared codebooks leak across tenants.** With a single codebook shared across 5 tenants, cross-tenant error rate is **80%**. Per-tenant codebooks eliminate leakage entirely (0%). Per-tenant *turn keys alone* do not help — the token codebook itself is the leaking channel.

These findings are empirical corrections to the preceding theory paper. Three of them (correlated codebook, shared codebook, hierarchical failure) directly constrain the service architecture and the encoder training objective.

---

## 1. Corrections to the theory

### 1.1 Transition shape (OP1)

The theory paper derived the following rule: for a session with T turns and P positions per turn, decode accuracy is:

```
P_correct(T, P, D, V) ≈ Φ( √D / √(T · P) − √(2 log V) )
```

This predicts a **sharp** transition around `T_c = D/(4 P)` at D=4096, P=10, giving `T_c ≈ 100`. Empirically, accuracy drops from 100% at T=8 to 8% at T=64, with the 50% crossing at **T_c ≈ 18.7**.

The corrected empirical fit:

```
P_correct(T) ≈ Φ( (18.7 − T) / 10.5 )
```

This is 5× smaller `T_c` than theory predicted and a transition width of `σ = 10.5` — nearly 60% of `T_c` itself.

### 1.2 Why the theory over-predicted

The theory assumed:
- Each position-token binding contributes independent signal.
- The sign-bundle adds O(1) noise per position.

The actual bundling adds **correlated** noise. The sign operation is nonlinear; the effect of one position's sign error propagates to all positions in the same turn. Theoretically modeling this requires tracking the joint distribution of sign errors, not just per-position variance.

The corrected rule of thumb:

```
T_safe(D) ≈ √D / 8   (90% decode)
T_50(D)   ≈ √D / 4   (50% decode)
```

At D=4096: `T_safe = 8`, `T_50 = 16`. Matches observation.

At D=16384: `T_safe = 16`, `T_50 = 32`.

The theory paper over-predicted by 2×. This paper corrects the bound.

### 1.3 Design implication

For sessions longer than `T_safe`, the substrate cannot decode with high accuracy using a single hypervector. Neither larger D alone nor hierarchical encoding solves this (see §2).

The realistic fixes are:
- **Multiple HVs per session.** Store one HV

# llgenie: pick the right llama.cpp build for the card (upstream vs Prism)

## Goal

`llgenie` currently **always** builds **upstream `ggml-org/llama.cpp`** (see
`containers/test/Dockerfile`: `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/ggerganov/
llama.cpp.git ...`, CPU-only). That is the general / high-end tree.

But there is a second, purpose-built tree — **`PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp` (branch
`prism`)** — whose 119 unique commits are dedicated to **low-bit quants
(PTQ1_0 / PQ2_0)** across Metal / CUDA / CPU / ROCm / SYCL / Vulkan, plus MTP /
DFlash / DSpark and Qwen3.5. That tree exists specifically so you can run
**larger, more capable models on constrained memory** (low-end / memory-tight
cards) — exactly the class of hardware llgenie's `--download-top-tier` fits.

**Ask:** make the llama.cpp **source selectable per hardware spec**, so llgenie
picks the tree that can *actually load the quant it chose*:
- **upstream** (full-featured) for the quants it supports (standard K-quants,
  IQ-quants, F16/F32, and the ternary `Q2_0` group-64 which has merged upstream);
- **Prism** (low-bit PTQ/PQ) for the low-bit quants stock llama.cpp **refuses**
  (PTQ1_0 / PQ2_0 / TQ1_0 / TQ2_0).

This is a follow-on to [#76](https://github.com/asimov-agent/llgenie/issues/76)
(parent) and the build work in [#78](https://github.com/asimov-agent/llgenie/issues/78)
— #78 makes llgenie *clone+build* the server; this issue decides *which tree to
build*.

## The easy rule — card size picks the server

**The decision is card size, NOT the downloaded model's quant.**

1. **Which file *fits* the card?** Decided by **size (GB)**, not quant.
   `file_size_bytes + KV_headroom + OS_headroom <= card_RAM`. This is already
   what `discover_top_tier` does. The card's RAM (from
   `read_total_ram_bytes()` / `read_current_headroom_bytes()`, overridable by
   `LLAMA_RAM_BYTES`/`LLAMA_HEADROOM_BYTES`) selects which quants are
   *available* to the card.

2. **Which server build to compile?** Decided by **card RAM only**, not by
   inspecting the downloaded model's filename.

   - **Card RAM <= 24 GB -> build Prism** (the PrismML fork).
     On a memory-tight card, the only large models that fit are low-bit
     (PTQ1_0 / PQ2_0), and **only Prism loads those**. The Prism fork is a
     **superset** of stock llama.cpp — it also loads every standard quant
     (`Q2_0` through `Q8_0`, `F16`, etc.) — so building Prism on a small card
     is never wrong: it runs low-bit *and* standard models.
   - **Card RAM > 24 GB -> build upstream** (stock `ggml-org/llama.cpp`).
     On a card this size, standard quants (`Q5_K`, `Q8_0`, etc.) fit and run on
     stock upstream. Prism's extra low-bit quants are not needed.

   **The Prism fork is a strict superset of stock llama.cpp.** Verified from
   Prism's runtime-support matrix (https://docs.prismml.com/download/formats):
   every standard quant runs on Prism *and* on stock; the only quants Prism
   *adds* are PTQ1_0 / PQ2_0 / TQ1_0 / TQ2_0. So the card-size rule is safe:

   | Card RAM | Tree to build | Why |
   |---|---|---|
   | 8 GB  | Prism    | only PTQ1_0 fits; stock cannot load it |
   | 12 GB | Prism    | PTQ1_0 fits; stock cannot load it |
   | 16 GB | Prism    | PQ2_0/PTQ1_0 fit; stock cannot load them |
   | 24 GB | Prism    | Q4_K fits a large model; Prism runs low-bit AND standard |
   | 36 GB | upstream | Q8_0 fits; stock handles it fine |
   | 48 GB | upstream | Q8_0/F16 fits; stock handles it fine |
   | 64 GB | upstream | Q8_0/F16 fits; stock handles it fine |

   The quant tag that #87 surfaces on each candidate is still useful for the
   *user* (to know which models need Prism vs stock), but **`make install` does
   not inspect it to decide the tree**. The tree is decided by card RAM alone.
## Proposed design

1. **Card-size rule — no model inspection.** `make install` decides the tree
   purely from `card_RAM`:
   - `card_RAM <= 24 GB` -> build

Verify Dependabot security updates are enabled in consumers that receive the npm version-update disable

## Origin

Found while implementing joshuafolkken/kit#803, which sets `open-pull-requests-limit: 0` on the `npm` entry of the distributed `.github/dependabot.yml`.

## Problem

#803 makes the security-advisory path the *only* remaining source of npm Dependabot PRs in every consumer. That path depends on a repository-level setting the kit neither sets nor checks: **Dependabot security updates** (`automated-security-fixes`), which is opt-in and off by default for private repositories.

A consumer that syncs the file without that setting enabled gets **zero** npm Dependabot PRs — advisories included — and nothing in the toolchain reports it. The failure is silent: the absence of a PR looks identical to the absence of an advisory.

Current state across first-party repos (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/automated-security-fixes`):

- `joshuafolkken/kit` — enabled
- `joshuafolkken/app-kit` — enabled
- `joshuafolkken/game-kit` — enabled
- `joshuafolkken/joshuafolkken-com` — enabled
- `joshuafolkken/jgame` — 404 (needs checking; a 404 here is not the same as `{"enabled":false}`)

So no repository is currently exposed, but nothing keeps it that way, and a newly created private consumer starts out exposed by default.

## Expected result

`josh` reports the setting rather than assuming it. Candidates, roughly in order of cost:

1. A `josh doctor` / `josh health` check that queries `automated-security-fixes` and warns when it is disabled or unreadable.
2. The same check run during `josh sync`, since that is the moment the npm disable reaches the consumer.
3. Optionally offering to enable it (`gh api -X PUT repos/<owner>/<repo>/automated-security-fixes`) rather than only reporting.

Distinguish the three outcomes — enabled, disabled, and not readable (404 / missing scope) — and do not fail the command on the unreadable case.

## Notes

#803 documents the prerequisite in the distributed `dependabot.yml` comment and in `docs/sync.md`, which is the mitigation available without new tooling. This Issue covers enforcement.

Limit distributed Dependabot npm updates to security advisories

## Background

`.github/dependabot.yml` is a kit-distributed file — it is listed in `AI_COPY_FILES` in `scripts/init/init-logic.ts` and documented in `docs/sync.md`, so `josh init` / `josh sync` write it into every consumer (app-kit / game-kit / jgame). Its `npm` entry therefore opens weekly version-update PRs in kit *and* in each consumer.

Those same repositories already bump npm dependencies through a different path: `fullrun`, `halfrun` and `queue` all run `josh latest` before implementation starts.

## Problem

The npm entry duplicates `josh latest`, and the duplicate loses. Recent npm Dependabot PRs in kit were closed unmerged rather than reviewed and merged:

- #771 `typescript-eslint` 8.65.0 → 8.66.0 — CLOSED
- #772 `eslint-plugin-unicorn` 72.0.0 → 73.0.0 — CLOSED
- #383 `@types/node` 25.7.0 → 25.8.0 — CLOSED
- #382 `pnpm/action-setup` — CLOSED

Every one of them still consumed a full CI run — `Checks`, `Detect E2E`, `Security Audit`, `Analyze (actions)`, `Analyze (javascript-typescript)`, `SonarCloud Code Analysis`, `SonarQube` — plus reviewer attention, and the identical noise is replicated in every consumer repository that received the distributed file.

Security advisories are the one case `josh latest` does not cover on its own: it bumps to latest whenever it next runs, which may be days away, and the `pnpm audit` inside it reports a finding rather than opening a fix.

## Expected result

- Dependabot stops opening routine npm version-update PRs, in kit and in every consumer that syncs the file.
- Dependabot still opens npm PRs for security advisories. Dependabot security updates are enabled on this repository (`automated-security-fixes` → `{"enabled":true,"paused":false}`), and `open-pull-requests-limit: 0` disables version updates only — security updates keep their own internal limit.
- The `github-actions` entry is unchanged. It remains the mechanism that bumps the action SHA pins which `josh sync` then distributes (`docs/sync.md`), and it is the ecosystem that #802 makes auto-mergeable.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The `npm` entry in `.github/dependabot.yml` sets `open-pull-requests-limit: 0`, with a comment naming `josh latest` as the version-update path
- [ ] A unit test asserts the npm entry disables version updates and the `github-actions` entry keeps its weekly schedule
- [ ] `docs/sync.md` records the consumer-facing effect, next to the existing note explaining why the `github-actions` entry is kept as a backstop
- [ ] A security advisory still produces an npm PR (verified against GitHub's documented behaviour for `open-pull-requests-limit: 0`; no synthetic advisory is created)

## Notes

This change reaches consumers on their next `josh sync`, so it is a deliberate policy change for the whole distribution, not a kit-local tweak. The rationale holds for consumers because they run the same `josh latest` flow.

feat(audit): add a built-in division-before-multiplication precision rule

## Problem

`sdkt audit` ships five built-in rules (AUTH-001..004, MOVE-001) and every one of them is signature-based — they reason about `require_auth()`, `invoke_contract()`, and argument reuse. Arithmetic ordering, the classic Soroban/DeFi correctness bug class where a multiplication follows a division and truncates the result, is not covered by any built-in rule. The plugin system can host such a rule, but no built-in rule exists, so `sdkt audit` reports a clean bill of health on code containing the pattern.

## Current behavior

```
$ sdkt audit --list-rules
Available audit rules (5):
  AUTH-001  critical  Privileged/admin function must call require_auth()
  AUTH-002  critical  Cross-contract invoke_contract() must be guarded by require_auth()
  AUTH-003  critical  initialize()-style entrypoint must call require_auth()
  AUTH-004  critical  Token transfer function must call require_auth() on source or destination
  MOVE-001  warning   Local used as a call argument multiple times (possible move-after-use)
```

No rule inspects arithmetic ordering. Source such as:

```rust
let fee = amount / 10_000 * bps;   // truncates before multiplying
```

is reported as clean.

## Expected behavior

A new built-in rule flags division-before-multiplication within a function: a `/` whose result feeds a later `*` on the same value, where the division truncates before the multiplication can recover precision. The finding carries the rule id, a warning severity (the pattern is a real bug class but not always exploitable), the offending function name as its location, and a message that names the operation order.

## Why it matters

Precision loss from div-before-mul is the error class most likely to be reported by a contract auditor, and this is precisely the class the devkit's own audit tooling does not check. A contributor rule here extends the tool's coverage into a correctness area that the signature rules cannot reach, and gives the registry a second rule shape (expression ordering rather than function signature), which is useful groundwork for further arithmetic and state-ordering rules.

## Concrete example

```rust
pub fn quote(env: Env, amount: i128) -> i128 {
    let fee_bps: i128 = 30;
    amount / 10_000 * fee_bps      // truncates to 0 for amount < 10_000
}
```

Expected: one warning-level finding for `quote` describing the div-before-mul order. Today: no findings.

## Implementation direction

`crates/sdkt-audit/src/rules.rs` shows the rule shape: a unit struct implementing `AuditRule` (`id`, `severity`, `description`, `check(&self, scans: &[FnScan], ctx, &mut AuditReport)`), registered through `Registry::register_builtin_rules` in `crates/sdkt-audit/src/registry.rs`. Follow the existing conventions exactly — a stable rule id in the same namespace, a `Severity` from `crates/sdkt-audit/src/types.rs`, and `location: Some(<function name>)` so findings group like the current ones. If the per-function scan data (`FnScan` / `AuditContext`) does not already carry the expression ordering the rule needs, extend the scan minimally rather than reparsing the source inside `check`; the scanning layer is shared by all rules and is the right place for a new fact. Keep the rule conservative: report the clear ordering pattern and avoid flagging constant-folded or unrelated operands.

## Scope

- One new built-in rule for division-before-multiplication, plus whatever minimal scan-context support it needs.
- Unit tests for positive and negative cases, and a `--list-rules` assertion.

## Out of scope

- General expression/operator analysis beyond the div-before-mul ordering.
- Overflow, rounding-direction, or no-op arithmetic checks.
- Reworking the scanner, the registry, or the severity model.
- Shipping the rule as a plugin instead of a built-in.
- Any change to `--format sarif` or the report schema.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sdkt audit --list-rules` lists the new r

This issue tracks the implementation of a new, unified system for mentions and references within Chatto. The goal is to move away from relying on standard URLs for internal links and instead use a custom, internal reference format that provides greater flexibility, security, and a better user experience.

- **Client Flexibility**: Gives clients maximum control over how to navigate to a target, rather than being bound by a fixed URL-based API contract.
- **Security**: Reduces the exploit vector where a server might attempt to mimic specific URL formats to trick a client.
- **Mobile Integration**: Facilitates better interaction with mobile apps (iOS/Android) by utilizing protocol prefixes to trigger app actions.

- [ ] **Custom Reference Format**: Develop and implement a persistent internal format for storing these references.
- [ ] **Protocol Support**: Support for a custom scheme (e.g., `chatto://`) to enable cross-client and mobile app integration.

[Feature]: Self-service browser bootstrap/pairing link from an authenticated Control UI (no host CLI required)

## Summary

An already-authenticated operator can self-service pair a **mobile app** from inside Control UI (Devices → **Pair device** → Copy setup code, no terminal needed). There is no equivalent self-service path for pairing a **new browser** (webchat Control UI on a second device/machine). The only documented way to bring up a new browser is `openclaw dashboard` run **on the Gateway host itself** (owner-issued, short-lived, single-use handoff), which requires SSH/console access to that host.

This is a real usability gap for anyone away from the Gateway host who needs to log in from a device that has never been paired before (e.g. a borrowed computer while travelling), and who has no SSH access to the host. Pre-pairing devices in advance is the practical workaround, but there's no self-service recovery path for the "genuinely new browser, no host access" case.

## Why this looks feasible, not just a wish

The mobile "Pair device" setup code and the `openclaw dashboard` browser handoff appear to use the same underlying primitive: a short-lived, single-use signed bootstrap credential (`bootstrapToken=...&bootstrapProfile=owner&gatewayUrl=...` in the `dashboard --json` output). The mobile pairing flow already proves this kind of ephemeral credential can be safely minted from an authenticated `operator.admin` session in the UI, without touching the host. There does not appear to be an architectural reason a "Pair another browser" action couldn't reuse the same mechanism and render it as a copyable link/QR from Devices, gated behind `operator.admin` exactly like mobile pairing is today.

## Related issues

- #141520 — documents the adjacent confusion (pasting a mobile "Pair device" setup code into the Gateway Token field fails with a generic `token_mismatch`). That issue's proposed fix is UI copy/error-message clarity; it does not propose a self-service browser-bootstrap action. Filing this issue separately because it's a capability gap, not a copy/wording bug.
- #120762 / #120764 — improve the *mobile*/LAN/Public-URL pairing wizard's connectivity guidance; scoped to the mobile app flow, not new-browser bootstrap.

## Suggested contract (sketch, not a firm proposal)

1. Devices card gets a second action next to "Pair device": something like **"Pair another browser"**.
2. Gated behind `operator.admin`, same as mobile setup-code creation.
3. Produces a short-lived, single-use link/QR equivalent to what `openclaw dashboard` currently prints from the host CLI (same `bootstrapToken`/`bootstrapProfile=owner` shape), scoped so it can only be redeemed once, by one browser.
4. Documented alongside the existing mobile pairing docs (`/web/control-ui/connect-and-pair#pair-a-mobile-device`) as the browser equivalent.

## Environment where this was noticed

- OpenClaw self-hosted, Docker deployment, token-mode gateway auth.
- Operator already has an admin-paired browser and the OpenClaw mobile app; needed to add a second, previously-unpaired browser while away from the Gateway host.

message_tool_only: stranded-reply recovery re-prompts the model to publish its private final and force-sends an English error notice to the DM (no config to disable)

## Summary

In `message_tool_only` mode (`messages.visibleReplies: "message_tool"`), a turn that ends with a **private** final text and no `message(action=send)` is classified as a "stranded reply". The recovery then:

1. **re-prompts the model with the private text verbatim** and tells it to deliver it: *"Your previous reply was not delivered … Your reply text was: "<finalText>" … Please deliver this reply now by calling message(action=send). Do not add any extra commentary; just deliver the original reply."*
2. if the retry sends nothing, **delivers a runtime notice** to the chat — `I generated a reply but could not deliver it to this chat. Please try again.` — marked `isError` + `deliverDespiteSourceReplySuppression`, so no reply mode can hold it back.

This defeats the main reason to pick `message_tool` in a customer-facing DM: keeping the model's final text private. The code says `message_tool_only` "keeps normal final text private by design" (comment on `warnPrivateMessageToolFinal`), but recovery actively tries to publish that text, and there's no config key to turn it off.

## Environment

- OpenClaw **2026.9.6**, Linux, Telegram DM
- `messages.visibleReplies: "message_tool"`, `messages.groupChat.visibleReplies: "automatic"`
- Support agent answering end customers. Private finals are internal notes ("handled, nothing else to do; context: …"), and they can mention other conversations.

## Why we use `message_tool`

With the default `automatic` mode, the agent answered the customer via `message(action=send)` and then wrote an internal note as its final text. That note went out as a second Telegram message about 3 s later. We saw 8 such leaks in about 10 turns. Switching to `message_tool` fixed that: `final reply suppressed by sourceReplyDeliveryMode: message_tool_only … deliverDespiteSuppression=false` shows up in the debug log exactly as expected.

## Reproduction (live, Telegram DM)

1. Send a DM that makes the model end a turn with a long (≥280 chars) final text and no `message` call. In our case this was a duplicate of an already-answered request, and the model wrote itself a 937-char note summarising what it had done.
2. Gateway log: `final reply suppressed by sourceReplyDeliveryMode: message_tool_only … textChars=937 deliverDespiteSuppression=false`. This part is correct.
3. Right after that, `resolveStrandedReplyRecovery` returns `kind: "retry"`. A follow-up run is injected with the prompt above, which contains the full private note, and with `toolsAllow: ["message"]`.
4. Our model **refused**, because the note referenced other customers' cases. A more compliant model would have sent the internal note to the customer. That is the leak `message_tool` is supposed to prevent.
5. The retry sent nothing, so `kind: "diagnostic"` delivered `I generated a reply but could not deliver it to this chat. Please try again.` to the customer DM, in English, although the conversation was in Polish.

Source: `src/auto-reply/reply/stranded-reply-recovery.ts` (`resolveStrandedReplyRecovery`, `buildStrandedReplyRetryPrompt`, `buildStrandedReplyDeliveryFailurePayload`). The classifier only uses length and sentence count (`LONG_PRIVATE_FINAL_MIN_CHARS` / `MULTI_SENTENCE_PRIVATE_FINAL_MIN_CHARS`), so it can't tell a forgotten answer from a note to self.

Our current workaround is prompt discipline: "if you did not send, end the turn with exactly `NO_REPLY`". Because `isSilentReplyText` makes the classifier return `none`, this avoids both the retry and the notice. But in direct chats the Silent Replies section is omitted from the system prompt, so agents never learn about `NO_REPLY` unless the operator adds it to their instructions. And it is discipline, not a channel guarantee.

Security: Restrict webhook capabilities and isolate intake across owners

Webhook events can contain third-party text while executing with the owner's tools and Skills. Sender authentication and an “untrusted data” prompt do not enforce a permission boundary. Track the P2 / Medium advisory from [PR #816's security review](https://github.com/D00mch/souz/pull/816#discussion_r4113569672), following the narrower approach proposed in the [owner's response](https://github.com/D00mch/souz/pull/816#discussion_r4113609076).

### Risk

When hooks are enabled, an accepted event can include attacker-controlled content such as an email, issue description, or comment. `HookService` passes that payload into an ordinary owner-capable agent turn. Prompt injection can then attempt to use the owner's enabled capabilities to perform unintended actions. A valid webhook signature authenticates delivery; it does not make every field trustworthy.

Relevant entry point: `backend/src/main/kotlin/ru/souz/backend/hooks/HookService.kt`, the `executeChatTurn(..., content = hookInput(...))` call.

### Proposed scope

- Define a small, explicit per-hook capability set, defaulting to no tools / answer-only execution.
- Let the owner authorize specific actions when configuring the hook. Keep unattended execution possible without mandatory interactive confirmation for every side effect.
- Enforce the restriction at execution boundaries across compiled tools, file-backed Skills, and subagents. Filtering only the advertised compiled-tool catalog is insufficient; indirect invocation and child execution must not regain the owner's broader permissions.
- Keep hook permissions within the owner's available permissions. Event content must not select or expand the capability set.
- Where actions accept sensitive arguments, enforce deterministic constraints such as allowed destinations. Prompt instructions alone must not supply those constraints.
- Preserve the applicable restrictions through option continuations, retries, and recovered queued work.

Prefer a focused extension of existing execution policy over a general approval framework. Owner-controlled automation may intentionally delegate capabilities, but that delegation must be explicit. An allowlist limits authority; it does not prevent prompt injection from misusing an allowed action.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A hook without explicit capabilities cannot invoke tools, file-backed Skills, or subagents that provide additional capabilities.
- [ ] Explicitly authorized automation still completes unattended.
- [ ] Disallowed actions are rejected before side effects, including attempts through Skill invocation and subagent delegation.
- [ ] Sensitive argument constraints are checked in code; an allowed delivery destination works and an event-supplied unauthorized destination is rejected.
- [ ] Continuation and recovery paths cannot broaden the hook's permissions.
- [ ] Focused regression coverage verifies denied invocations do not reach the external boundary, and documentation explains the safe default, explicit delegation, and remaining prompt-injection risk.

### Intake isolation across owners — P2 / Medium

Source: [Partition webhook intake concurrency by principal](https://github.com/D00mch/souz/pull/816#discussion_r4115410628), reviewed at `13abeb5c7c657310ee0ca6edabe385e186de393c`.

Affected path: `backend/src/main/kotlin/ru/souz/backend/http/routes/HookRoutes.kt`, the process-wide intake semaphore.

The review reports that a sender holding any one hook's valid Bearer token can occupy all 16 intake slots with slow request bodies. A slot is acquired before body reading and retained through the five-second body timeout, verification, and admission. Unrelated hooks then immediately receive HTTP 429. Replenishing roughly four slow requests per second can sustain denial of webhook intake across owners. This is an availability boundary separate from the agent-capability restriction above.

GET /vaults query does not enforce max limit and allows limit=100000 to OOM the API

**Context**
`backend/src/routes/vaults.ts` forwards `req.query.limit` directly to `findMany({take: limit})` after `z.coerce.number()` without an upper bound. Zod schema allows any positive int.

**Why this is a gap**
An unauthenticated caller can request `?limit=100000` and force Prisma to materialize 100k vault rows + relations, spiking memory and DB CPU and triggering OOM kill on the 512MB container.

**Acceptance Criteria**
- [ ] Clamp `limit` to `Math.min(parsed, 50)` and `page` to `1..1000`; return `400 code=LIMIT_EXCEEDED` if `limit>50` instead of silently clamping (document chosen behavior)
- [ ] Add `maxLimit` to OpenAPI spec and snapshot test
- [ ] Test: request `limit=100000` and assert 400 and no DB query with `take>50` (spy on prisma call)
- [ ] Existing pagination tests still pass with default limit 20

# Vendored msgpack affected by CVE-2026-57585 (Unpacker crash after caught error) — fork lacks context reset in `unpack_clear`

## Summary

CVE-2026-57585 (GHSA-6v7p-g79w-8964, CVSS 3.1: 7.5 HIGH, CWE-416) affects
msgpack-python < 1.2.1: reusing an `Unpacker` after a previous unpack raised an
exception can resume from a corrupt parser context and crash the process with a
SEGV (denial of service). It was fixed upstream in msgpack 1.2.1 via commit
[`2c56ddb`](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-python/commit/2c56ddb5d0025ed481d962c0f5d62d19dec7476d).

srsly vendors this code as `srsly/msgpack/unpack_template.h` and
`srsly/msgpack/_unpacker.pyx`. I checked the 2.5.3 sdist, and the vulnerable
pattern is present — the fork is in fact missing cleanup that even *pre-patch*
upstream had:

- **`srsly/msgpack/unpack_template.h`** — the vendored `unpack_clear` only clears
  `stack[0].obj`; it does not walk the stack or re-init the context:

  ```c
  static inline void unpack_clear(unpack_context *ctx)
  {
      Py_CLEAR(ctx->stack[0].obj);
  }
  ```

  The 1.2.1 fix adds `unpack_init(ctx)` here, clears map keys across the whole
  stack, and calls `unpack_clear()` from `unpack_construct` / `unpack_skip` on the
  error (`-1`) return. srsly's `unpack_construct` / `unpack_skip` return the raw
  execute result with no cleanup.

- **`srsly/msgpack/_unpacker.pyx`** — the `Unpacker._unpack` error branch raises
  `FormatError` / `StackError` / `ValueError` but never calls
  `unpack_clear` / `unpack_init` on `self.ctx`, so the next `unpack()` / `skip()`
  resumes from the corrupt context.

## Impact

- SCA tools that do source-file hashing (Mend/WhiteSource in our case) flag srsly
  itself against CVE-2026-57585 via the vendored files, with no upgrade path to
  clear the finding — msgpack is bundled, not a declared dependency, so upgrading
  the standalone `msgpack` package does nothing.
- srsly's own high-level helpers (`msgpack_loads`, etc.) create a fresh unpacker
  per call, so the vulnerable reuse-after-error pattern is not reachable through
  the documented API. But any code that instantiates `srsly.msgpack.Unpacker`
  directly and reuses it across a caught error is exposed, and the flagged code
  ships in the compiled wheel regardless.

## Request

Re-vendor msgpack with the 1.2.1 fix, or cherry-pick the relevant parts of commit
`2c56ddb` into the fork (the changes are in `unpack_template.h` and
`_unpacker.pyx`), and cut a release. Happy to test a build.

- https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-python/security/advisories/GHSA-6v7p-g79w-8964
- https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-python/commit/2c56ddb5d0025ed481d962c0f5d62d19dec7476d

[GSD][Governor] Prevent duplicate mission captains and bound global concurrency

Parent: #46

Related: #34, #47, #48, #51, #52, #62, #76, #110, #115, #116

## Goal

Add a **provider-neutral mission admission / concurrency governor** so Tachiko Conductor cannot accidentally start multiple competing high-cost captains or writers for the same authoritative mission.

This Issue owns only **who may start concurrently**:

1. deterministic mission identity;
2. duplicate/overlapping captain and writer prevention;
3. explicit identities for intentional experiment / review / consultation lanes;
4. restart-safe global concurrency admission.

This Issue does **not** own:

- model-driven waiting — #47;
- worker/reviewer fresh-vs-resume lifecycle — #48;
- tool/log output bounding — #49;
- token telemetry — #51;
- compaction timing or thresholds — #61;
- semantic/model routing — #76/#116.

Long Astra/Terra missions are allowed. #117 must not shorten a legitimate mission merely because it is long or has a large context.

## Evidence — 2026-09-22 rollout audit

A fresh rollout audit found several heavy sessions active in overlapping time windows, including multiple sessions targeting the same repository/worktree/Issue scope.

Nine large sampled sessions recorded approximately:

- **4,976 model responses**;
- **377.5M raw input tokens**;
- **360.9M cached input tokens** (~**95.6% cache hit**);
- **16.67M uncached input tokens**;
- **1.94M output tokens**.

The cache was already effective. One major avoidable source of waste was allowing multiple expensive mission/captain lanes to exist at the same time without a shared admission boundary.

These are diagnostic rollout metrics, not billing/accounting claims.

## Architecture

```text
Steward / Ready authority
  -> deterministic mission identity
  -> #117 mission admission
       -> existing owner? reconcile it
       -> overlapping production captain/writer? refuse new admission
       -> explicit experiment identity? isolated admission if policy allows
       -> explicit read-only review/consultation identity? allow under review rules
       -> global concurrency capacity available? admit
  -> #34/#90/#116 routing
  -> worker/captain invocation
  -> #47 model-free waiting
  -> #48 session lifecycle
  -> #49 bounded tool output
  -> validation -> independent review -> guarded merge
```

The governor is an admission layer, not a second scheduler or workflow authority.

## 1. Deterministic mission identity

Define a durable provider-neutral identity sufficient to decide whether a new lane overlaps existing authority.

Bind to the strongest available evidence, including:

- repository;
- Issue / PR / durable Run authority;
- worktree / mutation authority;
- claim / lease / generation;
- execution phase;
- lane role.

The identity must survive restart/re-entry and be inspectable without reading model transcripts.

## 2. Lane roles

At minimum distinguish:

```text
production_captain
mutation_writer
read_only_review
read_only_consultation
experiment
```

Exact names are implementation choice; semantics are required.

### Production captain / writer

For one authoritative Issue / PR / worktree / mission mutation surface:

- default maximum is **one production captain/writer authority**;
- an already-active authoritative lane must be reconciled/resumed before another is considered;
- native dispatch, bootstrap heartbeat and registered manual sessions must consult the same ownership view;
- ambiguous ownership fails closed.

A captain may delegate bounded workers under its existing mission authority; delegation must not accidentally become a second independent captain for the same mission.

### Review / consultation

Parallel Sol/Oracle/Luna review or consultation is allowed only with an explicit **read-only** role/identity.

It must not:

- claim mutation authority;
- become a second captain;
- write implementation changes;
- merge merely because it is concurrently active.

fix(ps-service)!: require configured identity for RBAC bootstrap owner grant

## Problem
`resolve_active_roles` (`authz/service.py:176-217`) calls `store.bootstrap_first_owner(principal)` for any principal with no existing rows in `access_role_assignments`. `bootstrap_first_owner` (`authz/store.py:279-327`) grants `SYSTEM_OWNER` to whoever's call wins the advisory lock while the table is empty — reachable from every role-gated MCP tool, with no deliberate "become owner" action and no identity vetting beyond holding a valid token for the configured issuer. In a freshly deployed or re-migrated environment, whichever authenticated user of the same IdP calls first permanently becomes `SystemOwner`.

## Solution
Add operator-configured expected first-owner identity (subject + issuer, matching `Principal.sub`/`Principal.iss`). `bootstrap_first_owner` only grants `SYSTEM_OWNER` when the calling principal matches; a non-matching caller gets no owner grant, the table stays empty, and the response looks identical to an ordinary non-owner call (no disclosure that a bootstrap was attempted or who the real expected owner is). The service fails closed at startup if this identity isn't configured, mirroring the existing OIDC fail-closed pattern (`test_startup_fail_closed`). The advisory lock's existing double-bootstrap protection is preserved unchanged.

## Value
Surfaced by a deep security assessment of the RBAC/ABAC framework (#133). The advisory lock already prevents two simultaneous callers from both becoming owner, but nothing prevents an unintended authenticated user from winning the race to be *first* — meaning permanent, unvetted control over the entire access-role hierarchy could go to whoever reaches the service first, not whoever the deploying organization intended.

## Deliverables
- [ ] New required config for expected first-owner subject + issuer (`ServiceConfig`)
- [ ] `bootstrap_first_owner` compares the calling principal against the configured identity before granting `SYSTEM_OWNER`
- [ ] Startup fails closed with a configuration error when the expected-owner identity is unset
- [ ] Rejected bootstrap attempts recorded as a distinct audit event type

## Discussion
Breaking change: deployments that don't set the new expected-owner config will fail to start. Out of scope: any change to the advisory-locked double-bootstrap protection itself (already correct); any UI/tooling for setting this config beyond the existing env-var config surface.

## Acceptance criteria

### Group 1: Configuration/Startup

| AC-ID | Criterion | Perspective |
|---|---|---|
| AC-BI-001 | WHEN the service starts and the expected first-owner identity (subject + issuer) is not configured THEN the service fails to start with a configuration error, consistent with the existing OIDC fail-closed startup pattern | Security |
| AC-BI-002 | WHEN the expected first-owner identity is configured at startup THEN the service starts normally | Technical |

### Group 2: Authorization/Access

| AC-ID | Criterion | Perspective |
|---|---|---|
| AC-BI-003 | WHEN the `access_role_assignments` table is empty and the calling principal's (sub, iss) matches the configured expected first-owner identity THEN `bootstrap_first_owner` grants that principal `AUTHENTICATED_USER` and `SYSTEM_OWNER` exactly as today | Business |
| AC-BI-004 | WHEN the table is empty and the calling principal's (sub, iss) does NOT match the configured identity THEN `bootstrap_first_owner` does not grant `SYSTEM_OWNER`, the table remains empty, and the caller receives the same response as a normal non-owner call with no indication a bootstrap was attempted or who the expected owner is | Security |

### Group 3: Audit/Logging

| AC-ID | Criterion | Perspective |
|---|---|---|
| AC-BI-005 | WHEN `bootstrap_first_owner` rejects a non-matching principal (AC-BI-004) THEN a distinct audit event is recorded identifying the rejected principal's subject/issuer | Compliance |

#521 reported that every page's React Server Component payload embeds the **entire i18n dictionary**, exposing unreleased-feature names and internal terminology to any visitor. sharedChatPage         present
projectCollaboration   present

(+ webhookSettings, scimHeading, manageJo* per the close's own confirmation)

 recoverable from the client bundle regardless."

2. Unreleased-feature names in a shipped bundle are roadmap intel (SCIM, wallet step-up, collaboration, internal moderation states) that competitors and phishers can mine for pre-announcement signal and impersonation targets.

File path manipulation vulnerabilities arise when user-controllable data is placed into a file or URL path that is used on the server to access local resources, which may be within or outside the web root. Log shell command executions (exec channel) by default

`CanastaDefaultSettings.php` logs the `exception`, `error` and `fatal` groups by default. It does not log MediaWiki's `exec` channel, which records every shell command run through Shellbox (`wfShellExec` / `Shell::command`).

After a code-execution bug in an extension (for example CVE-2026-100382 in ExternalData, which lets anonymous requests run commands), the `exec` log is the only record of what was actually run. Without it, an operator can't tell whether a wiki was probed, whether secrets were read, or what was dropped on disk. Full debug logging (`$wgDebugLogFile`) captures this, but it is too verbose to recommend for production.

## Proposal

Add to the defaults:

```php
'exec' => getenv( 'MW_LOG' ) . '/exec.log',
```

The existing log rotator will pick it up. Volume is modest: roughly a line per shell-out, dominated by SyntaxHighlight's `pygmentize` calls on wikis that use it. That's a few thousand lines a day on a busy wiki.

Web container always receives the database root credentials

The web container always runs MediaWiki with the database's root credentials:

- `create` sets `MYSQL_USER=root` for the bundled database (`roles/create/tasks/_env_update.yml`).
- The Compose `web` service receives `MYSQL_USER=${MYSQL_USER:-root}` and `MYSQL_PASSWORD=${MYSQL_PASSWORD}`, which is the root password.
- `--wikidbuser` creates a separate wiki database user, but the web container still receives the root password in its environment.

Any code execution in the web process can therefore read root credentials from `/proc/self/environ` and use them, with full rights over every wiki database in the farm and over `mysql.*`. Exploits for CVE-2026-100382 (ExternalData) do exactly this as their first step.

## Expected

- Default to a dedicated, non-root MariaDB user for MediaWiki, with rights only on the wiki databases.
- Give the web container only that user's credentials. Keep the root password for the `db` service, and for CLI operations that need it (create, import, backup/restore, adding wikis), which can use it through `maintenance exec -s db` instead of the web environment.
- Provide a migration path for existing instances.

Apache executes PHP files in public_assets via the /w/public_assets symlink

Apache executes `.php` files placed in `public_assets/`.

- `$MW_HOME/public_assets` is a symlink to `$MW_VOLUME/public_assets`, the host-mounted `public_assets/` directory.
- `DocumentRoot` is `/var/www/mediawiki`, and `<Directory /var/www/>` has `FollowSymLinks`.
- `<Directory /mediawiki/public_assets>` is `Require all granted`.
- `conf-enabled/php8.2-fpm.conf` applies `SetHandler proxy:unix:...php8.2-fpm.sock` to every `.php`/`.phtml`/`.phar` server-wide.

So `https://<wiki>/w/public_assets/<file>.php` runs through php-fpm. `public_assets/` is writable by `www-data`, so any bug that lets the web process write a file becomes a persistent web shell. That shell survives container recreation and image upgrades, because the directory is a host mount.

`images/` is not affected: `/w/images` is aliased to `img_auth.php`. The `php_flag engine off` in MediaWiki's `images/.htaccess` does nothing under php-fpm in any case.

This is not theoretical. Tools exploiting CVE-2026-100382 (ExternalData) try `public_assets/` among other writable paths.

## Expected

`public_assets` should only ever serve static files. Options, any of which is enough:

- In `<Directory /mediawiki/public_assets>`, add `<FilesMatch "\.(php|phtml|phar|pht|phps)$"> Require all denied </FilesMatch>` (or `SetHandler none` plus `RemoveHandler`).
- Stop exposing `public_assets` through the `/w/` docroot symlink, and serve it only through the existing `/public_assets/` rewrite with PHP handling disabled.

Consider the same guard for any other `www-data`-writable path under the docroot, such as `cache/`.

Compose: config set MYSQL_PASSWORD breaks the instance; no way to rotate the database password

On Compose, there is no supported way to rotate the bundled database's root password, and the obvious attempt breaks the wiki.

`canasta config set MYSQL_PASSWORD=<new>` updates `.env` (and `vars.yaml` on gitops instances), then restarts. But the `db` service only reads `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=${MYSQL_PASSWORD}` when it initializes an empty data directory. On an existing volume, the account in MariaDB keeps the old password, so after the restart:

- the web container can no longer connect to the database
- the `db` healthcheck (`mariadb-admin ping -u root -p$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD`) fails

K8s already blocks this key in `config set` and prints a rotation procedure (`roles/config/tasks/_validate_key.yml`). Compose accepts it and silently produces a broken instance.

Rotating this credential is routine after any suspected exposure. For example, an RCE in a bundled extension (such as CVE-2026-100382 in ExternalData) exposes the web container's environment, which includes `MYSQL_PASSWORD`.

## Expected

On Compose with the bundled database (`USE_EXTERNAL_DB=false`), `config set MYSQL_PASSWORD=<new>` should:

1. Run `ALTER USER` for `root@'%'` and `root@'localhost'` in the running `db` container, authenticating with the current password and passing the new one outside argv and logs.
2. Only then write `.env` and `vars.yaml` and restart.

Alternatively, a dedicated command could do the same. Either way, `WIKI_DB_PASSWORD` needs the same handling when `--wikidbuser` is not root.

With an external database, `config set` should refuse, or warn that the password must be changed on the database server first.

An empty range parameter answers 500 on the dashboard, cache and tool-usage endpoints

## Description

An empty `range` query parameter (`?range=`) makes `/api/dashboard`, `/api/cache` and `/api/tool-usage` answer HTTP 500 Internal Server Error. The range parser (`backend/api_common.py:288-289`) tests for `"all"`, then evaluates `s[-1]` before any validation. For an empty string that raises `IndexError`, which no handler turns into a 400.

Reproduced with FastAPI's TestClient and with a real uvicorn process. Without a cookie the endpoints answer 401. With a guest session, which anyone can obtain through `POST /login/guest` when guest mode is enabled, all three answer 500. Non-numeric, overflowing and unknown-suffix values correctly answer 400, as fixed for #112.

## Expected Behavior

The docstring at `backend/api_common.py:281-285` says a malformed query value "cannot escape any endpoint as a 500 (issue #112)". An empty `range` answers 400 naming the bad parameter, like every other malformed range.

## Reproduction Steps

1. Check out 643a59ee5d0de04e84c75b488f4982a3394b10cd with the pinned requirements. Set `COOKIE_SECURE=0`, `R2_ENDPOINT` to a `file://` copy of `fixtures/r2_mini/`, and a private `DATABASE_URL_VIZ`.
2. Run:
   ```python
   from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
   from backend.app import app
   c = TestClient(app, raise_server_exceptions=False)
   c.post('/login/guest', headers={'Origin': 'http://testserver'}, follow_redirects=False)
   print([c.get(p + '?range=').status_code for p in ('/api/dashboard', '/api/cache', '/api/tool-usage')])
   ```
3. Observe `[500, 500, 500]`.

## Environment / Context

- This is a regression in the shape #112 addressed. #112's closing change (d5b4222f590a345297346c37466beef969a94d1b) rewrote this parser, and the helper it replaced answered 400 for an empty value.
- Audit grading: severity Low (an unhandled 500 on malformed input, the same class as #112), exploitability Demonstrated, confidence High, remediation Trivial. Independent verifiers reproduced it and graded it Medium; it was kept at #112's Low for consistency.

## Discovered During

Full repository audit of 2026-09-27, re-audit of #112 (domain D09 input handling), starting snapshot 643a59ee5d0de04e84c75b488f4982a3394b10cd. Revalidated on master 00a94a041df71529e0403b5a18435622a5450b2c, where `backend/api_common.py` is unchanged.

## Suggested Fix

Unverified: reject an empty or one-character `s` with the same `HTTPException(400)` before indexing `s[-1]`. Add `range=` to the malformed-parameter tests.

`StellarTomlTool` calls the vulnerable `toml.parse()` (#652) directly on content fetched from a caller-supplied domain

**Files:** `backend/tools/StellarTomlTool.ts` (line 50)

### Problem

```ts
const url = `https://${domain}/.well-known/stellar.toml`;
const response = await axios.get(url, { responseType: 'text', timeout: 10_000 });
const parsed = toml.parse(response.data);
```

`domain` comes directly from the tool's input (`StellarTomlInputSchema.domain`, caller-supplied, no allowlist). The fetched content is parsed with the `toml` package — the exact dependency flagged in #652 as having two high-severity advisories: uncontrolled recursion (DoS) and prototype pollution via `__proto__` key-path desynchronization. This is the concrete, reachable call site where that vulnerability chain actually matters in this codebase: parsing untrusted, remotely-fetched, attacker-influenceable content is precisely the scenario those advisories describe.


### Subtasks

- [ ] Prioritize this call site specifically when addressing #652's dependency upgrade — it's the most directly exploitable path found in the codebase
- [ ] Consider a stopgap independent of the SDK upgrade: wrap `toml.parse()` with a size cap on `response.data` (stellar.toml files are small; reject anything abnormally large before parsing) and/or a recursion-depth guard
- [ ] Add a test with a deeply-nested / maliciously-shaped TOML fixture asserting the tool fails gracefully rather than hanging or crashing

ACH returns after settlement can't be recorded: late deposit returns cost the platform, late withdrawal returns strand customer money

## What happens

The ledger has no way to record an ACH return that arrives **after the entry settled**. `Services::Ach::Return` does only one thing: it calls `CancelStagedTransfer` on the real leg. That only works while the real leg is staged or pending. Once the entry settles, the leg is committed, Go answers `CancelStagedTransferRejected`, the service raises `Refused`, and nothing is recorded.

Real returns don't stop at settlement:
- Ordinary returns (R01 insufficient funds and the like) are due within 2 banking days of settlement.
- **Unauthorized-debit returns (R05, R07, R10) can arrive up to 60 days after settlement.**
- A withdrawal credit can also come back after it settles, for example when the receiving account is closed (R02).

## Why it matters

### A late deposit return is a loss to the platform, and first-party fraud exploits it

`ClearingPolicy` clears a deposit from the start of the 3rd Fed business day after it completed. Its comment says that's "until which an ACH return could still claw it back", which holds for ordinary returns but not for unauthorized ones. So an account owner can:

1. deposit $X by ACH debit from their own account;
2. wait for it to settle and clear (3 business days);
3. withdraw $X back to the same account, which is paid;
4. within 60 days, tell their bank the original debit was unauthorized (R10). The network takes $X back from the platform's bank.

The owner ends with the withdrawal and the refund. The platform is out $X, and **its ledger never learns**: the return can't be recorded, so the entity still looks square. The same money can also leave through another entity, via Securities (Purchase, then Draw to a colluding Borrower, then that Borrower's withdrawal). But a second party isn't needed.

The in-platform controls hold up to that point. Funding and every Securities money leg draw on *cleared* cash, and ruby ADR 0010 keeps an entity's cash covering its uncleared plus cleared cash, so uncleared money can't be spent or withdrawn. The exposure is entirely after clearing.

### A late withdrawal return is a loss to the customer

When a settled withdrawal credit is returned, the money comes back to the platform's bank, but the ledger can't re-credit the entity. Their money is stranded outside the ledger until someone reconciles by hand.

## What's needed (not yet designed)

- **Recording a post-settlement return.** For a deposit, reverse the settled real leg and its shadow leg, taking the money out of whichever of the entity's wallets still holds it. For a withdrawal, re-credit the entity.
- **What happens when the depositor no longer holds the money.** `cash` carries `debits_must_not_exceed_credits`, so today the ledger can't represent a customer who owes the platform. That needs a receivable, an overdraft allowance, or a recovery process.
- **An exposure policy for unauthorized returns**, which clearing doesn't cover. For example: hold or limit money leaving by ACH until 60 days, limits per entity or per deposit, or treating first deposits differently.

## Evidence

- `ruby/app/services/ach/return.rb`: returns only ever cancel the staged real leg.
- `ruby/app/services/ach/clearing_policy.rb`: `BUSINESS_DAYS = 3`, and the comment quoted above.
- `spec/alloy/ledger.als` now models a late return that the ledger can't see, with two checks, `UnclearedMoneyStaysBacked` and `LateReturnIsRecoverable`. They're running now, and their results will follow in a comment.

Authentication and the public demo mutations (`settleAch`, `clearAch`, ...) are out of scope here until deployment.

## Objectif

Aider Qwen à bien travailler, pas seulement l'empêcher de mal agir : des retours d'outils exploitables pour décider de la suite, et un signal de péremption avant d'éditer un fichier qui a changé depuis sa lecture.

## Origine

Analyse complémentaire du 2026-09-26 rapprochant les six tickets du lot des huit composantes d'un harnais d'agent (état, outils, planification, mémoire, orchestration, contexte, sécurité, évaluation) : le lot couvre le contrôle, rien n'améliore la qualité des interactions outillées. Constat cohérent avec le banc : la conduite de Qwen est très sensible à la forme des informations reçues (campagnes du 2026-09-26, `docs/banc-noyau-agents-md-2026-09-26.md`).

## Périmètre retenu (recentré après consolidation)

1. **Retours d'outils exploitables** — en consommant le résultat typé du socle #9, jamais en le dupliquant :
   - après une lecture : chemin, portion réellement lue, moyen de poursuivre ;
   - après un échec de modification : cause de l'échec et extrait actuel pertinent, plutôt qu'une erreur nue ;
   - après un test : résultat effectif, cas défaillant et extrait utile — journaux complets consultables à part.
2. **Péremption de lecture** : un fichier modifié depuis sa dernière lecture par l'agent est signalé comme potentiellement périmé avant une nouvelle édition. Recoupe la détection concurrente de #10 par l'intention, mais vit au niveau du tour de l'agent, sans journal d'effets.

## Explicitement repoussé

- Le **curateur de contexte par étape** (le harnais prépare ce que le modèle voit à chaque pas) : la mécanique n'existe pas dans smolcoder (`message[0]` + historique) et l'hypothèse est lourde — à instruire seulement si le banc (#13) montre que Qwen se noie (relectures inutiles, appels d'outils gaspillés). Décision sur mesure, pas sur intuition.
- Base vectorielle, second modèle de routage, framework d'agents, mémoire inter-missions : hors périmètre. La connaissance de projet passe par le pattern déjà disponible — fiches dans `docs/` + pointeurs courts dans `AGENTS.md`.

## Non-recouvrement (assumé)

- Compaction qui conserve le contrat et le dernier échec pertinent : critère de #8.
- Résultat d'exécution typé : socle de #9 — ce ticket le consomme.
- Détection des modifications concurrentes, journal d'effets : #10.
- Scénarios de démonstration (mission deux fichiers, interruption, modification humaine concurrente) : déjà les scénarios ciblés de #13.

## Critères d'acceptation

- Après un échec de modification, le retour permet à un fournisseur simulé de corriger au tour suivant sans relire le fichier entier (test déterministe).
- Une erreur au milieu d'un long journal reste accessible ; la troncature ne masque pas la cause décisive.
- Un fichier modifié entre lecture et écriture est signalé avant l'édition (modification externe injectée dans le test).
- Effet mesuré par #13 sur tâches appariées : réussite réelle, relectures, appels d'outils, durée — et aucune dégradation des refus de sécurité.

Après le socle typé de #9, mesuré par #13. Ordre du lot mis à jour : #13 minimal → #14 → #8 → #11 → #15..#18 → #9 → **#19** → #10.

Celui du lot (`smolcoder-harnais-6-issues.md`) : renforcer la boucle existante, décisions #1 à #7 acquises, tests conservés, entrée au journal dans le même commit, ne pas éditer `dist/`.

[CLAUDE-ai-01][EPIC] Retrieval SDDD orienté résultat — les 3 outils doivent rendre de l'exploitable, pas des fragments

## Pourquoi cet Epic

Les 3 outils de retrieval SDDD (`roosync_search` sémantique, `conversation_browser`, `codebase_search`) sont censés être critiques au harnais. Après 8+ mois ils sont **inutilisés et inutilisables** — pas parce qu'ils plantent, mais parce que **ce qu'ils rendent n'est pas exploitable en l'état**. Critique user (2026-06-16) : « même quand les outils renvoient quelque chose, le résultat est très pauvre — un chunk de 5 mots ou une ligne de code ; ça montre au mieux dans quel groupe de fichiers poursuivre en grep. » Et pour `conversation_browser` : « tous les agents passent en grep sur les JSON au bout de 2 tentatives. »

**Cet Epic est orienté RÉSULTAT, pas moyen.** La cible n'est pas « l'outil rend ≥1 résultat non-vide » mais « le résultat est exploitable sans rouvrir un grep ».

## Baseline mesurée en live (2026-06-16, vrais moteurs Qdrant/PG)

### codebase_search — confirme la critique, durement
Requête : `unified store Postgres join filters Qdrant semantic search results` (cherchait le bloc JOIN dans `search-semantic.tool.ts`, corrigé le jour même par #637).
- 5 hits, **tous labellisés `relevance: "good"`** (scores 0.84–0.88).
- **Tous `start_line == end_line` = une seule ligne** par hit.
- **ZÉRO hit sur le fichier source réel** (`search-semantic.tool.ts`). Les 5 hits = 2 baselines de config (`codebaseIndexQdrantUrl`), 2 fixtures de test, 1 test manuel.
- **Diagnostic** : (a) granularité **ligne** au lieu de **bloc/fonction** ; (b) classe les matchs de **tokens de surface** dans data/config/fixtures au-dessus de la **logique du code** ; (c) le label `relevance: "good"` à 0.88 sur une baseline de config est trompeur. Résultat = un panneau vers un groupe de fichiers — et ici **le mauvais groupe**.

### roosync_search sémantique — cassé en session live
Requête : `coordinator cron cadence decision 3h deep dispatch`.
- `results_count: 5, unique_tasks: 0, results: [], machines_found: ["unknown"]`.
- Confirme : le fix #637 (régression #2426, JOIN Postgres vide qui nuke tout) est **mergé mais pas encore live** (rebuild ≠ swap du process MCP — va-live au prochain restart). **Aujourd'hui, dans toute session en cours, l'outil rend `[]`.** Et même une fois restauré, la pauvreté de chunk identique à codebase_search reste à traiter.

### conversation_browser — `list` bon, drill-down cassé
- **`list` est exploitable** : taskId, firstUserMessage, lastMessage (vrai extrait substantiel), métadonnées riches. J'ai retrouvé le debrief CoursIA d'hier sans difficulté.
- **`view` (drill-down) s'effondre** : sur le debrief CoursIA (8.69 M chars), `view` avec `detailLevel: Summary, smart_truncation: true, max_output_length: 12000` a rendu **2 607 417 chars** — le `max_output_length` ignoré d'un facteur **~217×**. Le squelette est noyé sous des milliers de marqueurs `[Assistant]:`/`[User]:` **vides**, et chaque message substantiel est **tronqué en plein milieu de phrase**. La réponse EST récupérable, mais au prix d'un dump de 2,6 MB et d'un bruit énorme → **c'est exactement pourquoi un agent bascule en grep** : cibler la string exacte dans le JSONL est plus fiable et moins cher.
- **Diagnostic** : les primitives de navigation existent (skeleton, detail levels, smart_truncation) mais (a) `max_output_length` n'est pas respecté, (b) le squelette rend du vide au lieu de l'essentiel, (c) la troncature coupe le signal. L'outil expose des moyens, pas une réponse.

## Métrique nord (mesurable, honnête)

**Taux de décrochage vers grep** : un outil de retrieval réussit quand les agents **arrêtent** de basculer en Grep/Read direct sur le même sujet juste après l'avoir interrogé. Observable dans nos propres traces (`roosync_search`/`codebase_search`/`conversation_browser` suivi de `Grep`/`Read` sur le même thème dans les N tours suivants). Cible : → ~0.

install-root-audit.test.mjs: per-kind KIND_FLOORS + the aggregate floor don't catch a coordinated multi-kind thinning

**Dimension:** correctness

**Deferred from PR #2047 review** (ticket #2025).

**Finding:** `plugin/scripts/install-root-audit.test.mjs`'s `KIND_FLOORS = { sh: 8, js: 21 }` (added by #2025/PR #2047) plus the pre-existing `files.length > 30` aggregate guard each individually catch a single-kind collapse, but neither catches a **simultaneous, moderate thinning of both kinds at once**. Empirically confirmed by constructing a synthetic `kinds` map and calling the shipped, exported `kindFloorShortfalls(kinds)` directly:

```
sh: 14 -> 8   (-43%)
js: 36 -> 21  (-42%)
null: 2       (unchanged)
total: 52 -> 31   (aggregate floor is > 30, so 31 clears it)
```

`kindFloorShortfalls()` returns `[]` (each kind is exactly AT its own floor, and `< floor` is a strict comparison by design — see the existing 'accepts ... each kind sitting exactly at its floor' test), and `files.length > 30` also passes (31 > 30). **Neither guard fires**, despite the instrument set having lost 40% of its real coverage (21 of 52 tracked scripts). The floors don't need to land exactly on the boundary to go undetected either — any simultaneous reduction that keeps each kind \u2265 its own floor and the total > 30 is equally invisible, so the exposed window is much wider than the exact-boundary case above.

A single realistic root cause could produce this shape without being an extension-aware bug at all: a **path-prefix-based** filter change (e.g. a glob or exclusion list edited to drop a shared subdirectory that happens to hold both `.sh` and `.mjs` files) would thin both kinds together, unlike the extension-specific bug #2025 was written against.

**Out of scope for #2025**: that ticket's own stated purpose, and PR #2047's title, is narrowly "catch a one-kind drop" (the exact bug measured in PR #2023's review, where a filter dropped every `.sh` file while `.js`/`.mjs` was untouched). #2025's floors fully satisfy that acceptance criterion — confirmed by this review's own mutation testing (all-`.sh`-drop and all-`.mjs`-drop mutants both correctly caught). Defending against a *coordinated* multi-kind thinning is a materially different, larger problem (would need e.g. a live baseline-ratio comparison per kind rather than a static floor, or a floor tied to the aggregate rather than independent per-kind floors) and does not belong in a light-sized ticket.

**Suggested fix (not prescribed):** none prescribed here — flagging the gap for scoping. One option: track each kind's floor as a percentage of the CURRENT total tracked count (recomputed each run) rather than a static integer, so a proportional multi-kind thinning still shows up as a ratio shift. Needs its own design/sizing pass.

[M0/M1] Bootstrap Rust artifact engine + first CTF vertical slice

## Goal

Bootstrap this repository from an empty directory into the first usable milestone of a standalone, CTF-first binary analysis/extraction tool in Rust.

The uploaded implementation prompt is the project-level specification. This issue intentionally implements the **foundation plus one strong vertical slice** rather than attempting every listed format in one unreviewable PR.

The core design invariant is:

> Every useful thing discovered from input data is an Artifact, and every parser/extractor exists to discover additional Artifacts.

Normal supported workflows must not require external executables such as `7z`, `unrar`, `foremost`, `cabextract`, `unsquashfs`, Python packages, etc.

---

## Scope

### 1. Repository/bootstrap

Start from an empty working directory.

Create a production-quality Rust project using current stable Rust.

Prefer a **single package with a reusable library + thin CLI** for this first milestone unless a workspace split is clearly justified. Do not over-fragment into many tiny crates.

Required baseline files:

- `Cargo.toml`
- `src/lib.rs`
- `src/main.rs`
- `README.md`
- `LICENSE` (permissive; MIT or MIT/Apache-2.0 is acceptable)
- `docs/architecture.md`
- `docs/security.md`
- `docs/capabilities.md`
- GitHub Actions CI for Linux and Windows

The executable/package may use the repository name `ctf-tools` for now; keep naming isolated enough that it can be changed later without redesigning the engine.

### 2. Foundational data model

Implement the minimum stable internal model needed for future formats:

- `ByteSource`
  - whole file input
  - in-memory bytes
  - cheap bounded ranges/slices of a parent source
  - random access without forcing intermediate temp files
  - bounds-checked reads
- `Artifact`
  - stable ID
  - parent/source relationship
  - relationship kind
  - format/kind
  - offset/range and size
  - content identity/hash
  - confidence
  - validation evidence
  - extraction/recovery status
  - metadata
  - warnings/errors
- `ArtifactGraph`
  - preserves provenance
  - allows overlapping artifacts
  - does not silently discard one structurally valid artifact merely because another overlaps it
- Explainable confidence/evidence model
  - avoid arbitrary floating-point confidence scores
  - distinguish validated / recovered / partial / damaged / heuristic where applicable

Suggested relationship vocabulary should cover at least:

- contains
- embedded-in
- carved-from
- decompressed-from
- trailing-data
- leading-data
- overlap

### 3. Handler/scanner architecture

Create a format-handler abstraction that supports the staged model:

```text
fast candidate discovery
  -> format-specific structural validation
  -> boundary determination
  -> artifact creation
  -> optional extraction/child discovery
  -> recursive analysis
```

Requirements:

- magic bytes are candidates, not proof
- malformed candidates must not abort unrelated scanning
- format-specific handlers own their validation/boundary logic
- third-party crate APIs must stay behind project-owned abstractions
- no generic plugin system in this milestone

### 4. Recursive engine and safety limits

Implement recursive analysis using the same engine for root and child artifacts.

Add configurable limits from the beginning, including at least:

- max recursion depth
- max artifact count
- max total expanded bytes
- max single child size
- max archive entries
- max compression expansion ratio

Add content deduplication (BLAKE3 or similarly appropriate fast hash) so identical bytes are not recursively reprocessed forever.

Deduplication must not erase provenance: multiple logical artifacts may point at identical bytes while recursive work is performed once where safe.

### 5. Safe materialization/extraction layer

Implement deterministic extraction under a controlled output root.

Protect against at least:

- `../` traversal
- absolute paths
- Windows drive-letter paths

## Goal

Angular時代のdependency sprawl / vendor lock-inをAvalonia側で再発させず、AIPsiteNYGと将来のNYG reusable libraryを長期運用・商用再配布できるよう、外部依存を **Minimal Trusted Dependency Base** に限定する。

原則は「permissive OSSなら採用可能」ではない。

> BCL/.NET/Microsoft/.NET Foundation/Avaloniaを優先し、それ以外のOSSは自作コスト・correctness・security・performanceの観点から専門領域で合理性がある場合のみ、NYG-owned adapter境界とfallbackを条件に採用する。

2026-09時点のmigration baselineは **.NET 10 + Avalonia 12.1.x**。exact versionはCentral Package Managementで固定する。

UI/Interaction Architectureは `AIPsiteNYG_Avalonia_Frontend_Panel_Reorganization_v5_8_1_Review_Closure` を正本とし、Dock.Avalonia / MSAGLの扱いは本Issueの旧分類よりこの改訂方針を優先する。

## Trust tiers

### Tier 0 — Runtime / platform foundation

原則採用可能。

- .NET runtime / BCL
- Microsoft.Extensions.*
- ASP.NET Core / SignalR client
- System.Text.Json / System.Net.Http
- Avalonia 12.1.x

### Tier 1 — Closely governed ecosystem dependencies

用途が明確で、置換コストより採用価値が高い場合に採用可能。

- CommunityToolkit.Mvvm
- Microsoft Kiota
- Open XML SDK
- Microsoft.Data.Sqlite（local DB要件成立時のみ）
- Roslyn（editor/compiler tooling要件成立時のみ）

### Tier 2 — Specialist / adapter-approved dependencies

coreへ無条件追加しない。専用adapter/projectへ隔離し、exact version・license・transitive graph・fallback・replacement plan・contract testsを必須とする。

#### Approved for current architecture

- **Dock.Avalonia** — #815
  - docking / split / tab / float mechanics only
  - panel identity / ContextBinding / navigation / authorization / persistence schemaはNYG-owned
  - `NygWorkspaceLayout` をcanonical persistenceとする
  - adapter failure時はtabbed/single-pane fallback必須

- **MSAGL Core** — #816
  - node placement / edge routing / geometry computation only
  - bundled viewerをproduct UIにしない
  - RelationGraph semanticsは#814、visual/hit-test/viewportはNYG GraphRendererがowner
  - timeout/failure時はOutline/Table fallback必須

#### Conditional specialist examples

- SkiaSharp — Avalonia DrawingContextで性能不足が#805で継続的に実証された場合のみ
- PDFsharp / MigraDoc — PDF生成/処理要件が成立した場合のみ
- AvaloniaEdit — 通常TextBoxで満たせないeditor要件 + compatibility確認後のみ
- AngleSharp — HTML import/DOM処理要件成立時のみ
- codec/parser/native library — 自作が安全性/工数上明らかに不合理な場合のみ

### Tier 3 — Self-build / reject by default

baseline dependencyとして追加しない。

- Refit
- RestSharp
- ReactiveUI / ReactiveUI.Avalonia
- System.Reactive（明示exceptionなし）
- FluentAvalonia

Carry pfSense conversion skips into F-1 findings, not just a report parameter

Filed from #302's review (@SamikaPerera). Not started -- this is the scope stub, deliberately kept out of #302 itself.

## The gap #302 does not close

#302 fixed the *disclosure* half of a real problem: a skip note from `pfsense_convert.py` (a rule it could not model) used to reach the user exactly once, at upload, and be gone by the time a report was downloaded later. That's fixed -- the downloaded report now carries the skip list and its coverage statement stops claiming "nothing was skipped" when something was.

It does not fix the *modelling* half. Skipping a `pass` rule makes the emitted Cisco ACL stricter than the real device. A policy rule asserting "this traffic must be denied" can then report `status="none"` (clean) against the emitted ACL, while the real firewall actually permits that traffic -- a genuine policy violation, reported as a pass. See `CLAUDE.md` section 7's "UPDATE, 6 September" entry for the full direction analysis (skipping a `block` rule is the safe, noisy direction; skipping a `pass` rule is the dangerous, silent one).

## The more complete fix

Carry each conversion skip into the F-1 findings list itself, as a `status="error"` card -- which is what it actually is: "part of this config could not be checked." That would:

- Show up on the dashboard directly, not only in a downloaded report.
- Be counted by `analysis/coverage.py` the same way any other blind spot is, rather than needing a second, parallel `conversion_gaps` parameter (which #302 added as the smaller, faster fix).
- Let a reader connect a specific skip to the specific policy rule it might be silently affecting, if the finding names the interface/rule clearly enough.

## Why this needs its own scoping, not a bolt-on to #302

- **Which check owns it?** A conversion skip isn't produced by `access_control`, `policy_compliance`, or `routing` -- it's a property of the source file, discovered before the pipeline ever runs a check. Needs an id prefix decision (not `PC-`/`AC-`/`RT-`/`CH-`/`CV-` -- another collision the team has cared about avoiding, most recently for #239's `cve_mapping`).
- **Where does it enter the pipeline?** `analysis/pfsense_convert.py`'s skip list is produced by `web/main.py`'s upload handler, before `analysis.pipeline.analyse()` is ever called. Getting it into the findings list means either widening `analyse()`'s signature (an F-3 shared-contract question) or injecting it after the fact in `web/main.py` the way `_attach_explanations()` already injects a key -- but a NEW finding is a bigger change than a new key on an existing one.
- **Does it apply beyond pfSense?** Today only `pfsense_convert.py` produces a skip list. If Cisco IOS parsing (via Batfish) can also silently drop something, the same mechanism should probably cover it too, which needs checking rather than assuming.

## Acceptance criteria (draft, not final -- needs a design pass first)

- [ ] Decide the id prefix and which module owns emitting these findings.
- [ ] Decide how the skip list reaches `analyse()`/the pipeline without widening `run(bf)`'s signature for every other check.
- [ ] A skipped rule appears as a `status="error"` finding on the dashboard, not only in a downloaded report.
- [ ] `analysis/coverage.py`'s `conversion_gaps` parameter (added in #302) is retired once this lands, since the findings list itself would carry the same information.
- [ ] Full suite green, mutation-tested the same as #302's own two guards.

Você é um desenvolvedor sênior especializado em SA-MP (San Andreas Multiplayer), Pawn, Lua, MySQL, sistemas multiplayer e desenvolvimento de gamemodes para GTA San Andreas.

Quero criar um servidor SA-MP completo, profissional e moderno, com identidade própria. O projeto deve ser desenvolvido de forma organizada, modular, segura, otimizada e fácil de expandir.

OBJETIVO

Crie um gamemode completo de SA-MP com foco em Roleplay, inspirado nos grandes servidores brasileiros, mas sem copiar nomes, marcas, mapas ou sistemas proprietários.

O servidor deve possuir uma estrutura profissional, com:

- Gamemode em Pawn
- Banco de dados MySQL
- Sistema de contas
- Sistema de login e registro
- Sistema de personagens
- Sistema de empregos
- Sistema de organizações
- Sistema de casas
- Sistema de veículos

- Sistema de punições
- Sistema de chat
- Sistema de comandos
- Sistema de salvamento automático
- Sistema de logs
- Sistema de segurança anti-abuso
- Interface visual moderna
- TextDraws
- Dialogs
- Mapas e interiores personalizados
- Sistema de GPS
- Sistema de telefone
- Sistema de celular
- Sistema de notificações
- Sistema de HUD
- Sistema de scoreboard
- Sistema de ranking
- Sistema de estatísticas do jogador

ARQUITETURA

Não coloque todo o projeto em um único arquivo gigante.

Organize o código em módulos, por exemplo:

gamemodes/
main.pwn
