Hi! I maintain the python-roborock library and the Roborock integration in Home Assistant.

Roborock vacuums use a local protocol for direct commands, but they still route all map data strictly through the cloud (even though the map is stored locally). Even worse, if you try to block the vacuum from accessing the internet on your router, it will constantly reboot its Wi-Fi connection trying to re-establish a cloud connection, meaning you can't rely on just using a private local connection.

I built a self-hostable version of Roborock's cloud: https://github.com/Python-roborock/local_roborock_server

It works without having to open the device or root it, taking advantage of a couple of quirks during the onboarding process:

1) The vacuum has api-%s.roborock.com baked into its firmware. It injects the region directly into the string and this is the first exploit we take advantage of. The app will send in your region as a two letter code, e.g. 'us', 'eu', 'cn'. We send in a full URL ending with a '/' (e.g. 'example.com/'). The vacuum then treats "api-example.com" as the host and the rest as the URL path(e.g. 'api-example.com/.roborock.com'), directing its traffic to your server so long as there is a valid HTTPS certificate on that domain.

2) The second part of the handshake requires encrypting a message via a public key that is stored on Roborock's cloud where the private key pair is on the vacuum. We are able to reverse engineer the public key as the robot sends signatures with its message. Because of how RSA works, each signature is mathematically tied to the secret public key plus some extra noise. By gathering a few signatures across multiple onboarding attempts and taking their greatest common divisor, the noise cancels out and cleanly isolates the vacuum's actual public key which allows the server to encrypt its response and complete the pairing.

I have a full technical write up here: https://python-roborock.github.io/local_roborock_server/tech...

I wanted to share this on HN as I think this points to a very interesting thing that is happening. I have been playing with this idea for years in my head and I have not been able to get it to work (and I am not the only one who had looked into the api-%s avenue). I'm not a cryptography expert and had no idea that the signature exploit was even possible. I was stuck for long enough that I decided to throw the problem at some long-running agents, and they found the greatest common divisor exploit.

IoT companies put most of their security effort into the cloud, since that's what they actually run. The vacuum is just one device on someone's home network, so it gets less attention and corners get cut. I think LLMs that are willing to throw themselves at a problem for hours are going to make stuff like this a lot easier to pull off and a lot more common.

## Summary

Bring nodewright's container evidence to parity with the layout AICR settled on in [NVIDIA/aicr#2426](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aicr/issues/2426): a CycloneDX SBOM and an OpenVEX document attested to each **platform manifest** digest, with SLSA provenance on the index.

Nodewright is most of the way there already. The gaps are the attestation subject, a missing VEX document, and two cosign flags.

## Current state

`.github/actions/cosign-sign-sbom` already does the right things in the right order:

- `cosign sign` on the image
- `cosign attest --type cyclonedx` with a Syft-generated CycloneDX SBOM
- `actions/attest-build-provenance` for SLSA

Images are built multi-arch (`PLATFORMS: linux/amd64,linux/arm64`), and `operator-ci.yaml` resolves the **multi-platform manifest digest** and passes that as `subject-digest`.

## Gaps

### 1. Evidence is attached to the index, not the platform manifests

This is the substantive one, and it is the same defect AICR fixed in #2426.

`crane digest <tag>` returns the index. An SBOM describes exactly one root filesystem, so attaching a single SBOM to a multi-platform index means it cannot honestly describe either child. A consumer who resolves `linux/amd64` and enumerates referrers there finds nothing.

Fix: resolve each platform manifest with `crane digest --platform linux/<arch>` and attest that platform's SBOM to its own digest. AICR's `.github/actions/attest-image-from-tag` does this and fails closed if a platform is missing or resolves to the index digest, which catches a release that silently lost an architecture.

### 2. No VEX document

Nodewright publishes no OpenVEX (`.openvex.json` does not exist, zero references in the repo). Without one there is no way to say "this CVE does not apply to us and here is why", so every finding in a scan is either a real problem or unexplained noise.

AICR's `.openvex.json` plus the `aicr-managing-openvex` skill is the working model, including the constraint learned the hard way in [NVIDIA/aicr#2706](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aicr/issues/2706): the document is signed and published, so it carries triage statements only. Working notes belong in a separate state file with a lifecycle, or they grow without bound.

**Use OpenVEX, not CycloneDX, for the VEX.** `cosign attest --type cyclonedx` sets predicate type `https://cyclonedx.org/bom` regardless of whether the payload is an SBOM or a VEX, and a referrer descriptor has no name field. Two CycloneDX documents on one manifest are therefore indistinguishable in a referrers listing, and telling them apart means pulling and decoding every payload. OpenVEX gets `https://openvex.dev/ns`, so the listing stays self-describing.

### 3. `--new-bundle-format=true` is not set

Zero occurrences in the action. This controls whether the attestation publishes through the OCI referrers API or as a legacy `.att` tag, and it has moved between cosign releases. It should be an explicit decision rather than an inherited default. AICR sets it on every attest call and has a release-policy test pinning that.

### 4. No timeout on cosign calls

AICR bounds every `cosign attest` with `timeout --foreground 120s`, so a hung registry call fails the release instead of hanging the job.

## Worth copying, and worth not copying

**Copy:** the per-platform subject resolution with fail-closed checks; the OpenVEX guard that validates the document against the v0.2.0 contract before anything is signed, in both source and projection form; the digest-binding step that rewrites VEX product identifiers to `pkg:oci/<image>@sha256:<platform-digest>`; and the release-policy tests that pin attestation subjects and predicate types so a refactor cannot silently regress them.

**Do not copy:** AICR's `tooling` field history. See #2706 — an 8KB changelog accumulated in a field meant for a tool identifier, because the maintenance workflow required producing revision evide

## Priority: High | Effort: Small

SPINA gap review — approved ideas versus current implementation (22 September 2026)

## Review boundary

Requested by the owner before continuing signing work. Reviewed `main` at **6a33ab481574bf702920760610f803b59ffbd3ac**, tree **1c88730791d89e2798faef0f5e76fd2a5f081543**, against live Notion Current Project State, Create State decisions, and the [current Master296 scope amendment](https://github.com/GILBIC/spina-lending-app/issues/296#issuecomment-5627859431).

This is a broad, risk-focused source/decision review: repository structure and search, selected financial/source/renewal/role/document/release code, implementation records and acceptance requirements. It is **not an exhaustive line-by-line audit or a new full-suite/physical-device verification**. The working container could not clone the repository because external GitHub DNS was unavailable; connected GitHub source reads succeeded. Only an isolated copied JavaScript amount-normalization function was executed locally. No production database, private signing material or live accounts were inspected or changed.

The R numbers below are **recommended gap-review order, not a replacement or renumbering of frozen Master296**. Implementation choices and operational acceptance remain separate. No new code, PR, merge, deployment, payment, tax calculation or release authorization is created by this issue.

## Recommended priorities

### R1 — Connect approved tax/disclosure terms to the real loan lifecycle

**Classification: confirmed implementation/alignment gap.** The approved tax-itemized agreement candidate explicitly says source binding is not implemented. Runtime `FirstLoanTerms` has generic upfront deductions; its Regular schedule is principal plus contractual interest. `first_loan_documents.packet_fields` has generic deductions/net cash and interest totals, but no separate DST-upfront/GRT-within-repayments/tax-source mapping or Amount Financed/EIR fields. The renderer rejects unknown fields rather than inventing them. The tax projection helper exists, with synthetic proof/test consumers, but it is not called by this runtime renderer.

Minimal next work: bind the same authorized loan/tax calculation snapshot into approval, disclosure, agreement and complete schedule; preserve agreed installments; use existing calculators and reject unresolved inputs. Independently verify the protected accounting path for the chosen product/deductions rather than treating operational release as a posted journal. This review does not choose rates or declare tax/legal applicability.

**Done when:** exact supplied tax components reconcile across the locked packet, cash authorization, schedule, servicing and supported protected accounting; zero/unresolved remain distinct; stale-source and double-charge tests pass.

Sources: [tax candidate](https://github.com/GILBIC/spina-lending-app/blob/6a33ab481574bf702920760610f803b59ffbd3ac/docs/forms-documents/2026-09-16/templates/T02-cash-loan-agreement-r4-tax-itemization.md), [terms](https://github.com/GILBIC/spina-lending-app/blob/6a33ab481574bf702920760610f803b59ffbd3ac/gilbic_backend/src/gilbic_backend/first_loan_terms.py), [runtime renderer](https://github.com/GILBIC/spina-lending-app/blob/6a33ab481574bf702920760610f803b59ffbd3ac/gilbic_backend/src/gilbic_backend/first_loan_documents.py), [actual-book boundary](https://github.com/GILBIC/spina-lending-app/issues/443).

### R2 — Align renewal summaries with the authoritative signed schedule

**Classification: confirmed static source discrepancy; actual transaction impact not yet reproduced.** `_renewal_row` in `renewal_workflow_api.py` derives `contractual_total` from principal versus daily amount multiplied by product term (120 fallback), not the locked signed installments. `_payload` uses this total for paid percentage and `regular_50_percent_eligible`. This is not sufficient for variable/custom schedules or the newer 7x7 agreed-payment maturity. The Android renewal model consumes these fields.

- **B. An honest API detects a dishonest or misconfigured client.** The API rejects submissions that are unauthorized, malformed, or that honest clients would later refuse.

[Bug] Unimplemented SSRF Protection in URL Controller allows internal network scanning

### Description
The `controller/url.js` file contains a detailed `validateURL` function designed to prevent Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) by checking if a URL points to a private/internal IP address. 

However, this function is **never called** anywhere in the application. Additionally, the required `dns` and `net` modules are not imported, so if it were called, it would crash. 

As a result, when a user creates a short link pointing to an internal IP (e.g., `http://169.254.169.254` or `http://127.0.0.1:27017`), the `fetchWebsiteTitle` function executes a server-side `fetch()` against the internal network. This constitutes a Blind SSRF vulnerability, allowing attackers to probe internal services and metadata endpoints.

### Steps to Reproduce
1. Submit a request to create a short URL pointing to `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`.
2. Notice that the application does not reject the URL.
3. The server attempts to fetch the title of the page by making a direct request to the internal IP.

### Proposed Fix
1. Import the missing `dns` and `net` modules in `controller/url.js`.
2. Enforce the `await validateURL(url)` check inside `handleGenerateShortURL`, `handleGenerateShortUrlRender`, `handleUpdateShortURL`, and `handleBulkImport` before processing or saving the URL.
3. Add a fallback inside `fetchWebsiteTitle` to catch the rejection and fail safely.

Contract Telemetry, Authorization Guards, and Ledger Safety

Description:
  As a foundational smart contract library, our zero-knowledge verifier must be incredibly robust. Currently, the
  library lacks standardized event emissions (telemetry), strict access controls for state modification, and
  safeguards against network-level transaction limits.
  We need to implement a comprehensive security and observability layer. This involves standardizing how the
  contract emits diagnostic events during verification, strictly enforcing Soroban's require_auth mechanics on
  administrative functions, building automated rollback protections, and validating payload sizes before execution
  begins.

  Expected Behavior:
  The smart contract must clearly broadcast its state and verification results to off-chain indexers via events.
  All critical state changes (like updating a verification key) must be protected by cryptographic auth checks.
  Malformed or excessively large payloads should be rejected at the boundary before they burn excessive gas.
  Acceptance Criteria & Task Breakdown:

  Phase 1: Diagnostic Events & Telemetry

  [ ] Standardize and implement diagnostic event emissions during both successful and failed proof verification
  runs.
  [ ] Emit processing metrics (e.g., structural proof complexity, gas bound estimates) directly to the host ledger
  topics.
  [ ] Create standardized debugging topics that allow external wallets or block explorers to inspect the
  verification status across multi-step transactions.

  Phase 2: Authorization & Access Control

  [ ] Implement and enforce strict Env::require_auth() mechanics around all active parameter modification entry
  points (e.g., uploading a new verification key or updating structural reference strings).
  [ ] Build safety boundaries that prevent proof replay exploits across different ledger IDs (e.g., including chain
  ID and contract ID in the signed proof constraints).

  Phase 3: Ledger Bounds & Rollback Protections

  [ ] Code runtime structural size guards: before heavy parsing begins, validate that the incoming byte payloads
  strictly match the expected maximum ledger transfer capacities to prevent heap exhaustion or out-of-gas panics.
  [ ] Implement diagnostic rollback pipelines that safely and cleanly abort the standard transaction state if a
  proof fails, ensuring no partial state changes are permanently committed.
  [ ] Write integration tests simulating multi-contract topologies to confirm that malicious intermediary contracts
  cannot bypass the auth checks.

  Technical Constraints:

  • Event Bloat: While telemetry is important, emitting too many events costs gas. Ensure that diagnostic events
  are concise and structured optimally for Soroban's event serialization.
  • Fail-Safe execution: Rollback protections must guarantee that if a ZK proof is deemed invalid midway through a
  transaction, the exact error (ZkError) is returned gracefully, avoiding unhandled host panics.

This issue is therefore the durable integration owner for reviewer-convergence policy and CodeRabbit reviewer/remediation governance. It must not become an unbounded hardening PR itself.

---

## A. Autonomous review-convergence contract

Required operating rule for autonomous agents:

```text
initial implementation
→ exact-head CI/reviews
→ collect the whole current review epoch
→ ONE normal bundled root-cause correction wave
→ exact-head revalidation
→ terminal disposition / merge when safe
```

A later source-mutation wave is allowed only when the exact current head contains a demonstrable `CURRENT_REAL` correctness, security, data-integrity, merge-safety, or other release-invariant defect. Do not reject a real current defect merely to preserve an arbitrary wave count, but do not reopen a green exact head for speculative defense-in-depth.

After an exact head is green:

- historical/outdated findings are dispositioned, not reimplemented;
- provider quota/rate-limit/unavailability is never treated as clean-review evidence;
- reviewer silence is not `REVIEWED_CLEAN`;
- do not manually retrigger quota-exhausted providers merely to seek more comments;

The weekly rootfs sweep scans a rebuild, and the appliance has no published artifact to scan instead

Split out of #1313, which fixed this shape for the stack images and deliberately left the appliance alone. #1313's own body names it: "Same shape, deliberately out of scope here: `os-rootfs.yml`'s weekly sweep rebuilds the appliance rootfs from `develop-v2` and likewise never looks at the published RAUC bundle."

## The half that carries over

`os-rootfs.yml`'s Monday sweep runs `docker build -f os/rootfs/Dockerfile -t pithead-os-rootfs:ci` and points Trivy at that fresh build. A rebuild resolves apt at scan time, so it picks up Debian archive fixes that never reached the rootfs anyone actually booted — the same reason #1313 had to stop scanning `pithead-<service>:ci`.

It bites harder here than it did on the stack images. The appliance's Debian userland is frozen at bake time and has no apt at runtime, so this sweep is the only eye on podman, netavark, openssl and the kernel between releases. A sweep that silently re-resolves those packages is answering a question nobody asked.

## The half that does *not* carry over, and why this is its own issue

#1313's fix was available because the stack images are published: `release.sh` promotes them by digest to `ghcr.io/p2pool-starter-stack/pithead-<service>:vX.Y.Z`, so a sweep can resolve a tag to a digest and scan the exact published bytes. The appliance has no equivalent to point at. Checked rather than assumed:

- `scripts/release.sh`'s `IMAGES=(tor monero p2pool xmrig-proxy dashboard)` — the rootfs is not among them.
- Nothing under `scripts/` or `.github/workflows/` references `.raucb` at all.
- The bundle `pithead-os-vX.Y.Z.raucb` is produced by `os/rauc/mkbundle.sh` as part of the manual procedure in `docs/dev/appliance-release.md`, not by CI.

So there is no published artifact this sweep could be retargeted at today. That is the thing to decide, and it is a design question rather than a workflow edit — which is why it is not a line in #1313.

## What to weigh

1. Make the shipped rootfs addressable — publish the release's rootfs image (or the bundle) somewhere a digest scan can reach, and then the #1313 shape applies unchanged: resolve to a digest, scan the digest, apply the `.trivyignore` that shipped with it, report into a tracking issue rather than reddening a run.
2. Scan the artifact where it already lives — pull the release's `.raucb` at sweep time and scan the rootfs inside it. No publishing change, but the sweep has to learn the bundle format.
3. Record the gap and wait. The appliance has not shipped, so there is no fleet running an unscanned bundle yet. This is only acceptable while that stays true, and it stops being true at the first appliance release — which is the moment nobody will be thinking about it.

Whichever way it goes, the check that matters is the one #1313's report script already enforces for the stack: an artifact that could not be scanned must read UNCHECKED and fail the run, never count as clean.

## Not part of this

The engine pin. `os-rootfs.yml`'s Trivy step on `develop` is being pinned to `v0.74.0` separately (#1290's other half) — that is about which scanner runs, not which artifact it reads.

**Background:**
File path manipulation vulnerabilities arise when user-controllable data is placed into a file or URL path that is used on the server to access local resources, which may be within or outside the web root. If vulnerable, an attacker can modify the file path to access different resources, which may contain sensitive information. Even where an attack is constrained within the web root, it is often possible to retrieve items that are normally protected from direct access, such as application configuration files, the source code for server-executable scripts, or files with extensions that the web server is not configured to serve directly.

**Remediation:**
Ideally, application functionality should be designed in such a way that user-controllable data does not need to be placed into file or URL paths in order to access local resources on the server. This can normally be achieved by referencing known files via an index number rather than their name. If it is considered unavoidable to place user data into file or URL paths, the data should be strictly validated against a whitelist of accepted values. Note that when accessing resources within the web root, simply blocking input containing file path traversal sequences (such as dot-dot-slash) is not always sufficient to prevent retrieval of sensitive information, because some protected items may be accessible at the original path without using any traversal sequences.

## The problem

[ADR-0010](hyperion/docs/adr/0010-desktop-distribution-and-self-update.md) stages signing sensibly — M1 accepts Gatekeeper/SmartScreen first-install warnings, M2 adds Developer ID + notarization (macOS) and Azure Trusted Signing (Windows). **M2 assumes that when we arrive with a certificate, signing will work.** ADR-0014 shows it will not.

`codesign` refuses a dumped SBCL image — `main executable failed strict validation` — because `save-lisp-and-die :executable t` appends the Lisp core past `__LINKEDIT`, into the region the signature itself belongs in. A `.app` wrapping that image inherits the problem. This is the same root cause that stops `install_name_tool` working (ADR-0014).

**So the blocker is not the /yr and not the certificate. It is the shape of the artifact.** Today an Ouranos user holding a valid Developer ID still cannot produce a clean-installing Mac app; a Tauri user with the same certificate can. That is a capability our users cannot buy at any price, which makes this more than distribution polish.

## What is already verified

Measured on macOS 26 / SBCL 2.6.5 (recorded in ADR-0014's addendum):

- **Runtime + core as separate files signs and strictly verifies.** The SBCL runtime is an ordinary ~340K Mach-O: `codesign --options runtime --entitlements …` succeeds and `codesign --verify --strict` reports valid.
- **It still compiles at run time under hardened runtime**, given `com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit` (+ `allow-unsigned-executable-memory`). This matters more for us than for Electron — the Coalton REPL compiles on every input.
- **Hardened runtime enforces Team ID matching on every loaded dylib.** The libraries #78 carries must therefore be signed with the same certificate as the app. Ad-hoc signatures have no Team ID, so they do not match each other.
- **Hardened runtime strips `DYLD_*`**, which silently disables check 2 of `scripts/verify-bundle-macos.sh`. It will not fail — it will stop observing. A false green waiting for whoever turns hardening on.

## The trade, unmade

Runtime + core gives up the **single-binary property** ADR-0010's updater relies on (replace-and-re-exec becomes replace-two-files-consistently), and the runtime must locate its core when LaunchServices starts it with no arguments. That decision is the actual content of this issue.

Options worth costing: (a) runtime + core in `Contents/Resources/`, the Electron shape; (b) keep `:executable t` for CLI/dev artifacts and use runtime+core only for the signed `.app`; (c) accept right-click > Open on macOS indefinitely.

## The rule this implies for `cons desktop`

**Signing is a distribution-time parameter, never a build-time dependency.**

- `cons desktop build` must work with **zero credentials** — ad-hoc, first-install warning accepted. That stays the default and the contributor experience.
- `cons desktop ship` picks up a Developer ID / Azure identity from config or environment **only if present**, and says plainly what the user gets without one.
- Nobody should need an Apple account to build, test, or contribute.
- Notarization runs only on a Mac, so any CI story needs a macOS runner plus secrets — worth scoping alongside pre-publication issue 77.

## Not macOS-only

Windows SmartScreen wants Authenticode (ADR-0010 M2 names Azure Trusted Signing); whether a dumped SBCL `.exe` accepts an Authenticode signature is **unchecked** and is the exact analogue of this bug. Linux needs no signature at all. A Windows session should verify this — `signtool` on a dumped image — before M2 is planned in detail.

[Bug]: cua-s1-forms answers a confident skip outside its 55-concept label catalogue (97.5% in-distribution vs 29.3% held-out)

### Primary area

Documentation

### Summary

On a held-out set whose field concepts fall outside the 55-entry catalogue in `cua_s1/concepts.py`, `cua-s1-forms` scores 29.3% (12/41) while answering `skip` on 36 of 41 elements at 0.974 mean confidence. The same checkpoint scores 97.5% on in-distribution episodes from the repository's own `cua_s1.synth`. The model card's Limitations section says the checkpoint is "not validated on arbitrary real-world forms outside the demo set", but does not state that the failure outside the catalogue is a confident `skip` rather than a low-confidence or abstaining output, which is the part that matters for a downstream executor.

### Reproduction

1. Convert the published `.pt` (see #3977) to `ckpt/model.safetensors` + `ckpt/config.json`.
2. Run the scripts in https://gist.github.com/0xsline/2d492b5baa5b18110b97e733f0bb697d:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=src:. .venv/bin/python device_matrix.py   # device/batching control
PYTHONPATH=src:. .venv/bin/python ablate.py          # in-distribution baseline, option-count, vocabulary
PYTHONPATH=src:. .venv/bin/python ablate2.py         # 2x2x2 over doc label / form label / form title
```

`heldout.py` contains 41 decisions over 5 forms (logistics, hardware, DevOps, veterinary, and one Chinese form). Contexts are rendered with the package's own `cua_s1.schema.render_context`, and options with `Entity.option()`, so the input format is identical to training. The action mix is 25 fill, 7 skip, 4 check, 5 click.

### Expected behavior

The model card documents the operating boundary in a way a downstream integrator can act on: which label vocabulary the checkpoint depends on, and what it does when an element falls outside it.

### Actual behavior

```
in-distribution (cua_s1.synth, seeds 900000-900119, 3070 decisions) : 2993/3070 = 97.49%
  per action: skip 1632/1638 · fill 1137/1208 · click 120/120 · check 104/104

held-out label vocabulary (41 decisions)                            :   12/41 = 29.27%
  per action: fill 2/25 · skip 7/7 · check 2/4 · click 1/5
  36 of 41 predictions are `skip`; mean confidence 0.974
```

`skip` scores 7/7 only because the model emits `skip` almost everywhere. `check` and `click` also fail on held-out forms, for example `Button "Register Device"` and `CheckBox "Register for firmware updates"`, even though those decisions do not depend on any document entity.

### Environment

```
Cua component and version/commit: libs/cua-s1 @ b7f7e2d (PR #3964), artifact cua-ai/cua-s1-forms @ 2026-09-18T19:35:43Z
Operating system and architecture: macOS 27.0.0, arm64 (Apple M5)
Python / torch: CPython 3.13.2, torch 2.14.0, safetensors 0.8.0
```

### Evidence

Three controls rule out the obvious harness explanations.

**Device and batching.** Identical predictions across all four combinations, so this is not an MPS or padding artifact:

```
cpu/one batch  29.3%   mps/one batch  29.3%
cpu/batch=1    29.3%   mps/batch=1    29.3%      41/41 identical predictions
```

**Harness correctness.** The same code path reaches 97.49% on `cua_s1.synth` episodes, so the context and option rendering are right.

**Option count.** The held-out forms expose 6 entities + 3 fixed actions, against a mean of 20.4 options in-distribution. Trimming in-distribution option lists to the same width does not move accuracy, so width is not the cause:

```
full option lists (~20 options) : 2993/3070 = 97.49%
trimmed to 6 entities + 3       : 2998/3070 = 97.65%
```

**What does move it** is the label wording. Holding structure, shape, values, and action mix fixed and only renaming labels to phrases from `concepts.py`:

```
held-out labels (logistics/DevOps/veterinary/Chinese) : 12/41 = 29%
same shape, in-catalogue labels                       : 11/11 = 100%
```

[Security] PyQt6-Qt6 6.11.2 — MEDIUM: CVE-2026-79680 Qt VNC Server password-authentication bypass (fixed in Qt 6.11.3, no wheel yet; Linux artifacts bundle libqvnc.so)

## Summary

A scheduled dependency CVE scan (2026-09-29) over the full pinned snapshot found **one new** vulnerability affecting a current pin and **no Critical or High findings**.

`requirements/constraints.txt` pins `PyQt6-Qt6==6.11.2`. That pin is inside the affected range of **CVE-2026-79680**, an authentication bypass in the password mechanism of the **Qt VNC Server** platform plugin, published 2026-09-24 — i.e. *after* the previous scan (#1079, 2026-09-20). The three Qt advisories published since that scan were checked; the other two (CVE-2026-78253, CVE-2026-79616) are fixed *in* 6.11.2 and do not affect the pin.

All 49 pinned Python distributions are otherwise clean (see below). CVE-2026-15037 (LOW) remains open and is already tracked in #1079 — not duplicated here.

---

## The finding

### CVE-2026-79680 — authentication bypass in Qt VNC Server (`qvnc` platform plugin)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Component** | Qt VNC platform plugin (`plugins/platforms/libqvnc.so`, qtbase), vendored by `PyQt6-Qt6==6.11.2` |
| **Affected** | Qt 6.4.0 – 6.8.8 and 6.9.0 – **6.11.2** (our pin is in range) |
| **Fixed in** | Qt **6.11.3** (and the 6.8 LTS line after 6.8.8) |
| **Severity** | **Medium / Moderate** — CVSS 4.0 base **4.5** (GitHub Advisory Database rating: Moderate) |
| **CWE** | CWE-288 Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel |
| **Advisory** | [GHSA-wc8f-vjgx-jxrw](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wc8f-vjgx-jxrw) (GitHub DB, *Unreviewed*, published 2026-09-24) |

**Description.** An attacker using a specially modified VNC client that violates the RFB protocol can bypass the password authentication of Qt's VNC server and gain unauthorized remote access to the shared application, compromising the confidentiality and integrity of that session. The VNC server is only ever active when the application is started with the `vnc` QPA platform (`-platform vnc` or `QT_QPA_PLATFORM=vnc`).

---

## Exposure assessment

- **bgremover never selects the `vnc` platform.** Repo-wide grep: no `QT_QPA_PLATFORM=vnc` / `-platform vnc` anywhere in `bgremover/`, `scripts/`, `packaging/` or the docs. The only mentions of `vnc` are `preview3d_capability.NON_RENDERABLE_PLATFORMS` (which *refuses* 3D on that platform) and its documentation. `qt_plugins.py` only sets `QT_QPA_PLATFORM_PLUGIN_PATH`; the platform choice is left to Qt/the environment.
- **The vulnerable plugin ships in the Linux artifacts.** Verified in the installed `PyQt6-Qt6` 6.11.2 Linux wheel (`manylinux_2_34_x86_64`): `PyQt6/Qt6/plugins/platforms/libqvnc.so` is present (122 KiB) alongside `xcb`/`wayland`/`offscreen`/`minimal`/`eglfs`/`linuxfb`/`vkkhrdisplay`/`minimalegl`. `build_appimage.sh` bundles the wheel unchanged and `build_deb.sh` wraps that AppImage, so **both Linux AppImages and both `.deb`s carry the vulnerable code**; `_stage_platform_plugins` copies every file of the `platforms` directory into its staging tree at start-up, so the staged copy carries it too.
- **The macOS DMG is not affected.** The `PyQt6-Qt6==6.11.2` `macosx_11_0_arm64` wheel was downloaded and listed today: its `platforms/` directory contains only `libqcocoa.dylib`, `libqminimal.dylib` and `libqoffscreen.dylib` — no VNC plugin, so the code is absent from the macOS bundle.
- **Attack precondition:** a user must deliberately start BgRemover under the VNC platform (e.g. `QT_QPA_PLATFORM=vnc ./BgRemover.AppImage` on a headless Raspberry Pi to reach the UI remotely) *and* rely on the plugin's password option for access control *and* expose the VNC port. Nothing in the shipped app or docs suggests or enables that setup. Exposure is therefore **opt-in by the user, not application-triggered** — but the bytes are in the artifact, and the Pi is a supported target where a headless-VNC workflow is not far-fetched.

低

A

## Summary

Make dependency, action, runtime, package-manager, and container inputs explicit and continuously reviewed. Reduce avoidable toolchain ambiguity and add supply-chain controls appropriate for a public production site and future MDX compilation pipeline.

## Priority

**P1 — preventative security and reproducibility.** Begin after PR #51. Some cleanup can land with #52, but this issue owns policy and ongoing enforcement rather than repository formatting.

## Current state

Completed by #152:

- `flake.nix` / `flake.lock` own the development and CI toolchain;
- GitHub Actions owns required validation on minimal Dubnium JIT runners;
- Cloudflare Pages Functions / Wrangler own production runtime and deployment;
- GitLab is mirror-only and the divergent GitLab CI pipeline is removed;
- Docker is explicitly a secondary local portability path;
- Node 24, Yarn 1.22.22, Playwright 1.60.0, TypeScript 5.9.3, and Wrangler 4.114.0 authority is mechanically checked;
- frozen installs are enforced on CI/secondary install paths;
- stale scaffold metadata, drifting version claims, and mixed `npm run` indirection are resolved;
- build-only MDX/compiler content remains proven absent from request/browser runtime surfaces.

- #157 adds immutable external Action pins, Dependency Review, and CodeQL; do not mark these complete until exact-head required CI is green and the PR merges;
- secret-scanning / push-protection posture still requires repository/organization settings evidence;
- dependency grouping/supersession remains shared-policy work in `hackelia-micrantha/.github#106`;
- artifact/SBOM scanning should be added only where an operational release artifact justifies a durable inventory/scanning contract.

## Goals

- Establish one documented and reproducible JavaScript toolchain.
- Detect vulnerable, malicious, stale, or unexpectedly expanded dependencies before merge.
- Keep CI actions and build inputs pinned and reviewable.
- Produce software inventory for deployed artifacts where useful.
- Clarify whether Docker is operational and scan it accordingly.
- Prevent build-only content tooling from entering runtime/browser dependency surfaces.

## Dependency and action controls

- Ensure secret scanning and push protection are enabled where repository/organization settings permit.
- Pin third-party GitHub Actions to immutable commit SHAs or document justified exceptions.
- Keep workflow permissions read-only by default and grant narrow job-level permissions only when required.

[P1] Respect custom Django filter overrides before reporting vulnerable built-ins

A custom template filter named `striptags` is still attributed to `django.template.defaultfilters.striptags`. This can produce an `exploitable-vulnerability` finding for a vulnerable implementation that the template never calls.

Observed on engine 0.18.0, commit `5610778`.

### Reproduction

Use a Django dependency version covered by an advisory whose entry point is `python.django.template.defaultfilters.striptags` (the existing template-flow fixture uses Django 4.2.16).

```python
# app/templatetags/custom.py; include the package __init__.py files
from django import template

register = template.Library()

@register.filter(name="striptags")
def replace(value):
    return "constant"
```

```django
{% load custom %}
{{ bio|striptags }}
```

Render that template from a view with `{'bio': request.POST['bio']}` as the context.

Actual result: the built-in `python.django.template.defaultfilters.striptags` is reported as exploitable. Expected: the local filter registration overrides the built-in; this application is not evidence of a call to the vulnerable built-in.

### Location and ownership

[Filter applications are resolved by name alone](https://github.com/CoreTrace/coretrace-python-analyzer/blob/5610778/src/coretrace_python/taint/templates.py#L477-L488).

Resolve filter identity using the template's loaded libraries and registration precedence. Reuse semantic information for project definitions where possible. If a library's definitions cannot be resolved, preserve uncertainty rather than asserting a built-in target. The same resolved identity must feed reachability and taint evidence.

### Acceptance criteria

- The custom override above produces no reachable/exploitable claim naming the built-in for this application.
- The same template without an overriding library still recognizes the built-in.
- Unknown libraries do not manufacture proof of a built-in call or unsupported proof of absence.
- Loading order and selective imports such as `{% load striptags from custom %}` are handled consistently.

[P2] Preserve parent template flows rendered through block.super

When a child overrides a Django template block and renders `{{ block.super }}`, filter applications in the parent block are removed from render-context flow analysis even though Django executes them.

Observed on engine 0.18.0, commit `5610778`.

### Reproduction

```django
{# app/templates/app/base.html #}
{% block body %}{{ bio|striptags }}{% endblock %}
```

```django
{# app/templates/app/profile.html #}
{% extends 'app/base.html' %}
{% block body %}{{ block.super }}{% endblock %}
```

Render `app/profile.html` with `{'bio': request.POST['bio']}` as the context, using the vulnerable Django/advisory setup for the `striptags` entry point.

Actual result: the filter remains reachable, but the exploitable context-to-filter flow disappears. A child that leaves the parent's block intact preserves that flow.

### Location and ownership

- [Replaced blocks are excluded](https://github.com/CoreTrace/coretrace-python-analyzer/blob/5610778/src/coretrace_python/taint/templates.py#L374-L380)
- [The overridden set is propagated to the parent](https://github.com/CoreTrace/coretrace-python-analyzer/blob/5610778/src/coretrace_python/taint/templates.py#L439-L453)

Model `block.super` in template inheritance/context-flow composition so parent applications are retained when the child renders them. Do not retain every overridden parent block unconditionally: a complete replacement must still exclude the parent flow.

### Acceptance criteria

- The reproduction retains the flow from `bio` to the parent's `striptags` application, with the parent template location as evidence.
- A replacement block without `block.super` still excludes that parent flow.
- Unrelated overridden blocks do not become reachable through another block's `super`.
- Nested inheritance preserves the appropriate parent chain without duplicate findings.

Local storage serves untrusted HTML inline on the application origin

## Problem
Local storage accepts an uploader-controlled Content-Type, persists it, and serves that type inline from the application's storage route without an attachment or sandbox policy. Uploading HTML and opening its download URL produces an executable same-origin document.

**Priority: P1 / high when untrusted uploads share the application origin (stored script execution).**

## Affected components
`engine.go`: `StorageHandler` PUT and GET branches; `storage/local/local.go`: `ServeFile`.
Audited commit: b838998a4affdfe7fac3b2be8a265daff29344a2.

## Evidence / reproduction
Validated via public storage callbacks and httptest requests with the local adapter:
1. Obtain an upload capability and a download capability through StorageCtx.
2. PUT `<script>document.title='audit'</script>` with `Content-Type: text/html` to the upload URL.
3. GET the download URL without Origin (as with ordinary document navigation).

Both responses return 200. The download headers include `Content-Type: text/html` and the body contains the unchanged script. There is no Content-Disposition attachment or sandbox CSP. The GET route intentionally accepts requests without Origin, so its CORS checks do not prevent navigation to this content. This probe validates the HTTP response; no browser exploit was executed.

## Why it matters
An application that grants upload/download capabilities to users and mounts storage on its own origin can turn a shared file link into stored script execution under that origin. Capability expiry controls access to the file, not the privileges of the rendered document. This finding is specific to same-origin local serving; S3 redirects have a different origin boundary.

## Remediation direction
Default untrusted downloads to attachment with a safe Content-Type and nosniff, or enforce an appropriately sandboxed response. Provide an explicit opt-in for inline active content and recommend a separate untrusted-content origin. Add storage tests for HTML/SVG uploads and response security headers.

providers/macos-dev: replace child_process.exec(commandString) with the execFile argv shape

Surfaced by: #185 review

`providers/macos-dev/src/shell.ts:44` runs commands with `child_process.exec(commandString)`, which
spawns `/bin/sh -c` on an interpolated string. `providers/docker/src/shell.ts:43` does the same job
with `child_process.execFile(cmd, args, …)`, where arguments reach the OS directly and no shell parses
the assembled string.

macos-dev is the only provider that executes on the developer's host, with the operator's privileges.
It is the one where the difference matters most, and it is the one still on the weaker shape.

## What this is not

Not a claim that the current code has an exploitable injection today. The trust boundary is the
Launchfile itself, and `provider.ts:438,454` already run `build`, `install`, `dev`, `start` and
`release` from it. #185 moved `bootstrap` onto the argv-vector `spawn("/bin/sh", ["-c", command])`
shape rather than routing it through `shell.ts`, precisely to avoid widening this surface.

The point is that `execFile(cmd, args)` is provably safe regardless of input, whereas
`exec(interpolatedString)` is safe only as long as every caller stays careful — and static analysis
(CodeQL, CWE-78) flags the second shape whatever the runtime guarantees.

## Proposal

1. Change `shell()` to `shell(cmd: string, args: string[], opts?)`, matching
   `providers/docker/src/shell.ts` exactly (P-5: the two reference providers should handle this the
   same way).
2. For call sites that genuinely need a shell — a Launchfile `command` string, which `SPEC.md`
   § Command interpretation says a POSIX shell interprets — pass the command as a single argv
   element: `shell("/bin/sh", ["-c", command], …)`.
3. Audit every call site; build the argument arrays before the call rather than concatenating.

## Acceptance

- `grep -n "cpExec(" providers/macos-dev/src/` returns nothing.
- The existing macos-dev suite stays green, plus argv-shape assertions on the migrated call sites,
  mirroring what #185 added for `bootstrap`.

feat(audit): CEI-001 — flag external invocations preceding state writes

## Problem

The built-in audit engine currently has no rule identifying the Checks-Effects-Interactions ordering hazard where an **external contract invocation occurs before a later state write** in the same function.

This is a classic reentrancy-preco pattern in Soroban contracts: a contract call that pulls control flow away (where the callee may re-enter) placed before a state mutation creates a window where the invariant guarded by the write can be violated.

The existing `FnVisitor` in `crates/sdkt-audit/src/audit.rs` already walks `ExprCall` and `ExprMethodCall` nodes in source order, providing a foundation for an ordering-aware rule. There is no rule today that uses that ordering information to flag this pattern.

Concrete example:

```rust
pub fn swap(env: Env, to: Address) {
    // External invocation FIRST
    env.invoke_contract(&pool, sym!("withdraw"), ...);
    // State write AFTER — vulnerable window
    env.storage().set(...);
}
```

Expected: CEI-001 warning that the external invocation precedes a state write in the same function.

```rust
pub fn swap_safe(env: Env, to: Address) {
    // State write FIRST (effects before interactions)
    env.storage().set(...);
    // External invocation AFTER — no hazard
    env.invoke_contract(&pool, sym!("withdraw"), ...);
}
```

Expected: no CEI-001 finding.

## Current behavior

`sdkt audit` reports AUTH-001..004 and MOVE-001. There is no ordering check for external-call-before-state-write.

## Why it matters

- CEI ordering is a primary correctness invariant for Soroban contracts, especially token/balance bookkeeping.
- The AST visitor infrastructure already collects call and method-call nodes in order; an ordering rule is a natural, bounded addition.
- It fills a coverage gap distinct from the existing AUTH family (auth presence) and MOVE-001 (move semantics).

## Scope

- Add a `CEI-001` built-in rule (id, severity, description, registration) following the existing rule pattern in `rules.rs`.
- Detect the relevant **external contract invocation pattern** (e.g. `invoke_contract` / `invoke_contract_light`) using the existing method-call counting approach.
- Detect **state-write patterns** supported by the existing source analysis (e.g. `storage().set` / `.write` style method calls, or whatever write pattern the current visitor can reliably identify — document the chosen set).
- Flag **only** when both patterns occur in the same function AND the external invocation precedes the state write (ordering-sensitive).
- Preserve full support for rule registration, `--disable CEI-001`, severity output, and normal audit output formats.
- Clearly document the heuristic nature and its limitations in the rule description and docs.
- Use **Warning** severity (matching the spirit of MOVE-001's ordering signal; if the repo's `Severity` enum lacks a Warning level suitable here, map to the closest equivalent and document it).
- Emit a single finding per function (not one per violation pair) to keep output bounded.

False-positive boundary: The rule must require **both** an external invocation and a later state-write pattern. Do not flag functions containing only one of those patterns.

## Out of scope

- Redesigning `FnVisitor` to track new node kinds beyond what is needed for this rule.
- Full symbolic reentrancy analysis.
- Interprocedural analysis (cross-function).
- Proving exploitability or producing a runnable PoC.
- Redesigning the audit engine or registry.
- New rule IDs beyond CEI-001.

## Implementation direction

Follow the `Auth001`/`Move001` pattern: a unit struct implementing `AuditRule`, registered in `all_rules()`. Extend the `FnScan` or add a small per-function ordered-marker list if the current counters (`invoke_contract`, etc.) are insufficient to capture *order*. The rule body then scans the ordered list, finds an external-invocation marker followed by a state-write marker, and emits one finding.

Netty's STOMP codec (io.netty:netty-codec-stomp) contains a ByteBuf leak in StompSubframeDecoder. Once a frame's declared content-length has been fully read, the decoder allocates a chunk buffer from the channel allocator and parks it in an instance field while waiting for the single NUL byte that terminates the frame. If that byte never arrives, the buffer is never released: the replay Signal thrown by skipNullCharacter extends Error rather than Exception, so the decoder's catch(Exception) release path does not run, and StompSubframeDecoder overrides neither handlerRemoved0 nor channelInactive, so the buffer also survives channel teardown. A remote peer can leak one allocator buffer per connection by sending a complete, well-formed frame body and withholding its terminating NUL byte; with the default pooled allocator the memory is never returned to the pool or reclaimed by garbage collection, so the leak accumulates for the lifetime of the process and can lead to memory exhaustion. This affects versions up to and including 4.1.137.Final and versions 4.2.0.Final through 4.2.17.Final; it is fixed in 4.1.138.Final and 4.2.18.Final.

WGSL is_finite_value NaN/Inf guard is a float self-comparison that fast-math may fold away (activation.wgsl, relu.wgsl, bias.wgsl)

<!-- finding-id: SEC-e8e1dd84a447 -->
<!-- cwe: CWE-754 -->

Three WGSL kernels detect NaN / ±Inf with a float self-comparison helper,
`is_finite_value` (`value != value`, then `abs(value) <= MAX_F32`). WGSL does
not guarantee IEEE-754 NaN/Inf semantics at runtime — an implementation may
assume they are absent and an overflowing result is indeterminate, which is
why WGSL has no `isNan`/`isInf` builtin — so a backend compiling with
fast-math is free to fold both comparisons to "finite" and delete the guard.
Severity low (numeric integrity of discovery statistics only, no memory
safety impact: every index is still bounds-guarded), confidence low (reasoned
from the WGSL rules and wgpu-hal's Metal compile options, not reproduced on a
Metal device).

Found by the chunk 9 security sweep, Issue #2290 (shader layer #2232, tracker #2094).

## Why it matters

- `src/shaders/activation.wgsl:35` (`is_finite_value`), used at L210 (input
  skip) and L223 (the output guard that sets `valid = 1u`).
- `src/shaders/relu.wgsl:35`, used at L63 (input skip).
- `src/shaders/bias.wgsl:38`, used at L253, L264 and L273 — the only
  non-finite handling in that kernel (its `epsilon` uniform is never read).

Inputs are already filtered finite on the host
(`src/analysis/diagnostics/target_data.rs:74`–`:75`), so the guards that
matter are the *output* guards: a finite input can still overflow inside the
kernel — `incoming_weight * activation` (`activation.wgsl:216`–`:217`,
`bias.wgsl:261`), `gelu`'s `x * x * x` (`activation.wgsl:44`), and every
`x * x` square. When the guard is folded away, an Inf/NaN output is marked
`valid = 1u` and summed into the per-workgroup partial sums
(`activation_reduce.wgsl:44`–`:47`), so one overflowing sample poisons the
whole candidate's aggregate instead of being dropped as the CPU path drops
it. The host applies no finiteness check to the reduced sums in
`src/analysis/gpu/activation_evaluation.rs` (its two `is_finite` calls, L339
and L443, filter inputs only).

wgpu-hal 30's Metal backend builds shaders with a default `MTLCompileOptions`
(`wgpu-hal-30.0.1/src/metal/device.rs:272`) and never disables fast math,
which is Metal's default.

## Attacker model

A caller of the FFI analysis entry points who controls the recorded
activations / errors of a creature. FFI validation only requires them to be
finite (Issue #2135), so large finite values are accepted. No privilege
beyond submitting a discovery run.

## Trigger

A recorded activation (or `orientation * scale` / `incoming_weight`) large
enough that the kernel's product or square overflows f32 (|x| ≳ 1.8e19 for a
square, ≳ 7e12 for GELU's cube), analysed on a backend that compiles the WGSL
under fast-math (Metal by default).

## Exploit sketch

1. Submit training records where one sample's source activation is 1e20
   (finite, so FFI validation passes).
2. `activation.wgsl` computes `output_sq = output_val * output_val = +Inf`;
   the L223 guard, folded to `true`, marks it `valid = 1u`.
3. `activation_reduce.wgsl` adds `+Inf` into that workgroup's partial sum;
   the host totals it and the candidate's statistics become Inf/NaN, so the
   candidate is mis-scored (NaN never wins a `>` comparison; Inf can) instead
   of the single sample being skipped.

## Suggested fix

Replace the float self-comparison with an integer test that fast-math cannot
fold: `(bitcast<u32>(v) & 0x7f800000u) != 0x7f800000u` is `true` exactly for
finite `v`. Share it across `activation.wgsl`, `relu.wgsl` and `bias.wgsl`
(and `matching.wgsl` if it survives removal). Add a naga-validated CPU test
pinning the helper's body, and a GPU-gated test feeding an overflowing sample
that asserts `valid == 0`.

# Feature Specification: Pin lbug extension bytes and diagnose ABI staleness in stage-lbug-extensions.sh

**Feature Branch**: `fabrik/issue-593`
**Created**: 2026-09-15
**Status**: Specified
**Input**: User description: "scripts/stage-lbug-extensions.sh trusts whatever the CDN serves — pin the extension bytes and assert their ABI version"

## Background

`scripts/stage-lbug-extensions.sh` downloads the lbug `vector` and `fts` extensions from `extension.ladybugdb.com` at build time and stages them into the release archive. It currently verifies only that the downloaded files exist and are non-empty — it does not verify **which** files it got.

That is unsound because upstream publishes extensions at a per-minor path and overwrites them on patch releases: the files served at `v0.20.0/win_amd64/` are 0.20.2-era builds served under a `v0.20.0` path, and `LBUG_EXTENSION_VERSION` (the lbug minor) means every 0.20.x patch resolves to that same path and gets whatever was most recently built there. The extension ABI a build picks up therefore depends on *when* the build runs, not on anything in this repository.

This has real, observed consequences on Windows:

| core | CDN extensions (0.20.2-era) |
|---|---|
| 0.20.0 | crashes at `LOAD EXTENSION` |
| 0.20.2 | works |
| 0.20.3 | works |
| 0.20.4 | loads, then crashes at `CREATE_VECTOR_INDEX` / `CREATE_FTS_INDEX` |

A silent upstream overwrite can turn a working bundle into a process-crashing one with no change on this repository's side, and critically, no build failure — the staging script succeeds, Linux/macOS CI passes, and only Windows users find out. The currently-shipping v0.15.0 release depends on this exact accident of upstream's publishing schedule (0.20.2-era extensions happen to be ABI-compatible with the pinned 0.20.3 core), and upstream is expected to rebuild and republish that per-minor path again when it cuts 0.21.x.

## User Scenarios & Testing *(mandatory)*

### User Story 1 - Pin and verify extension bytes (Priority: P1)

As the maintainer of the release build, I need `stage-lbug-extensions.sh` to fail immediately when the bytes it downloads from the CDN differ from a known-good, checked-in set, so that an upstream overwrite at the shared per-minor CDN path can never silently change what ships without a build failure.

**Why this priority**: This alone closes the vulnerability described in the issue. Without it, a build can silently bundle ABI-incompatible extensions with no CI signal — exactly the 0.20.4-vs-0.20.2-era-extension pairing already observed to crash on Windows.

**Independent Test**: Run the staging script against a pin file with a deliberately wrong sha256 for one platform/extension pair and confirm the build fails with a clear error before staging any files. Run it again with correct pins and confirm the build succeeds unchanged.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** a checked-in pin file with the expected sha256 for each staged platform+extension pair, **When** `stage-lbug-extensions.sh` downloads an extension from the CDN, **Then** it computes the sha256 of the downloaded file and fails the build with a non-zero exit if it does not match the pinned value.
2. **Given** the downloaded bytes match every pinned hash, **When** the script completes, **Then** staging proceeds exactly as it does today, with the extensions placed in the release archive unchanged.
3. **Given** a new platform is added to the staging matrix, **When** no pin exists yet for that platform+extension pair, **Then** the build fails rather than silently accepting unpinned bytes.

GPU_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS is defined twice as independent literals (shaders.rs, device.rs) with no equality pin

<!-- finding-id: SEC-4b2140a0cd91 -->
<!-- cwe: CWE-1041 -->

`GPU_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS` is defined twice as independent `u64` literals — `src/analysis/gpu/shaders.rs:143` and `src/analysis/gpu/device.rs:54` — with no assertion pinning them equal. Severity **low**: both copies are `30` today and there is no external attacker path; the defect is redundant code that can silently diverge. Confidence **high**: both literals, every consumer and every assert were read directly.

Found by the chunk 9 security sweep, Issue #2291 (shader layer #2232, tracker #2094).

## Why it matters

The doc comment at `shaders.rs:141-142` claims the constant "is also available from `gpu/device.rs` for backwards compatibility. Both locations reference the same value." That is false: `device.rs:54` is a second literal, not a re-export. Every production consumer reads the **shaders** copy (`analyzer.rs:17`/`:433`, `queue/scheduling.rs:14`/`:80`/`:93`); the **device** copy has no production consumer and is only re-exported from the crate root at `mod.rs:54` (the shaders copy is re-exported as `SHADER_GPU_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS` at `mod.rs:93`). The asserts do not pin equality — `shaders.rs:324-325` bound the shaders copy to `5..=60`, while `device.rs:623`, `mod.rs:134` and `mod.rs:162` only check `> 0`. A maintainer who tunes the device copy (the one exported under the unprefixed name) changes nothing at run time — a dead lever of exactly the kind `AGENTS.md` warns against.

## Attacker model

No external attacker. The constants are compile-time; no FFI input, environment variable or config file reaches them. The actor is a maintainer or operator acting in good faith on the misleading comment.

## Trigger

Edit `src/analysis/gpu/device.rs:54` (for example to lengthen the init timeout on a slow host) and rebuild. The build and every existing assert still pass.

## Exploit sketch

1. A slow adapter repeatedly hits "GPU initialisation timed out after 30s" (`queue/scheduling.rs:93`).
2. A maintainer finds `neat_ai_discovery::analysis::gpu::GPU_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS`, follows it to `device.rs:54`, and raises it to `60`.
3. The build passes; `analyzer.rs` and `queue/scheduling.rs` still read `shaders::GPU_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS = 30`, so the timeout is unchanged and the fault persists while the code appears fixed.

## Suggested fix

Make a single source of truth: replace the literal at `device.rs:54` with `pub use super::shaders::GPU_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS;` (or delete it and the `mod.rs:54` re-export, since nothing outside `src/analysis/gpu/` uses it). If the second definition must stay, add `const _: () = assert!(device::GPU_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS == shaders::GPU_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS);`. Either way, correct the comment at `shaders.rs:141-142`.

[B] Hash samples in a single chunked pass instead of reading the file three times

Part of #26 (Tier B: hygiene and robustness).

## Problem
`get_md5`, `get_sha256` and `get_ssdeep` in `malware_sample.py` each read the whole file into memory with `f.read()`, so every load reads the sample three times and holds all of it in memory. For large samples such as installers, disk images or memory dumps, this uses a lot of memory and is slow.

## Proposal
- Read the file once in fixed-size chunks (for example 1 MiB) and update the MD5 and SHA256 hashes on each chunk.
- On Python 3.11 and later, `hashlib.file_digest` is also an option, but it computes only one digest per pass. Python 3.9 and 3.10 still need a manual loop.
- ppdeep only hashes a complete buffer or file, so the ssdeep hash still needs its own read. Check whether a streaming ssdeep implementation is worth using, or put a size limit on fuzzy hashing.
- Return a small result object, such as a dataclass `Hashes(md5, sha256, ssdeep)`.

## Acceptance criteria
- Hash values are unchanged; existing tests plus a known-answer test on a fixed file confirm this.
- Memory use for MD5 and SHA256 stays roughly constant regardless of file size.

<!-- finding-id: SEC-d3bf886bc1d3 -->
<!-- cwe: CWE-248 -->

The `map_async` callbacks in the helpful and harmful batch evaluators end in `.expect("Failed to send map_async result")` (`src/analysis/gpu/helpful_evaluation.rs:443`–`:447`, `src/analysis/gpu/harmful_evaluation.rs:373`–`:377`). When `wait_for_buffer_maps_batch` returns `Err` on a timeout, the `?` early return drops the receivers **before** the staging buffers. Dropping a `wgpu::Buffer` whose map is still pending runs the callback synchronously with `MapAborted`. Because the receiver is already gone, `send` fails and `.expect` panics. If two or more mappings are pending, the second callback panics while the first panic is unwinding, and Rust **aborts the whole host process**.

Severity **medium**: the trigger is routine deadline pressure, not an attacker, but the result is an uncatchable abort of the process that loaded the library, not a clean `Err`. Confidence **medium**: this was traced through the wgpu 30.0.1 / wgpu-core 30.0.1 sources and Rust's drop order. It has not been executed, because the sweep host has no GPU adapter.

Found by the chunk 9 security sweep, Issue #2237 (evaluation slice, tracker #2094). The same callback pattern is at `bias_evaluation.rs:195`, `relu_evaluation.rs:185` and `activation_evaluation.rs:297`/`:666`, which is left to the sibling slice #2238.

## Why it matters

The drop order is deterministic:

1. **Early return.** `wait_for_buffer_maps_batch(...).context(...)?` (helpful L455–456, harmful L383–384) returns early on `"GPU batch buffer mapping timed out after …"` (`device.rs:382`).

5. **The process aborts.** The panic unwinds out of the drop while the `Vec` keeps dropping its remaining elements. `evaluate_helpful_batch_with_budget` and `evaluate_harmful_batch_with_budget` size their GPU buffers directly from the length of each sample set. Found by the chunk 9 security sweep, Issue #2237 (evaluation slice, tracker #2094).

Introducing the Life Sciences Verification Program
Today, we are introducing the Life Sciences Verification Program (LSVP), which gives life science professionals access to our Mythos, Opus, and Sonnet models with a refined set of safeguards more permissive for biology-related work. We have already onboarded dozens of organizations through an early-access program, and are now opening applications to the broader life science community (apply here). The program is launching in beta, initially for teams and institutions. We will continue to improve the program and expand access to individual Pro and Max plans over time.
The LSVP is designed to enable life science professionals to use our models across a wide range of tasks that are currently blocked in our generally available Fable models, like drug discovery, research biology, clinical development, and manufacturing. It’s built for teams of all kinds—from academic labs to startups, pharma companies, and more.
Verification and access types
To qualify for these grants, each applicant goes through a verification process that includes a review of their research credentials, security standards, and ethical research oversight. Once verified, teams may apply for two types of LSVP grants, “Standard Use” or “High-risk Use,” depending on their access needs. These grants can be used through all our product surfaces, including Claude Science, Claude.ai, Claude Code and the API.
Standard Use grants are suitable for most life science work, including the majority of biology research and development workflows. These grants can be extended to entire teams for diverse, daily workloads, and are renewed once a year. They give those teams access to our Mythos, Opus, and Sonnet models, with refined classifiers that are more permissive for science tasks than our generally available models. Standard Use grants apply to Mythos 5.1, Opus 5, and Sonnet 5 today, and to future models as they launch. They’re specifically designed to enable the full breadth of life science activities in areas spanning basic science, R&D, supply chain and manufacturing, clinical development, quality assurance, regulatory affairs, investing and diligence, and more.
Although we expect Standard Use to cover the majority of access needs, some work carries a higher potential for misuse and therefore requires additional vetting.
High-risk Use is an add-on grant for teams working in areas blocked under Standard Use. It removes all safeguards that block life sciences requests. This grant applies to a single research project as opposed to a full team, and must be renewed every six months. Typically, a single researcher with dual-use work would have access to one Standard Use grant for diverse, daily activities, and one or more High-risk Use grants which only apply to work on specific projects (for example, characterizing how one specific family of viral vectors is recognized by human immune pathways).

[audit:medium] Restore fallbacks can overwrite a raced destination

Audit date: 2026-09-27
Audited commit: `c6aee6244b18a6db973dddc875a99cf583575e7b`
Priority: P2-medium

## Problem and impact

After checking that a destination is absent, restore falls back from renameat2 to plain rename on ENOSYS/EINVAL and to fs::copy on other failures. Both branches can replace, truncate, or follow a destination created during the check-to-use window.

An attacker who can write the destination directory and win the race can corrupt a victim-created file or redirect restored bytes, but exploitation requires concurrency and a fallback path.

## Confirmed behavior

Confirmed by independent source validation of both fallback branches and their syscall semantics.

Confidence: **high** — The no-replace check, replacing rename fallback, and truncating copy fallback are directly visible and independently traced.

## Root cause

Fallback implementations do not preserve the atomic no-replace property of the primary renameat2 operation.

## Proposed correction

Never use a replacing rename as a no-replace fallback. Pin the destination parent, copy to a private temporary file, and atomically publish with a no-replace primitive; use O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW where a name must be reserved.

## Acceptance criteria

- Force ENOSYS/EINVAL and preserve a concurrent destination.
- Force EXDEV and race a file and symlink into the destination.
- Keep the trash entry intact after failed publication.

RUSTSEC-2026-0068: tar-rs incorrectly ignores PAX size headers if header size is nonzero

> tar-rs incorrectly ignores PAX size headers if header size is nonzero

Details |  
-- | --
Package | `tar`
Version | `0.4.44`
Date | 2026-03-19
Patched versions | `>=0.4.45`

As part of [CVE-2025-62518](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2025-62518), the [astral-tokio-tar](https://github.com/astral-sh/tokio-tar)
project was changed to correctly honor PAX size headers in the case where it
was different from the base header. This is almost the inverse of the
astral-tokio-tar issue.

Any discrepancy in how tar parsers honor file size can be used to create
archives that appear differently when unpacked by different archivers. In this
case, the tar-rs (Rust tar) crate is an outlier in checking for the header size
— other tar parsers (including e.g. Go [`archive/tar`](https://pkg.go.dev/archive/tar)) unconditionally
use the PAX size override. This can affect anything that uses the tar crate to
parse archives and expects to have a consistent view with other parsers.

This issue has been fixed in version 0.4.45.

See [advisory page](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0068.html) for additional details.

ci: smoke-tests/bun.lock is installed frozen on every PR but has no Dependabot entry

`smoke-tests/bun.lock` is installed with `--frozen-lockfile` inside a check that runs on every pull request, but `/smoke-tests` has no Dependabot entry. A stale lockfile there fails a required check, and nothing updates it.

## The install that matters

`.github/workflows/ci.yml:187` sets `working-directory: smoke-tests` for the "Search + mermaid render on the built site" step, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml:203` runs:

```
bun install --frozen-lockfile
```

That step lives in the `websites` job, which runs on `pull_request` and `push`. So a `smoke-tests/package.json` that drifts from `smoke-tests/bun.lock` breaks a PR-gating check.

## Why the gap exists

`.github/dependabot.yml` has six entries after #497: `/`, `/www-dev`, `/www-org`, `/www-shared`, `/catalog/test`, and `github-actions`. There is no `/smoke-tests` entry. `smoke-tests` is not a member of the root Bun workspace either — `package.json` declares `workspaces: ["sdk", "providers/*", "packages/*"]` — so the root entry does not cover it. It carries its own tracked `smoke-tests/bun.lock`.

## Correcting the record

The steward's accepted verdict on #469 said a `/smoke-tests` entry was optional, on this reasoning:

> A `/smoke-tests` entry is optional — `smoke-test.yml:63` installs without `--frozen-lockfile`, so a stale lockfile can't break it.

That reasoning cited the wrong workflow. `.github/workflows/smoke-test.yml` does install unfrozen, but it fires only on `workflow_dispatch`, `schedule`, and `push` to `main` — never on a pull request. `ci.yml` is the one that gates PRs, and it installs frozen. PR #497 correctly implemented the shape it was given; this is a defect in the verdict's reasoning, not in that PR.

## A second reason to add the entry

`.github/workflows/ci.yml:182` keys the Playwright browser cache on `hashFiles('smoke-tests/bun.lock')`:

```yaml
key: playwright-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('smoke-tests/bun.lock') }}
```

The comment above it explains that `smoke-tests/bun.lock` pins the Playwright version, so the lockfile hash is the correct cache key. Leaving that lockfile unmanaged means the pinned Playwright version drifts out of date with nothing offering to bump it.

## Proposed change

Add a `/smoke-tests` entry to `.github/dependabot.yml` using `package-ecosystem: bun`, so Dependabot regenerates `smoke-tests/bun.lock` alongside any `package.json` bump. Match the shape of the `/catalog/test` entry, which is the closest analogue: a test harness with its own lockfile, not a site.

Note the known limitation this does not solve: Dependabot's security-update path keys off the advisory's ecosystem, so `package-ecosystem: bun` never applies to it. #469 and the header comment in `.github/dependabot.yml` document the manual runbook for that case.

Force-deleted quorum queue stalls every connection that had published to it

### Describe the bug

When a quorum-queue delete falls back to force delete (`Could not delete quorum ... Attempting force delete`)
and the queue is re-declared with the same name, a channel that had already published to it keeps its old
enqueuer session. The new queue answers every message from that session with `not_enqueued`
(`out_of_sequence` in `rabbit_fifo:maybe_enqueue`), so:

1. **All versions tested (3.13.7 → 4.3.6):** that publisher's messages never reach the re-declared queue.
2. **4.1.5 and later:** the rejected pre-settled messages also stay in the client's `pending` map
   forever. It passes `SOFT_LIMIT`, the session goes `slow`, and the connection enters `flow` and is
   never read again. **Every** message on that connection is lost, to any queue. The client gets no
   `connection.blocked`, no channel close, no error.

4.1.4 is not affected by (2), 4.1.5 is. The change is in `rabbit_fifo_client:seq_applied/2` from #14589, which
keeps `not_enqueued` pre-settled commands pending for a later resend. After a forced delete that resend can
never succeed.

As far as we can tell the root cause is that the forced path (`force_delete_queue/1` in `rabbit_quorum_queue`)
never runs `rabbit_fifo:state_enter(eol, ...)`, so enqueuers are never told the queue is gone.

### Reproduction steps

Run `repro.py` (attached [repro.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32761498/repro.py)) needs Docker and `uv`. It starts a throw-away broker, publishes pre-settled messages on
one connection to two quorum queues `H` and `Q`, and then deletes `Q`. To force the timeout fallback it suspends
`Q`'s Ra server first. It then re-declares `Q` and keeps publishing, counting what arrives on `H`.

```
uv run --with pika==1.3.2 python repro.py --image rabbitmq:4.1.4   # no stall
uv run --with pika==1.3.2 python repro.py --image rabbitmq:4.1.5   # STALL
uv run --with pika==1.3.2 python repro.py --image rabbitmq:4.3     # STALL
uv run --with pika==1.3.2 python repro.py --mode clean             # normal delete: no stall
```

Output on 4.3.6:

```
broker logged "Attempting force delete": True
  + 10s  P sent to H:   198  H received:   127  | Q session: pending=154 slow=true next_enqueue_seq=296
  + 30s  P sent to H:   644  H received:   127  | Q session: pending=154 slow=true next_enqueue_seq=296
connection states on the broker: ['flow', 'running']
connection.blocked sent to P: False
messages from P that landed in the re-declared Q (sent 644): 0
```


### Expected behavior

After a queue is deleted, forced or not, existing channels should drop their session for it, or be
told to reset their sequence. Messages to the re-declared queue should be enqueued. A resend that can never
succeed should never be able to block the whole connection.


### Additional context

We hit this in production on a single-node 4.2 broker. Quorum queues with `x-expires` expire while their
application restarts. Some of those deletes log `[{timeout,...}]`, `[{error,shutdown}]` or
`[{error,noproc}]` and are force-deleted. Long-lived processes that were publishing to those queues then go
silent ~30 min later until they are restarted.

It would be very nice if the fix is backported to 4.2 (if possible).

[Security] enforce filesystem root denials for descendants

## Summary
DefaultPathValidator preserves a filesystem root's trailing separator during normalization, but appends another separator for descendant containment checks. A non-glob root denial therefore misses descendants, which can subsequently be permitted by the workspace fallback.

## Evidence
Current main `d67942adf9e3886b7e78c9f132198408eb0272e1`:
- `src/gateway/BotNexus.Gateway/Security/DefaultPathValidator.cs:309-333`: NormalizePath returns a filesystem root unchanged. IsUnderPath first checks equality, then tests StartsWith(configuredPath + DirectorySeparatorChar) and the equivalent alternate separator.
- `CanAccess` at lines230-247 rejects IsDenied matches first, then permits workspace containment. A descendant that misses a root denial can reach that fallback.
- An isolated evaluation of the exact containment expression on Windows used a drive root and a descendant path. The expression returned false for denial membership where descendant containment should be true. This is an expression-level reproduction, not a whole-validator or tool exploit execution.
- The same source shape gives a double slash prefix for POSIX root. Linux behavior is source-derived, not executed in this audit.

PR #3870 composes plugin ceiling denials into this existing validator. Its root-preservation test covers grants/fence output, not actual root-denial enforcement. The underlying validator defect is already in main; plugin production registration is still absent, so no deployed plugin exploit is claimed.

## Expected behaviour
A normalized non-glob filesystem-root denial covers the root and every descendant. Ordinary directory denials still respect path-segment boundaries, and denials retain precedence over workspace or explicit grants.

## Impact
A configured filesystem-root deny can fail to restrict otherwise allowed workspace descendants. This is a security-policy enforcement gap for that configuration, not evidence of observed data access or a production incident.

## Proposed fix
Correct containment in the existing shared validator without adding a parallel path checker. Preserve normalization, platform case comparison, glob semantics and the existing link-resolution checks. Coordinate plugin composition tests with the #2685 / PR #3870 owner rather than creating a competing plugin-fence implementation.

## Acceptance criteria
1. Real DefaultPathValidator read/write tests reject descendants of a configured root denial, including otherwise permitted workspace descendants, on supported Windows and Linux platforms.
2. Root equality, ordinary directory boundaries, sibling-prefix nonmatches, explicit grants, platform case rules and existing symlink/dotdot assertions remain correct.
3. Plugin ceiling composition tests cover root denials with omitted, null and explicit plugin policies through the real validator; preserve no-extra-grants semantics and existing tests.
4. The regression fails against the current separator-appending behavior and under a task-owned mutation restoring it, by name.
5. Compile affected projects locally, then validate only through a separately admitted authoritative remote gate; no local test hosts or assertion weakening.

## Files
- src/gateway/BotNexus.Gateway/Security/DefaultPathValidator.cs
- tests/gateway/BotNexus.Gateway.Tests/Security/PathValidatorTests.cs
- tests/gateway/BotNexus.Gateway.Tests/Security/PathValidatorSymlinkEscapeTests.cs
- tests/extensions/BotNexus.Extensions.Plugins.Tests/PluginAgentDescriptorFenceTests.cs

## Related
- #2406 fixed symlink-then-dotdot resolution, a different mechanism.
- #3612 concerned inherited denial propagation; this defect concerns containment of an already retained root denial.
- #3941 concerns relative plugin grant interpretation; #3969 concerns omitted-policy denial preservation. Neither repairs root-prefix matching.
- PR #3870 owns plugin integration; ordinary code validation remains held on #3918 sender start
